Accordingly, the court granted the Department of State's motion and transferred the case to the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia under 28 U.S.C. § 1631, despite Steele's pending petition before the Merit Systems Protection Board, because no judicially reviewable action had occurred within 120 days of his Board appeal under 5 U.S.C. § 7702(e)(1)(B).

cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' judgment for the United States, holding that in a Fifth Amendment takings case arising from a Notice of Interim Trail Use (NITU) under the National Trails System Act Amendments of 1983, the "before" condition for calculating just compensation must account for the continued operation of an intrastate scenic railroad service that was operating on the corridor both before and after the NITU issued, preventing property owners from receiving windfall compensation. The court applied the before-and-after valuation method and rejected the owners' argument that they were entitled to damages where they failed to prove that the fair market value of their property actually decreased as a result of the government's taking, given that the burden of proving loss with reasonable certainty rests on the property owner.

The Federal Circuit transferred Bennett's case to district court pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1631, holding that federal district courts have exclusive jurisdiction over discrimination claims under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2) where an employee alleges that a covered basis for removal under 5 U.S.C. § 7702 was involved, as established in Perry v. Merit Systems Protection Board. Because Bennett continued to pursue a disability discrimination claim alongside his appealable removal action, the Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction and transferred the matter to the Eastern District of California to address the discrimination allegation and any timeliness concerns.

cases.case_name: General Access Solutions, Ltd. v. T-Mobile USA, Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal in this patent case between General Access Solutions and T-Mobile USA/Ericsson pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), which permits dismissal when the parties stipulate to settlement or abandonment of the appeal. The order contains no substantive ruling on the underlying patent claims or issues litigated in the district court, and each party bears its own costs of appeal.

The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of May's complaint seeking a share of a 2012 settlement, holding that the claims were barred by issue preclusion and fell outside the Court of Federal Claims' limited jurisdiction, the same defects that doomed May's first appeal. The court rejected May's attempt to revive his claims by invoking 31 U.S.C. § 5323 (whistleblower payment provisions), the Inflation Reduction Act of 2022, and legislative history under the False Claims Act, finding these invocations presented no cognizable basis for relief and that May's challenges were frivolous under the summary affirmance standard set forth in Joshua v. United States.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit denied Core Scientific's petition for a writ of mandamus seeking to compel transfer of the patent infringement case from the Eastern District of Texas to the Western District of Texas under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). The court held that Core failed to satisfy the "clear and indisputable" right to relief prong of the mandamus standard because Core's petition did not address the amended complaint and third-party complaint, both of which alleged infringement based on Core's ongoing activities in the Eastern District of Texas, and because Malikie's venue allegations were grounded in Core's actual operations in that district rather than unilateral manipulation. Additionally, the court found Core's argument about venue manipulation was waived because it was raised for the first time in the reply brief.

The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of Polinski's complaint under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1491, holding that his claims arising from alleged actions by state and local officials failed to establish any cognizable claim against the United States within that court's limited jurisdiction. The court rejected Polinski's general assertion that the United States serves as "guarantor of individual rights" and found that his tort-based allegations regarding allegedly unlawfully retained bonds could not satisfy the Tucker Act's requirement that claims be based on sources of substantive law mandating federal compensation and not sounding in tort.

cases.case_name: Fulkerson v. New Mexico Department of Justice
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of Fulkerson's $50 million civil rights complaint against the New Mexico Department of Justice and state officials, holding that it lacked subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9) because the case involved neither patent law, Patent and Trademark Office review, nor the enumerated damages claims against the United States within the Federal Circuit's limited appellate jurisdiction. Rather than decide the case on the merits, the court transferred the matter to the Tenth Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1631, the appropriate forum for appeals of district court decisions in general federal question cases lacking Federal Circuit jurisdiction.

The Federal Circuit transferred Cooke's case to the United States District Court for the District of Maryland because the court lacked jurisdiction over her discrimination claim, which falls within the exclusive jurisdiction of federal district courts under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2) when an employee appeals a Board-appealable action and alleges the action was based on covered discrimination such as retaliation for prior EEO complaints. The court agreed with both USPS and Cooke that transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1631 was appropriate and that the district court would be better positioned to assess timeliness issues.

cases.origin: Department of Justice
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit granted the Department of Justice's motion to remand Cramer's appeal challenging a December 2025 Bureau of Justice Assistance decision, allowing the agency to reconsider its position after purporting to sua sponte rescind that determination in March 2026. The court exercised its discretion to remand under the standard articulated in SKF USA Inc. v. United States to preserve party and judicial resources without addressing the merits of the underlying dispute. Each party bears its own costs on remand.

The Federal Circuit transferred this civil rights case to the Ninth Circuit and vacated its consideration of the appeal, holding that it lacks subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a) because the appeal does not involve patent law, Patent and Trademark Office review, or the specified damages claims against the United States. The court reasoned that civil rights disputes fall outside the Federal Circuit's statutory mandate to review only patent-related matters and certain monetary claims against the federal government, and therefore the case was improperly filed in the Federal Circuit rather than the appropriate circuit court of appeals.

cases.case_name: Power2b, Inc. v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Power2b's appeal from a Patent Trial and Appeal Board decision in an inter partes review proceeding pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), which permits dismissal when the parties stipulate to settlement. The court ordered each party to bear its own costs, leaving the underlying PTAB decision undisturbed.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's decision holding that attorney Jackson was not entitled to fees under 38 U.S.C. § 5904(c)(1) because the statutory triggering event for collecting attorney's fees is the notice of the agency of original jurisdiction's most recent initial decision in the matter, here the December 2021 rating decision granting benefits, and Jackson sought no fees for work performed after that decision. The court rejected Jackson's argument that the fee trigger should be the original March 2008 rating decision, concluding that under the plain language of § 5904(c)(1) and the structure of the Veterans Appeals Improvement and Modernization Act of 2017, the relevant "initial decision with respect to the case" refers to the most recent decision being appealed from, not a prior unrelated rating decision.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) on three independent grounds: Pellegrino lacked authority to represent the estate pro se under Rule 83.1(a)(4) because he conceded he was suing on behalf of an entity rather than himself; the court lacked jurisdiction over his claims challenging IRS administrative misconduct because they sound in tort and are unreviewable, and his refusal claim failed to plausibly allege overpayment under the Tucker Act by providing no information about the estate's income or tax calculation; and his submission of fiduciary documents and a power of attorney did not cure either defect or violate due process. The court declined to reach Pellegrino's alternative arguments regarding sections 6402 and 6103(e)(6), equitable powers, or Department of Justice standing.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Green's petition for review of an MSPB decision because Green failed to comply with the court's April 24, 2026 order requiring her to submit a copy of the underlying decision within a specified timeframe. The court applied its procedural rules regarding petition filing requirements, finding that Green's non-compliance warranted dismissal of the entire petition.

cases.case_name: Commscope Technologies LLC v. Belden Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed CommScope's appeal from a Patent Trial and Appeal Board inter partes review decision pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b)(1), based on the parties' joint stipulation of voluntary dismissal. The court's order indicates the parties settled their dispute before appellate resolution, with each side bearing its own costs and any pending motions denied as moot.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's decision, holding that radiculopathy constitutes a separate disability from spondylolisthesis under 38 C.F.R. § 4.71a and § 4.25, requiring separate rating and appellate designation, and therefore Ms. De Hart's 2009 notice of disagreement addressing only spondylolisthesis did not place her radiculopathy claim into appellate status under the requirements of 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a) and applicable veterans benefits procedure. The court reasoned that because the regulations mandate separate evaluation of neurological abnormalities associated with spine conditions, Ms. De Hart was required to file a separate notice of disagreement in 2019 to challenge the effective date of her radiculopathy determination, and her failure to do so precluded appellate review of that issue.

The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' denial of Sanders's motion to proceed in forma pauperis and dismissal of his complaint under the Prison Litigation Reform Act's three-strike provision, 28 U.S.C. § 1915(g), which bars IFP status for prisoners with three or more prior dismissed frivolous or malicious actions unless they face imminent danger of serious physical injury. Sanders's opening brief on appeal raised no cogent, non-frivolous argument challenging the trial court's determination that he had not satisfied the imminent-danger exception and instead largely consisted of arguments for why he should be released from prison, while his single legal argument (regarding access to courts) was expressly rejected by controlling precedent that Sanders himself appeared to cite.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Burke's appeal from the Veterans Claims Court under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to terminate the proceeding. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs, and no precedential decision was issued regarding the underlying veterans benefits dispute.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Diallo's petition for review of a Merit Systems Protection Board decision under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) pursuant to a stipulated agreement by the parties. The court imposed no costs on either party, leaving the underlying MSPB decision undisturbed.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Szymanski's petition for review of an MSPB decision for failure to comply with Federal Circuit Rule 15(c)(3), which requires filing a Statement Concerning Discrimination. The court applied the sanction of dismissal for failure to prosecute in accordance with the court's procedural rules, without reaching the merits of the underlying personnel management dispute.

cases.case_name: Gotv Streaming, LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed GOTV Streaming's appeal from two Patent Trial and Appeal Board inter partes review decisions against Netflix under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), which permits dismissal when the parties stipulate to settlement. Each party bore its own costs, and the dismissal is nonprecedential.

cases.case_name: In Re EAGLE VIEW TECHNOLOGIES, INC.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit granted the USPTO's motion to remand the appeal from a Patent Trial and Appeal Board inter partes review decision in IPR2022-00734, reversing the panel's prior consideration of the merits. The Court's order indicates that the case will return to the PTAB for further proceedings, though the brief opinion provides no substantive reasoning regarding the underlying patent validity issues or grounds for the remand.

The Federal Circuit denied Hovgaard's petition for a writ of mandamus under the extraordinary remedy standard established in Cheney v. U.S. District Court for D.C., holding that he failed to demonstrate either a clear and indisputable right to relief or that normal appellate procedures were inadequate to address his challenge to a Veterans Court extension of time granted to the Secretary of Veterans Affairs. The court found that Hovgaard had not shown the delay was egregious enough to warrant this extraordinary remedy, and therefore the petition was denied.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Gilmer's appeal from the United States Court of Federal Claims pursuant to a May 15, 2026 order requiring submission of the appellate filing fee, which Gilmer failed to pay. The dismissal was based on Gilmer's non-compliance with the court's procedural requirement to pay the filing fee necessary to proceed with the appeal.

cases.case_name: In Re SEAGATE TECHNOLOGY HOLDINGS PLC
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit granted Seagate Technology's motion to withdraw its petition for a writ of mandamus against the United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas, with each party bearing its own costs. The order is nonprecedential and does not address the underlying merits of the mandamus claim, which would have required showing that the district court acted in excess of its jurisdiction or refused a clear duty under law.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of Utech's post-award bid protest, holding that Utech lacked statutory standing as an "interested party" under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(b)(1) because it chose not to submit a proposal before the deadline and therefore could not qualify as either an actual bidder or a prospective bidder, and that Utech waived its opportunity to challenge the solicitation under the Blue & Gold Fleet waiver doctrine by failing to protest before the proposal deadline. The court reasoned that to establish a "direct economic interest" required for interested party status, a party must show it had a substantial chance of winning the contract, and since Utech deliberately chose not to bid based on competitive considerations, it could not later establish prospective bidder status merely by stating an intention to bid in a hypothetical resolicitation.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal of Sansone's pro se complaint against the USPTO under Federal Rules of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), holding that the motion to dismiss was timely filed (sixty days from the last required service date of April 17, 2024) and that Sansone's allegations—whether construed as claims under criminal statutes, tort law, or as ultra vires administrative action—failed to state a plausible claim for relief under the Ashcroft v. Iqbal standard. Although the court acknowledged it must liberally construe pro se complaints and apply the strongest reasonable interpretation of ambiguous allegations, it found no error in the trial court's interpretation of the complaint and concluded that any misconstruction was harmless because Sansone's claims were inadequately pleaded under any reasonable interpretation.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the Board's 2019 remand order on chronic sinusitis and allergic rhinitis claims was not a reviewable "decision" under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a), and the unadjudicated vertigo and sleep apnea claims similarly did not constitute decisions because the Board neither granted nor denied them but instead left them for regional office consideration. The court concluded that Stiles failed to establish how the Veterans Court's statutory jurisdiction under § 7252 could be invoked to enforce the Board's regulatory duty under 38 C.F.R. § 20.904(b) to refer unadjudicated claims to the regional office, as the sources and governmental bodies involved were different.

cases.case_name: Pact Xpp Schweiz Ag v. Intel Corporation
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of noninfringement on both patents, holding that PACT forfeited a capability-based infringement argument on the '301 patent by failing to raise it at the summary judgment stage and that the district court correctly construed "physically dedicated connection" on the '593 patent based on PACT's own prosecution history statements, which supported a requirement that the entire end-to-end connection be inaccessible to other cores and memories. The court also rejected PACT's factual dispute argument regarding where the dedicated connection begins and ends, finding no evidence supporting PACT's proposed distinction between "interfaces" and the core-to-memory pathways.

cases.case_name: Maxeon Solar Pte. Ltd. v. Hanwha Solutions Corp.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal by agreement of the parties pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), which permits dismissal when the parties stipulate to termination of the proceeding. Each party bears its own costs, and the mandate issued the same date as the order.

cases.case_name: Enanta Pharmaceuticals, Inc. v. Pfizer Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment invalidating all claims of Enanta's '953 patent as anticipated, holding that the patent was not entitled to priority from Enanta's earlier provisional application because the '048 provisional's disclosure of —NHC(O)—C2-C12-alkyl did not provide adequate written description support under 35 U.S.C. § 112 for the '953 patent's narrower disclosure of —NHC(O)—C1-C12-alkyl, since C1 is categorically different from C2 and the provisional application explicitly excluded one-carbon alkyl groups. The court rejected Enanta's arguments that the change represented a correction of an obvious typographical error, holding that patent priority determinations turn on the written description standard rather than the court's power to correct errors under 35 U.S.C. § 251, and that Enanta presented no genuine dispute of material fact on whether a skilled artisan would recognize the difference as a typographical error.

cases.case_name: Via Transportation, Inc. v. Rideco Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) following the parties' stipulation to dismiss, with each side bearing its own costs. Because the case was dismissed by agreement rather than on the merits, the decision establishes no precedent and provides no ruling on the underlying patent or substantive legal issues between Via Transportation and Rideco.

cases.case_name: Pom Group Inc. v. Schedule a
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Pennsylvania
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss, with each side bearing its own costs. Because the dismissal was by stipulation rather than by judicial resolution of the merits, the order is nonprecedential and does not establish any substantive legal holding regarding the underlying dispute between POM Group Inc. and the defendants.

cases.case_name: Via Transportation, Inc. v. Rideco Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) following a stipulated agreement between Via Transportation and Rideco, with each party bearing its own costs. The nonprecedential order does not address the underlying merits of the case, as the parties resolved their dispute before appellate adjudication. This dismissal represents a settlement-based termination of the cross-appeal that arose from the Western District of Texas litigation.

cases.case_name: Clear Imaging Research LLC v. Google LLC
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Clear Imaging Research's appeal against Google pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss. Each party bears its own costs, and the order is nonprecedential.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that 12 U.S.C. § 4208's non-reviewability provision clearly and convincingly bars judicial review of the Attorney General's determination that Jacobson's FIAFEA whistleblower declaration was deficient. The court rejected Jacobson's argument that Fisher v. United States required the lower court to first determine whether FIAFEA is a money-mandating statute before addressing the jurisdictional bar, finding that Fisher's money-mandating analysis does not apply when a statute explicitly strips the Court of Federal Claims of jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: Ironburg Inventions Ltd. v. Valve Corporation
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit reversed and remanded the district court's grant of estoppel under 35 U.S.C. § 315(e)(2), holding that the district court relied on insufficient evidence to establish that Kotkin was reasonably discoverable through Valve's own pre-petition search efforts, and that the district court improperly applied hindsight bias in finding Raymond discoverable by considering forward citations created after Valve's IPR petition was filed. The court reaffirmed that the burden rests on the patent holder to prove that an IPR ground "reasonably could have been raised" using a skilled searcher standard employing merely reasonable diligence, not extraordinary or "scorched earth" search tactics.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Harrow's six-day furlough under 5 U.S.C. § 7513(a), holding that the "efficiency of the service" standard was satisfied because the furlough represented a reasonable management solution to sequestration-mandated budget constraints, even though Harrow argued it decreased departmental efficiency. The court assumed without deciding that the 60-day filing deadline in 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1) is non-jurisdictional and subject to equitable tolling following the Supreme Court's reversal in Harrow v. Department of Defense (2024), but found Harrow's merits argument foreclosed by binding precedent in Einboden v. Department of the Navy, which established that agencies need not show their furlough decisions were optimal, only that they were reasonable responses to financial constraints applied fairly across similarly situated employees.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of Gomez's Whistleblower Protection Act retaliation claims under 5 U.S.C. § 2302, holding that Gomez failed to establish protected disclosures because his allegations regarding a purported conspiracy to circumvent veterans hiring preferences lacked credibility and corroboration, his grievance claim was unrelated to protected whistleblowing activity, and his objections to management's discretionary refusal to convert a position classification amounted to mere disagreement with agency decisions rather than protected disclosures of illegal activity. The court applied the deferential "virtually unreviewable" standard to the administrative judge's credibility determinations while reviewing the Board's jurisdiction determinations de novo, ultimately finding substantial evidence supported the Board's conclusions on each alleged protected action.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Powell's petition for review of an MSPB decision for failure to pay the required docketing fee within the time prescribed by Federal Circuit Rule 52(d). The court applied a procedural dismissal standard based on non-compliance with mandatory filing requirements, finding that Powell's failure to timely prosecute the appeal warranted dismissal under the Federal Circuit's local rules.

cases.case_name: Boston Scientific Corp. v. Stryker Corporation
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's denial of a preliminary injunction against Stryker's OptaBlate BVN device, holding that Boston Scientific failed to establish a likelihood of success on the merits of its induced infringement claim under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b) because substantial questions exist regarding claim construction and infringement of the '166 patent's claims 16 and 21. The court found no abuse of discretion in the district court's preliminary determination that the term "reaches" in the claimed introducer limitation was facially ambiguous, the parties had presented minimal substantive argument or evidence on the proper construction, and Boston Scientific therefore failed to meet its burden of demonstrating likely success on the merits at the preliminary injunction stage.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit granted petitioners' petition for en banc review of a Merit Systems Protection Board decision involving federal employees Jackler and Jaroch against the Department of Justice and Office of Personnel Management, though the opinion does not specify the underlying substantive issues or legal doctrines at stake. The court ordered new briefing from the parties and amici curiae on an expedited schedule, with oral argument to be scheduled later, effectively vacating the panel's prior decision and indicating the full court will reconsider the case. This procedural order reveals significant judicial interest in the case—as evidenced by the acceptance of numerous amicus briefs from labor unions, senators, and whistleblower advocates—but provides no information about the merits or reasoning behind the en banc grant.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Rorie's appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2) because the claimant forfeited his arguments by failing to raise them in his opening brief before the Veterans Court, and his brief challenge on appeal merely contested an application of law to fact rather than a pure legal issue. The court held that it lacks jurisdiction to review factual determinations or applications of law to particular facts in appeals from the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, distinguishing between reviewable legal interpretations of 38 C.F.R. § 3.157(b) and non-reviewable fact-specific applications.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Secrest's petition for review of an MSPB decision for failure to comply with procedural requirements, specifically his failure to pay the docketing fee mandated by Federal Circuit Rule 52(d) and his failure to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination under Federal Circuit Rule 15(c)(3). The court determined that these failures to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's rules warranted dismissal of the petition.

cases.case_name: Latham v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs
cases.origin: Department of Veterans Affairs
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the VA's regulations governing the Program of Comprehensive Assistance for Family Caregivers under 38 U.S.C. § 1720G, holding that the Lathams had standing as legacy participants facing potential discharge from the program but their facial challenges to the regulations failed under the deferential arbitrary-and-capricious standard of the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706. The court rejected their arguments that the VA exceeded its statutory authority in adopting the GS pay scale for stipend calculations and using in-home visits for reassessment procedures, and held that § 502 limits review to facial challenges to rules and their promulgation, not fact-specific as-applied disputes.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision that claims 1–3, 9–13, and 16–17 of the '578 patent were unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, rejecting Medmix's arguments regarding both claim construction and motivation to combine. The court held that the term "at least two ramps" does not require an "inclined plane" shape as a matter of claim construction under the Phillips standard, as the plain language of the claims and specification contain no such limitation, and the prosecution history amendment was directed to achieving axial guidance rather than limiting shape, supporting the Board's obviousness finding based on a combination of Keller '574, Heusser, and Yu references.

cases.case_name: 3s Americas Inc. v. Cooper New Energy Co. Ltd.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' agreement, with each side bearing its own costs. The dismissal was entered as a nonprecedential order, meaning the underlying dispute between 3S Americas and Cooper New Energy (which originated in the District of Arizona) was resolved through stipulation rather than appellate adjudication on the merits.

cases.case_name: Yangtze Memory Technologies Company, Ltd. v. Micron Technology, Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Appeal No. 2026-1110 pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b)(1) based on the parties' joint stipulation of voluntary dismissal, with each party bearing its own costs. The court deconsolidated the two appeals and granted the parties' motion to realign Micron as appellant in the remaining Appeal No. 2026-1596, setting Micron's opening brief deadline for July 27, 2026.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding the Office of Personnel Management's denial of McGowan's application for disability retirement benefits under the Federal Employees' Retirement System (FERS), 5 U.S.C. § 8451, finding that the Board properly excluded McGowan's medical evidence based on credibility determinations rather than categorical rejection of subjective evidence, and that the court lacked jurisdiction to review the underlying factual disability determination. The court rejected McGowan's argument that the Board improperly focused on the cause of his alleged PTSD and excluded medical evidence solely because it was subjective, distinguishing the case from Vanieken-Ryals on grounds that the Board's exclusion rested on its credibility assessment of McGowan's testimony regarding his military service, not a blanket rule against subjective evidence.

cases.case_name: Foras Technologies Ltd. v. Bmw of North America, LLC
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Foras Technologies' appeal from the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in two inter partes review proceedings under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss. Each party bears its own costs, and the order is nonprecedential.

The Federal Circuit dismissed James's appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a), holding that the court's appellate authority is limited to patent cases, Patent and Trademark Office reviews, and certain damages claims against the United States not exceeding $10,000, none of which applied to her $50,000,000 employment discrimination damages suit against federal judges. The court declined to transfer the case under 28 U.S.C. § 1631, noting that James already had a pending appeal in the Third Circuit, which was the appropriate venue for her claims.

The Federal Circuit granted Scott's motion for voluntary dismissal of his appeal from the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), lifting the stay and dismissing the appeal with each party bearing its own costs. The decision is nonprecedential and contains no substantive analysis of the underlying veterans benefits claim, merely disposing of the procedural motion to withdraw.

The Federal Circuit denied Ecto World's petition for a writ of mandamus directing the International Trade Commission to terminate or stay its Section 337 investigation into alleged unfair competition based on PACT Act violations, holding that Ecto World failed to satisfy the demanding three-prong mandamus standard requiring a clear and indisputable right to relief, lack of adequate alternative remedies, and extraordinary circumstances warranting the drastic remedy. The court found that Ecto World could adequately raise its jurisdictional arguments before the Commission or in a post-final determination appeal, and that the Commission did not clearly abuse its considerable discretion in managing its docket by declining to stay the investigation pending resolution of a related appeal.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Pena's appeal for lack of jurisdiction because his challenges involved only the Veterans Court's procedural discretion and application of law to facts, which fall outside the court's limited appellate authority under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(c) and (d)(2), which permits review only of statutory or regulatory validity and interpretation issues or non-frivolous constitutional claims. Pena's arguments that the Veterans Court improperly allowed the Secretary an extension and failed to enter judgment in his favor, along with his invocation of "due process," were characterized as procedural complaints and factual disputes rather than legal errors requiring appellate review.

cases.case_name: Dynapass Ip Holdings LLC v. Bank of America Corporation
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal with prejudice of Dynapass's patent infringement suit against Bank of America, holding that the district court correctly construed the claim term "receiving the password" in U.S. Patent No. 6,993,658 under the intrinsic evidence standard. The court reasoned that the plain language of claim 1, which requires generating a password from a passcode and token before receiving it, unambiguously precludes the alternative embodiment disclosed in the specification where the passcode and token are submitted separately, and the specification's repeated juxtaposition of "password" against its component parts confirmed this construction.

cases.case_name: Inneos LLC v. Opticis Co., Ltd.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision in an inter partes review proceeding under 35 U.S.C. § 311 et seq., though the specific merits are not disclosed in this nonprecedential summary order issued under Federal Circuit Rule 36. The affirmance was entered without opinion, indicating the panel found no reversible error in the PTAB's determination regarding the validity or patentability issues at stake in IPR2023-01256.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Doe's appeal from the Court of Federal Claims' rejection of a "Certificate of Service" filed in a closed case, holding that the Court of Federal Claims lacked appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(3) because the order was a ministerial administrative decision performing housekeeping functions rather than a final decision subject to review. The court reasoned that following precedent from Ayestas v. Davis and related authorities, ministerial orders and administrative decisions fall outside the scope of appellate jurisdiction and therefore cannot be appealed.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision against Shawn Burns in his employment dispute with the Department of Homeland Security, applying the deferential standard of review for MSPB decisions under the Administrative Procedure Act. The court issued this nonprecedential affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, which permits summary affirmance without opinion when the panel finds the lower decision correct and no new precedent is needed.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's dismissal of Coleman's individual right of action (IRA) appeal under the Whistleblower Protection Enhancement Act of 2012, 5 U.S.C. § 2302, for lack of jurisdiction. The Board properly found that Coleman failed to establish the jurisdictional requirement that a protected disclosure was a contributing factor to an adverse personnel action, because all eleven of his protected disclosures were made after the January 24, 2015 decision to discontinue his hazardous duty pay supplement, and the Board correctly rejected his "continuing reprisal" theory on the ground that subsequent consequences of a discrete personnel action do not constitute separate actionable violations.

The Federal Circuit denied Johnson's petition for a writ of mandamus challenging various actions by the Veterans Benefits Administration and the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims, holding that mandamus is an extraordinary remedy requiring a petitioner to demonstrate both a clear and indisputable right to relief and the absence of adequate alternative remedies. The court found Johnson failed to satisfy this demanding standard under the doctrine established in Cheney v. U.S. District Court for D.C. because he had available regular appeal procedures before the Veterans Claims court and this court, and he did not demonstrate that any delay in handling his cases was so egregious as to justify extraordinary relief.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.case_name: Ningde Amperex Technology Ltd. v. Zhuhai Cosmx Battery Co., Ltd.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeals in this patent dispute between Ningde Amperex Technology Ltd. and Zhuhai Cosmx Battery Co., Ltd. under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs, and the dismissal is nonprecedential.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's obviousness rejection of claims 1–22 of the automated kitchen system patent application under 35 U.S.C. § 103, holding that substantial evidence supported the examiner's motivation to combine the Buehler and He '660 references based on articulated benefits such as automation, space minimization, and labor cost reduction. The court rejected the applicant's arguments that the references taught contradictory configurations and that the proposed combination would be physically incompatible, reasoning under the doctrine established in In re Keller that obviousness analysis focuses on what the combined teachings would suggest to a skilled artisan, not whether features can be bodily incorporated into a primary reference.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's dismissal of Gonzalez's appeal challenging the Board of Veterans' Appeals' denial of his dependency and indemnity compensation claim under 38 C.F.R. § 3.356(a). The court held that the Veterans Court lacked jurisdiction to entertain Gonzalez's clear and unmistakable error motion because the underlying issue of DIC eligibility had already been decided by a court of competent jurisdiction, consistent with the rule established in Winsett v. Principi that revision based on CUE is improper when a higher court has already decided the challenged issues.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Cantu's appeal for lack of jurisdiction because he failed to raise a non-frivolous legal question challenging the Veterans Court's decision under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(c)-(d), which limits Federal Circuit review to challenges to the validity or interpretation of statutes or regulations. The Veterans Court properly dismissed Cantu's mandamus petition as moot under L.A. County v. Davis since the Board had issued the decision he sought to compel, and Cantu's subsequent arguments about statute and regulation violations were not actually interpreted or relied upon by the Veterans Court in its dismissal order.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision denying Sanicola's whistleblower reprisal claim under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), holding that although Sanicola established a prima facie case by showing she made protected disclosures and that relevant officials had knowledge of them, the VA satisfied its burden under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e)(2) by proving by clear and convincing evidence that it would have terminated her employment for multiple speeding violations even absent the protected disclosures. The court rejected Sanicola's arguments that the Board failed to consider relevant facts or erred in accepting telematics data (rather than her state driving record) to establish the speeding violations and found no reversible error in the Board's reliance on VA Directive 0637, which does not purport to limit agencies' use of telematics monitoring for employee driving behavior.

cases.case_name: Centripetal Networks, LLC v. Keysight Technologies, Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in two inter partes review proceedings, upholding the Board's determinations regarding the patentability challenges raised by Keysight Technologies and Palo Alto Networks against Centripetal Networks' patents. The court provided no substantive opinion, issuing only a nonprecedential affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, which permits summary affirmance when the panel believes oral argument and published opinion are unnecessary.

cases.case_name: State of Mississippi v. United States
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of Mississippi's takings claim under the Tucker Act, holding that the trial court improperly converted the Government's summary judgment motion into a Rule 12(b)(1) motion to dismiss without notice to the parties or opportunity to respond, thereby violating procedural fairness and the applicable rules of court. The court affirmed the trial court's discovery orders denying Mississippi's motions to compel documents withheld under the deliberative process privilege, finding no abuse of discretion where the court applied the correct legal framework and Mississippi failed to make document-by-document showings of particularized need to overcome the qualified privilege.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit granted the United States' request to withdraw its petition for a writ of mandamus directed at the Court of International Trade and dismissed the petition accordingly. The court did not reach the merits of the underlying mandamus claim, as the petitioner's voluntary withdrawal mooted the case for appellate review.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Hays's removal from his position at USPS, finding no violation of due process under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c). The court held that USPS satisfied the essential due process requirement of notice by mailing the notice of proposed removal to Hays's address of record on file, and Hays failed to provide convincing evidence to rebut the presumption of receipt that arose from proper mailing, even though he resided at a different address during his incarceration.

cases.case_name: Atlas Global Technologies LLC v. Lianzhou Technologies Co., Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment in favor of Atlas Global Technologies in this patent dispute against Lianzhou Technologies (formerly TP-Link), though the specific claims and reasoning are not detailed in this nonprecedential summary judgment. The court's per curiam affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, which permits affirmance without opinion when the decision is obvious or presents no significant question, indicates the lower court's decision was sound but offers no precedential guidance on the underlying patent law issues.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit reversed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decisions holding Google's patents directed to hotword detection in multi-device systems unpatentable, finding that the Board's anticipation findings under 35 U.S.C. § 102 lacked substantial evidentiary support because the prior art reference (Rosenberger) did not clearly disclose devices exchanging confidence scores while remaining in a low-power mode as required by the claimed limitations. The court declined to address Sonos's alternative theory regarding a different interpretation of "low power mode" and remanded for the Board to consider that theory in the first instance, rather than making factual findings sua sponte.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board
United States District Court for the Eastern District of Washington

cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Vaughns's appeal from the Veterans Court for lack of jurisdiction, holding that his arguments challenged factual determinations and the application of law to specific facts rather than pure legal questions reviewable under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(1)-(2). The court found that Vaughns's challenges to herbicide exposure findings, harmless-error analysis, medical opinion adequacy, and the VA's duty to assist under 38 U.S.C. § 5103A all involved factual disputes or fact-dependent legal applications outside the Federal Circuit's limited appellate authority over veterans benefits cases.

cases.case_name: Knoa Pharma LLC v. Accord Healthcare, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that dependent claim 18 of the '908 patent was invalid under 35 U.S.C. § 103 for obviousness, rejecting Purdue's arguments on de novo review of the legal conclusion while applying clear error review to underlying factual findings. The court held that using a coating pan to heat abuse-deterrent oxycodone tablets—rather than the tablet press taught in the prior art reference Bartholomäus—would have been an obvious design choice to a person of ordinary skill in the art, since coating pans were known devices already used in pharmaceutical tablet production and offered the practical advantage of scalability for commercial production.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction, holding that the Tucker Act does not provide jurisdiction over takings claims based on alleged copyright infringement because 28 U.S.C. § 1498(b) provides an exclusive statutory remedy for copyright infringement by the government. The court reasoned that § 1498(b)'s specific remedial scheme displaces Tucker Act jurisdiction under the Supreme Court's framework in United States v. Bormes, which holds that a specific statutory remedy supersedes the Tucker Act's gap-filling role, and that Dr. Aljindi's single passing reference to § 1498(b) in a complaint expressly grounded only in Tucker Act takings theory was insufficient to invoke jurisdiction under that statute.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in two inter partes review proceedings, upholding the Board's determinations regarding the patentability challenges to Zentian's patents that Apple raised under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and/or § 103. The court issued a nonprecedential affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating that the Board's factual findings and legal conclusions regarding anticipation and/or obviousness were not clearly erroneous and the Board did not abuse its discretion.

cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's dismissal of Dr. Mathai's Fifth Amendment Takings Clause claim, holding that his expectations regarding a retention bonus and his objection to organizational reassignment do not constitute cognizable property interests protected by the Takings Clause because his compensation and employment terms were governed exclusively by statute rather than contract, and federal employers retain managerial discretion to reassign employees without triggering takings liability. The court reasoned that under precedent like Adams v. United States, Dr. Mathai possessed only a unilateral expectation to receive a retention bonus that neither statute nor VA regulations created as a legal entitlement, and that VA's organizational restructuring—even if premeditated—fell within the agency's ordinary managerial authority to reassign work duties and did not appropriate any protected property right.

cases.case_name: Melinta Therapeutics, LLC v. Nexus Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Nexus's generic antibiotic product infringed Melinta's U.S. Patent No. 9,084,802 under 35 U.S.C. § 271(e)(2) (the Hatch-Waxman Act infringement provision), rejecting Nexus's claim construction argument that a diluent added during administration fell outside the patent's "consists of" language and finding no clear error in the district court's written description analysis under 35 U.S.C. § 112. The court also declined to reach issues concerning the second patent and affirmed the permanent injunction against Nexus's ANDA product.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed-in-part and dismissed-in-part the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decisions finding three patents owned by Carolyn Hafeman unpatentable, holding that the Board's institution decision under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) is unreviewable even when the real party in interest violates a Sotera stipulation post-institution, but remanding the substantive patentability determination for reconsideration of the Board's claim construction of "without assistance by a user" and its treatment of secondary considerations of non-obviousness. The court rejected Ms. Hafeman's arguments that Jenne disclosed the "without assistance" limitation and that she had adequately established nexus for her secondary considerations evidence, finding the Board's narrow construction of that limitation—limiting it to the act of changing return information rather than establishing the remote communication itself—was supported by the claim language and specification.

The Federal Circuit reversed the Veterans Court's denial of attorneys' fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act (EAJA), 28 U.S.C. § 2412(d)(1)(A), holding that Greenidge was a "prevailing party" despite the absence of a formal remand order. The court reasoned that the touchstone of prevailing party status is whether there has been a material alteration of the legal relationship between the parties, and here, the Veterans Court's vacatur of the Board's ultra vires decision and dismissal of the appeal removed an obstacle to Greenidge's properly noticed CUE motion, thereby materially altering his legal relationship with the government and satisfying EAJA's requirements.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of International Trade's dismissal of International Rights Advocates' Administrative Procedure Act claim alleging unlawful withholding or unreasonable delay by Customs and Border Protection in investigating cocoa imports from Côte d'Ivoire for forced child labor violations under section 307 of the Tariff Act of 1930, holding that IRAdvocates failed to establish organizational standing. The court concluded that IRAdvocates' alleged injuries—financial harm from conducting investigations and expended resources—were insufficient to confer Article III standing because they did not flow from Customs' failure to act on the petitions themselves but rather from the underlying problem of forced child labor in the cocoa industry.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Reynolds's indefinite suspension without pay under 5 U.S.C. § 7513(a), holding that the agency established reasonable cause to believe Reynolds committed a crime for which imprisonment could be imposed (based on his indictment for sexual abuse) and that the suspension would promote the efficiency of the service, as the alleged misconduct directly implicated his duties as a federal law enforcement officer. The court rejected Reynolds's arguments that mitigating factors under the Douglas standard (his clean disciplinary record, lack of prior conviction, and eventual case dismissal) warranted a lesser penalty, and found no error in the agency's restoration of his paid status within fifteen days of the criminal charge's resolution, satisfying the requirement under Morrison v. National Science Foundation that suspension pending criminal proceedings be terminated within a reasonable time.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Shandler's petition for review of the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of his disability retirement annuity benefits as untimely under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1), which imposes a 60-day deadline for filing petitions to review. Although the Supreme Court held in Harrow v. Department of Defense that this deadline is not jurisdictional and thus potentially subject to equitable tolling, Shandler failed to satisfy the equitable tolling standard established in Menominee Indian Tribe of Wisconsin v. United States because he made only a conclusory statement about diligent pursuit and presented no explanation of extraordinary circumstances beyond his control that prevented timely filing.

cases.case_name: Arendi S.A.R.L. v. Oath Holdings Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's judgments that all asserted claims of the four patents ('843, '854, '356, and '993) are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, applying the two-step Alice/Mayo framework. The court held that the claims recite an abstract idea—collecting, analyzing, and using information to search external sources—and lack a specific technical solution to a technological problem, instead merely using generic computer functionality as a tool to perform an abstract information-processing task, such that improving user convenience or experience does not render the claims directed to patent-eligible subject matter.

cases.case_name: Chandan Steel Ltd. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of International Trade's decision upholding Commerce's antidumping order on stainless steel flanges from India, holding that substantial evidence supported Commerce's use of total adverse facts available ("AFA") under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e(a) and (b) against Chandan Steel for failing to submit complete window period sales data across multiple questionnaires despite repeated opportunities to do so. The court reasoned that Chandan's repeated omissions of requested sales data constituted both a failure to provide information under § 1677e(a)(2)(B) and a significant impediment to the proceeding under § 1677e(a)(2)(C), and that Chandan's inattentive reporting despite its experience in Commerce proceedings demonstrated failure to cooperate to the best of its ability under § 1677e(b), thereby justifying assignment of the same 145.25% dumping margin applied to another uncooperative respondent.

cases.case_name: Ollnova Technologies Ltd. v. Ecobee Technologies Ulc
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit vacated the infringement and damages judgments and remanded for a new trial, holding that the jury verdict form impermissibly combined infringement findings for all asserted patents into a single question without identifying which patent(s) were infringed, violating principles requiring clear jury verdicts on each patent. The court also vacated and remanded for further proceedings on whether the '495 patent's claims satisfy step two of the Alice test under 35 U.S.C. § 101, while affirming that the '887 and '371 patents' asserted claims are not directed to abstract ideas under § 101 and affirming the denial of non-infringement judgment for the '371 patent.

cases.case_name: Life Spine, Inc. v. Globus Medical, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit reversed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision in an inter partes review proceeding under 35 U.S.C. § 319, holding that the term "complementary with one another" in claims 10–14 of Globus Medical's '731 patent should be construed to encompass ramped portions with mirrored angles, not merely portions that "complete one another" as the Board had adopted. The Court applied the Phillips v. AWH Corp. framework for claim construction and determined that the specification's embodiments depicted in Figures 40–44, when read in context as a person of ordinary skill in the art would understand them, supported Life Spine's broader construction, making the claims obvious under the undisputed prior art and thus unpatentable.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Michael Thorogood's indefinite suspension from the Navy under 5 U.S.C. § 7701, finding that substantial evidence supported the Board's determinations that his position required a security clearance, the Navy complied with the procedural requirements of 5 U.S.C. § 7513 in providing notice and an opportunity to respond, and no abuse of discretion occurred in the administrative hearing. The court applied deferential review under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c), emphasizing that when suspension results from security clearance revocation, it may only review whether a clearance was denied, whether it was required for the position, and whether statutory procedures were followed—not the underlying merits of the security clearance decision itself.

cases.case_name: Fox Logistics and Construction Co. v. United States
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's summary judgment for the United States, holding that Fox Logistics failed to establish either an implied-in-fact contract with the Air Force or a genuine dispute of material fact regarding breach of the February 2014 agreement between the Air Force and Lakeshore. The court reasoned that the February 2014 agreement imposed obligations only on Lakeshore (to submit invoices, obtain subcontractor payment certifications, and pay subcontractors upon receipt of government funds), not on the Air Force, and the undisputed record showed the Air Force performed its obligations by processing and paying all four invoices submitted by Lakeshore—making Lakeshore's subsequent bankruptcy and failure to pay its subcontractors a matter of Lakeshore's nonperformance, not the Air Force's breach.

cases.case_name: Amsted Rail Company, Inc. v. Squires
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in two inter partes review proceedings (IPR2023-00538 and IPR2023-00539) brought against Amsted Rail Company. The court did not issue a precedential opinion, instead entering a summary affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, which indicates the panel found no reversible error in the PTAB's patentability determinations.

cases.case_name: David Boland, Inc. v. Secretary of the Army
cases.origin: Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals' decision against David Boland, Inc. in its dispute with the Secretary of the Army regarding government contracts, though the court issued only a summary affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36 without written opinion. Because the decision is nonprecedential and contains no substantive reasoning, the specific legal doctrines or statutory provisions governing the contract dispute cannot be identified from this disposition.

cases.case_name: Euro-Notions Florida, Inc. v. United States Customs and Border Protection
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.case_name: AGS Company Automotive Solutions v. United States Customs and Border Protection
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.case_name: Grant & Bowman, Inc. v. United States Customs and Border Protection
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Peternel's petition for review of an MSPB decision for failure to comply with mandatory procedural requirements under Federal Circuit Rules 52(d) and 15(c)(3), specifically the failure to pay the docketing fee and file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination. The court exercised its authority to dismiss for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules, finding these procedural defects fatal to the petition's viability regardless of the merits of the underlying MSPB case.

The Federal Circuit dismissed English's appeal from the Court of Federal Claims for failure to file his opening brief within the time required by Federal Circuit Rule 31(d). The court exercised its authority to dismiss appeals for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's procedural rules, treating the procedural default as fatal to the continuation of the appeal.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Robison's appeal for lack of jurisdiction because her challenge to the Veterans Court's decision constituted an impermissible application-of-law-to-facts review under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), as she conceded that controlling precedent under Haines v. West and Crews v. McDonough bars survivors from bringing clear and unmistakable error claims regarding a deceased veteran's benefits. The court held that while it may review rules of law and statutory interpretations under § 7292(a), it lacks authority to review whether the Veterans Court correctly applied established precedent to her particular factual circumstances.

cases.case_name: Mimedx Group, Inc. v. Surgenex, LLC
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal in this case pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) because the parties stipulated to dismissal by mutual agreement. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs, and the order was issued as a mandate on the same date.

cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1500, which bars the court from reviewing claims when the plaintiff has a substantially similar suit pending in another court. Although Markham's employment contract dispute fell within the Tucker Act's general grant of jurisdiction to the Court of Federal Claims, his filing of the same breach-of-contract action in federal district court before filing at the Claims Court divested the latter court of jurisdiction, and the timing of the district court dismissal after the Claims Court action was filed did not retroactively cure this defect.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Covington's appeal for lack of jurisdiction because he failed to raise a clear and unmistakable error claim before the Veterans Court and his remaining arguments challenged only the application of regulations to his particular factual circumstances, which falls outside the Federal Circuit's limited appellate jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2). The court held that it may review only constitutional issues and challenges to the validity of laws or regulations as applied generally, not factual determinations or regulations as applied to specific cases.

cases.case_name: Agi Suretrack LLC v. Farmers Edge Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Nebraska
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment that AGI SureTrack's asserted patents claiming automated systems for capturing, processing, and sharing farming data are directed to patent-ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101, applying the two-step Alice test and concluding that the claims recite only generalized steps of collecting, analyzing, and presenting information using conventional computer components without improving computer functionality itself. The court vacated and remanded the district court's determination that the case was not exceptional under 35 U.S.C. § 285 for purposes of attorney's fees, finding an abuse of discretion in that conclusion.

cases.case_name: Collision Communications, Inc. v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Kelley's petition for review of an MSPB decision for failure to comply with Federal Circuit Rule 31(d) by not timely filing the required brief. The court applied the procedural dismissal doctrine, treating the petitioner's failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's rules as grounds for dismissal rather than addressing the merits of the underlying MSPB case.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Keefer's appeal for failure to pay the required docketing fee within the timeframe prescribed by Federal Circuit Rule 52(d). The court treated this procedural default as fatal to prosecution of the appeal, applying the rule mechanically without addressing the merits of the underlying veterans benefits dispute.

cases.case_name: Eregli Demir Ve Celik Fabrikalari T.A.S. v. Itc
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of International Trade's three judgments against Erdemir, upholding the International Trade Commission's denial of reconsideration of its original material injury determination, its refusal to institute a changed-circumstances review under 19 U.S.C. § 1675(b), and its non-revocation determination in a sunset review under 19 U.S.C. § 1675(c). The court reasoned that a changed-circumstances review could provide no relief not already available in the sunset review, and that the Trade Court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over challenges to the Commission's denial of reconsideration, while the merits of the sunset review determination were sustainable based on the statutory framework governing antidumping investigations and revocation proceedings.

cases.case_name: Zhang v. Parties Identified on Schedule A
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Southern District of Florida
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Zhang's appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss the proceeding. The court ordered each side to bear its own costs and issued the dismissal as a mandate, rendering this a nonprecedential order that provides no guidance on the merits of the underlying dispute.

The Federal Circuit dismissed Reyes's appeal for failure to comply with procedural requirements under Federal Circuit Rule 52(d), specifically the failure to pay the required docketing fee and file an Entry of Appearance form by a court-admitted attorney. The court's order was based solely on non-compliance with its procedural rules and did not address the merits of the underlying veterans benefits dispute.

cases.case_name: Veterans Legal Advocacy Group v. Collins
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's denial of Veterans Legal Advocacy Group's application for attorney fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act (28 U.S.C. § 2412(d)(1)(A)), holding that VetLAG was not a "prevailing party" because the VA's voluntary corrective actions lacked the requisite judicial imprimatur under the standard articulated in Buckhannon Board & Care Home, Inc. v. West Virginia Department of Health & Human Resources. The court rejected VetLAG's argument that a court order requiring the VA to submit affidavits confirming those already-voluntary corrective actions constituted sufficient judicial imprimatur, reasoning that the order served only to help assess mootness rather than materially alter the legal relationship between the parties or conclusively resolve the claim.

cases.case_name: Future Link Systems, LLC v. Realtek Semiconductor Corporation
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal by stipulated agreement of the parties pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), with each side bearing its own costs. Because the parties agreed to dismissal, the court did not address the underlying merits of the dispute between Future Link Systems and Realtek Semiconductor regarding what appears to be a patent matter from the Western District of Texas.

cases.case_name: Go1 Pty, Ltd. v. Opensesame, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the Board's final written decision rejecting Go1's obviousness challenge under 35 U.S.C. § 103 to OpenSesame's e-learning patent (U.S. Patent No. 8,784,113). The Board had determined that the prior art combination of Sperle and Madison failed to teach the claimed sequence of verifying a user's license validity before providing a location designator for content access, but the court found this reasoning insufficient because the Board did not adequately address whether a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine the references despite their reversed sequence or whether the sequence difference was material to obviousness. The decision turned on whether the Board properly analyzed the motivation to combine and the reasonable expectation of success under the PTAB's § 103 analysis framework.

cases.case_name: Pantech Corporation v. Oneplus Technology (Shenzhen) Co., Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' stipulation to dismiss, with each side bearing its own costs. This nonprecedential order indicates the parties settled or otherwise agreed to terminate the underlying patent dispute between Pantech Corporation and OnePlus Technology before the appellate court reached the merits of the case.

cases.case_name: Insulet Corp. v. Eoflow, Co. Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts
cases.summary: Held: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's judgment and entered judgment as a matter of law for EOFlow on Insulet's Defend Trade Secrets Act claim because under 18 U.S.C. § 1836(d), applying the discovery standard established in Merck & Co. v. Reynolds, a reasonably diligent company should have discovered the misappropriation more than three years before Insulet filed suit in August 2023, making the claim time-barred as a matter of law. The court also established jurisdiction over the appeal despite the nominally "without prejudice" dismissal of patent claims because that dismissal was effectively with prejudice under 35 U.S.C. § 286's six-year statute of limitations, which had expired for the alleged June 2018 acts of infringement before the January 2025 dismissal.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of Chafin's application for Federal Employees' Retirement System disability benefits under 5 U.S.C. § 8451(a)(1)(B), holding that an employee's inability to commute to work need not be considered when determining whether she can render "useful and efficient service" in her position, as the commuting area requirement appears only in the separate reassignment provision of § 8451(a)(2)(A), and applying the canon of expressio unius est exclusio alterius demonstrates Congress intentionally omitted commuting considerations from the disability definition. The court also rejected Chafin's factual challenge to OPM's disability determination as barred by 5 U.S.C. § 8461(d), which precludes Federal Circuit review of OPM's factual findings in physical disability cases.

cases.case_name: Sight Sciences, Inc. v. Ivantis, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

cases.case_name: Clearplay, Inc. v. Dish Network L.L.C.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Utah
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment as a matter of law (JMOL) of noninfringement, holding that ClearPlay failed to prove infringement of either the '970 Patent or the '799 Patent under the claim constructions given to the jury. For the '970 Patent, the court found that the trial evidence established AutoHop does not directly disable individual navigation objects but instead operates on categorical background conditions (whether AutoHop is enabled and the device is in play mode), which does not satisfy the "direct disabling" requirement. For the '799 Patent, the court found insufficient evidence that AutoHop's announcement files contain the requisite structure where each individual navigation object contains its own start position, stop position, filtering action, and configuration identifier within the same object or data structure.

The Federal Circuit granted the Merit Systems Protection Board's motion to remand the case for reconsideration of its dismissal of Bernstein's appeal, exercising its discretion under the standard articulated in SKF USA Inc. v. United States to allow the agency to reconsider its previous position without reaching the merits. Each party bears its own costs, and the court expects the Board to address the matter promptly upon remand.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York

cases.case_name: Calderon Lopez v. Commissioner of Social Security
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit dismissed Calderon Lopez's appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that decisions of the Ninth Circuit fall outside the Federal Circuit's appellate authority and therefore cannot be reviewed by this court. The court applied the jurisdictional limitation established in 28 U.S.C. § 1295, which restricts Federal Circuit review to matters within its enumerated categories, which do not include appeals from other circuit courts' decisions.

The Federal Circuit denied McBride's petition for a writ of mandamus challenging the Veterans Claims Court's denial of her petition regarding discontinuation of her total disability rating based on individual unemployability (TDIU), instead treating her filing as a timely notice of appeal under Federal Rules of Appellate Procedure Rule 3 and transferring the case to the normal appeals docket. The court also denied her motion for a stay and/or injunction pending appeal under the four-factor test established in Nken v. Holder, finding she had not shown such interim relief was warranted, because mandamus is not an adequate alternative remedy when direct appeal is available.

cases.case_name: Pictometry International Corporation v. Roofr Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision holding all claims of U.S. Patent No. 9,183,538 unpatentable for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. § 103, rejecting Pictometry's arguments that the term "predominant pitch" requires a weighted average of all roof sections and that Bailey's prior-art reference does not disclose this limitation. The court concluded that "predominant pitch" within its ordinary and customary meaning encompasses a weighted average calculation, that Bailey's teaching of "predominant slope" reasonably discloses this concept, and that a skilled artisan would have been motivated to combine Bailey with Pershing's teachings regarding area calculations to render the claims obvious.

cases.case_name: Pictometry International Corporation v. Roofr Inc.
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision holding all claims of the '800 patent unpatentable for obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §§ 311–319 (inter partes review), rejecting Pictometry's argument that the prior-art reference Abhyanker did not teach the claimed "user-acceptance" limitation because Abhyanker's marker-locking feature was not temporally responsive to the user's marker designation. The court reasoned that Abhyanker's locking mechanism was functionally similar to the patent's confirmation feature and that, as a matter of logic, the lock option would only be operationally meaningful after the user designated a location, thus satisfying the "responsive to" temporal requirement regardless of when the feature was initially displayed on screen.

cases.case_name: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Michigan
cases.summary: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment reducing Versata's trade secret damages award from $22.4 million to zero and remanded for a new trial, holding that the district court legally erred under the Defend Trade Secrets Act and Michigan Uniform Trade Secrets Act by precluding Versata from pursuing unjust enrichment damages and by restricting recovery to a reasonable royalty model based solely on the parties' licensing history. The court reversed the district court's reduction of the breach of contract damages from $82.3 million to three dollars and reinstated the jury award, while affirming the district court's denial of Ford's motion for judgment as a matter of law on trade secret misappropriation liability.
