Performance appraisals alone were insufficient to overcome the removing official's determination that unfit couriers pose mission liability.

The Court held that DOE's rejection of Senter's waiver request was in accordance with law, as DOE properly considered the request and reasoned that it was inapplicable given Senter's failure to satisfy the safety-performance requirement under § 339.204.

The Court found Senter could not establish harmful error because even assuming DOE erred in not conducting an 'actual comparison' between NMC role requirements and Senter's abilities, he failed to show DOE was likely to reach a different conclusion on waiver entitlement under the harmless-error standard of Ward v. United States Postal Service, 634 F.3d 1274 (Fed. Cir. 2011).

summary.holding: Affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Senter's removal from his DOE position for failure to meet physical fitness qualifications, finding substantial evidence supported the denial of his waiver request and no harmful error in the agency's procedures or legal analysis.

segments.text: The court reversed the Board's dismissal of the petition for enforcement as untimely, holding that under 5 C.F.R. § 1201.182(a), the reasonableness of time to file a PFE depends on the circumstances of each case, and a party need not file immediately upon becoming aware of a breach if actual harm has not yet materialized. The court concluded that the ten-month period from November 2016 (when Reyes learned of the VA HR officer's disclosure) to September 2017 (when he learned of the harmful consequence—DHS revocation of his job offer) was reasonable, as was the subsequent four-month period during which he retained counsel and contacted the VA.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit clarified the standard for timeliness of petitions for enforcement of settlement agreements under 5 C.F.R. § 1201.182(a), holding that reasonableness depends on case-specific circumstances and that a claimant is not required to file a PFE upon bare awareness of a breach before suffering identifiable harm—only after learning of actual adverse consequences must the filing deadline begin to run. This decision modifies prior Board practice that treated initial awareness of a breach as the triggering event regardless of whether harm was yet apparent.

cases.case_name: Shamoon v. City of San Antonio
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas
United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board

segments.text: The Board erred in construing "acquiring interest data" in claim 19 as requiring that at least some of the interest data acquired be active data. Under plain language analysis and the patent's explicit definition of "interest data" as "active or passive data, whether available or acquired," the phrase properly means obtaining any data qualifying as interest data, including wholly passive data. The verb "acquiring" has its ordinary meaning of obtaining, and its object "interest data" is expressly defined to encompass both active and passive data types.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit reversed the Board's determination that claim 19 is not unpatentable, finding the Board's claim construction of "acquiring interest data" erroneous as a matter of de novo review under Martek Biosciences Corp. v. Nutrinova, Inc., 579 F.3d 1363, 1380 (Fed. Cir. 2009), which requires that an explicitly defined claim term be construed according to the patentee's definition in the specification.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed by consent under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b); each party bears its own costs.

segments.text: The Court of Appeals dismissed the notice of appeal pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) because appellant failed to pay the required docketing fee within the time permitted by the rules. The dismissal was ordered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules.

The notice of appeal is dismissed for failure to pay the docketing fee required by Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) within the permitted timeframe. The dismissal is entered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit rules.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed the Trade Court's dismissal of the second lawsuit on claim preclusion grounds. All three prongs of the claim preclusion doctrine were satisfied: identical parties, final judgment on the merits in the first suit, and the second claim based on the same transactional facts (whether Mr. Chae deserved credit for Question 27). The court held that Mr. Chae was entitled to one full and fair opportunity to litigate the matter, and his second claim should have been brought in the first action.

segments.issue: Waiver of New Unsettled Law Argument
segments.text: The court held that Mr. Chae waived his argument that claim preclusion should not apply because the law was unsettled at the time of his 2018 examination, based on subsequent changes in U.S. v. Baxter. Although the court noted it applies a more lenient standard for pro se litigants, it declined to exercise discretion to overlook the argument's first presentation on appeal rather than before the lower court.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Trade Court's dismissal of Mr. Chae's second lawsuit challenging Customs' denial of credit for Question 27 on his Customs Broker License Examination on the ground of claim preclusion, holding that the second action should have been brought in the earlier litigation.

segments.text: The court granted the appellant's unopposed motions to voluntarily dismiss the appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b). Each party bears its own costs.
The court ordered that each party shall bear its own costs in connection with the dismissal of the appeal.

cases.case_name: National Steel Car Ltd. v. Greenbrier-Concarril LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Oregon

segments.text: The district court construed 'floor panel' as 'floor sheet, or floor sheets joined together, that may have one or more integral floor extensions,' and upon reconsideration clarified that extensions 'may be integral, or which can be separate,' with no requirement that pieces be 'abutting.' The court further clarified at summary judgment that 'separate' meant not requiring abutting contact, not permitting non-contacting extensions, and that floor panel extensions must still physically touch the floor panel itself. The Federal Circuit affirmed this construction as consistent with the court's prior orders and intrinsic evidence.

The district court granted summary judgment of non-infringement because Greenbrier's accused railroad cars do not meet the claim requirement that the side wall web physically contact the floor panel. Instead of direct contact, Greenbrier's design uses side post gussets (which do not touch the floor panel due to an intervening side sill) to support side posts connected to the side wall webbing. The Federal Circuit affirmed the summary judgment, finding no genuine dispute of material fact under the construed claims and the undisputed design of Greenbrier's cars.

summary.holding: Affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment of non-infringement of U.S. Patent Nos. 7,434,519 and 7,878,125, finding that the claim construction requiring physical contact between the side wall web and floor panel was correct and that Greenbrier's accused products do not satisfy this limitation.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Colorado

segments.text: The court reversed the district court's judgment and held that claim 30 of the '270 patent lacks adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a). Although the specification describes billions of possible PGF analogs, claim 30 narrowly covers only 1,620–4,230 compounds, yet the specification fails to disclose even a single example of a claimed compound or sufficient structural features common to all members of the claimed subgenus to allow a skilled artisan to identify them.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that when a patent genus claim covers a vastly narrower scope than the specification's broad disclosure, the specification must provide either representative species or common structural features with enough precision for a skilled artisan to visualize or recognize the claimed members; the absence of even a single disclosed embodiment of the narrow claim, combined with no identified common structural features, constitutes clear and convincing evidence of inadequate written description under the standard articulated in Regents v. Gilead.

segments.text: The petition for review was dismissed pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) because petitioner failed to pay the required docketing fee. The Court found failure to comply with this mandatory procedural requirement warranted dismissal for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules.

Petitioner also failed to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination, which constituted an additional independent ground for dismissal under the Federal Circuit's procedural rules. The omission of this required filing contributed to the Court's decision to dismiss the petition for failure to prosecute.

summary.holding: Petition for review of the Merit Systems Protection Board decision dismissed for failure to pay the docketing fee and failure to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination.

segments.text: The Veterans Court correctly determined that the Board of Veterans' Appeals lacked jurisdiction to consider Mr. Young's clear and unmistakable error (CUE) claims because the regional office had not yet considered them. The court vacated and remanded the Board's findings based on this jurisdictional defect.

The Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction to review Mr. Young's newly raised finality arguments under 38 U.S.C. § 5109A and 38 C.F.R. § 3.105 because the Veterans Court expressly declined to reach those issues on appeal. Under longstanding appellate doctrine, the Federal Circuit cannot review legal questions on which the lower court did not rule.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction to review finality arguments that the Veterans Court declined to consider.

segments.text: The court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), holding that it lacks authority to review the Veterans Court's factual determinations or application of law to fact. The appellant's challenges were limited to factual issues—whether the veteran's sickle cell disease was service-connected and whether his condition worsened during service—which fall outside the Federal Circuit's exclusive jurisdiction over statutory, regulatory, and constitutional questions.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because appellant presented only factual challenges and requests to reweigh medical evidence, which are beyond the Federal Circuit's appellate authority over Veterans Court decisions.

cases.case_name: Swank v. Secretary of the Navy

segments.text: The court dismissed the appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' agreement to do so. The dismissal was entered as a mandate effective immediately.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal by agreement of the parties under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b), with each side bearing its own costs.

cases.case_name: Nutricia North America, Inc. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the Court of International Trade's classification of medical foods under HTSUS chapter 21, subheading 2106.90.99, and held instead that the products qualify as medicaments under chapter 30, heading 3004, resulting in duty-free entry. The court reasoned that the exclusionary provision in chapter 30, note 1(a)—which excludes generic "foods or beverages" but carves out "nutritional preparations for intravenous administration"—does not exclude medical foods, which are specially formulated pharmaceutical-grade products administered enterally for specific therapeutic management of serious metabolic and medical conditions, as defined by Congress and the FDA.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that HTSUS chapter 30 note 1(a) applies its exclusion of generic "foods or beverages" only to ordinary dietary or nutritional products, not to medical foods that meet the statutory and regulatory definition under 21 U.S.C. § 360ee(b)(3) and 21 C.F.R. § 101.9(j)(8)—i.e., specially formulated products administered under medical supervision for therapeutic management of specific diseases with distinctive nutritional requirements. The holding distinguishes medical foods as a unique category occupying a middle ground between ordinary food and traditional pharmaceuticals, subject to classification as medicaments despite their food-like delivery mechanism and nutritional composition.

cases.case_name: Kaptan Demir Celik Endustrisi Ve Ticaret A.S. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed Commerce's final remand decision not to cross-attribute subsidies from Nur (an affiliate shipbuilder) to Kaptan's rebar production under 19 C.F.R. § 351.525(b)(6)(iv). Commerce found that steel scrap, though provided exclusively to Kaptan's production chain, was not "primarily dedicated" to rebar because it was a common input used across industries, unprocessed, and Nur's shipbuilding business was far removed from rebar production—thus failing to satisfy the regulation's requirement that the input be "merely a link in the overall production chain" and produced "dedicated almost exclusively to the production of a higher value-added product."

The court applied the substantial evidence standard to Commerce's remand findings, reviewing for whether a reasonable person might accept them as adequate to support the agency's conclusion. Commerce's determinations regarding the five factors for assessing whether an input is primarily dedicated, its finding that Nur's scrap was not a mere link in production, and its conclusion that Nur's business activities weighed against cross-attribution were all affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.

The court reviewed de novo the proper interpretation of the "primarily dedicated" requirement in 19 C.F.R. § 351.525(b)(6)(iv), applying the agency's preamble explanation that inputs must be dedicated almost exclusively to downstream production—analogous to stumpage for lumber or semolina for pasta—and not common inputs like plastics in automobiles. The court upheld Commerce's interpretation that steel scrap, though essential to rebar production, qualified as a common input rather than a specialized link because of its wide use across industries.

summary.holding: This decision affirms the Federal Circuit's deference to Commerce's regulatory interpretations in countervailing duty cross-attribution cases, confirming that the "primarily dedicated" analysis requires both practical dedication of inputs to downstream production and a characterization of the input as a narrow link in a specific production chain rather than a broadly used commodity, even when vertically integrated and exclusively supplied. The case does not establish new law but clarifies that Commerce's five-factor framework for assessing primary dedication—including consideration of whether an input is a common commodity and whether the supplier's business activities align with downstream production—is a reasonable and adequately explained approach under the 1998 regulation.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Ms. Chisum filed her notice of appeal 113 days after the Claims Court entered judgment, exceeding the mandatory 60-day deadline under 28 U.S.C. § 2522 and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(B). The taking of an appeal within the prescribed time is mandatory and jurisdictional, with no opportunity for waiver or equitable tolling.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely filing.

segments.text: The appeal was dismissed pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) based on the parties' joint stipulation of voluntary dismissal. Each party shall bear its own costs for purposes of the appeal in the Federal Circuit.

summary.holding: The parties' joint stipulation to voluntarily dismiss the appeal was granted, and each side bears its own costs in the Federal Circuit, with Franklin reserving the right to seek attorney fees under the Equal Access to Justice Act before the U.S. Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's dismissal of Akerman's second IRA appeal as barred by collateral estoppel under the four-part test from Shell Petroleum. Akerman did not dispute that his present appeal raised identical issues already litigated and finally decided in his prior '459 proceeding, and he had a full and fair opportunity to litigate those issues in the first action.

The court held as moot Akerman's challenge to the Board's December 2 denial of his request to certify an order for interlocutory appellate review, finding that because the Board's proceedings have already concluded and Akerman has obtained independent appellate review under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), granting relief on the interlocutory issue would have no practical impact.

The court rejected Akerman's motion for a filing fee refund under the Uniformed Services Employment and Reemployment Rights Act (USERRA), 38 U.S.C. § 4323(h)(1), holding that while USERRA waives fees for persons claiming rights under that chapter, Akerman filed only an IRA and identified no record evidence that he brought a USERRA claim before the Board.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's dismissal of Akerman's second IRA appeal as barred by collateral estoppel is affirmed; challenges to the Board's denial of interlocutory certification and its rulings on motions are moot; and Akerman is not entitled to a USERRA-based filing fee waiver.

cases.case_name: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. v. Power2b, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board

segments.text: The Board did not abuse its discretion in determining that Samsung presented a new obviousness ground in its reply briefing by arguing that Geva's planar element 14 would simply be placed on top of Keely's LCD without relying on Keely II's digitizer. Under 37 C.F.R. § 42.23(b), a reply may only respond to arguments raised in the patent owner's opposition and may not submit new evidence or arguments that could have been presented in the petition to establish unpatentability. The Board correctly found that Samsung's petition relied on Keely II's digitizer technology for position determination, making the reply's shift to a different combination a new and forfeited argument.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Board's Final Written Decisions in both inter partes reviews, finding no abuse of discretion in the Board's determination that Samsung forfeited its new obviousness theory by introducing it impermissibly in reply briefing rather than in the original petitions.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Northern District of California

segments.text: TetraMem's motion to dismiss the appeal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) was granted, and the appeal was dismissed. The appellate court found no objection from the appellee and granted the motion on the merits.
Each party was ordered to bear its own costs in connection with the dismissed appeal. This allocation was made consistent with TetraMem's motion requesting that each side bear its own costs.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed TetraMem's appeal and ordered each party to bear its own costs.

segments.text: The court affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment of noninfringement for Ninebot's second-generation unicycles, holding that no reasonable jury could find these models contained "leg contact surfaces" that protruded from the sides of the device as required by the claim construction of claims 1 and 18.

The court dismissed Ninebot's appeal of the district court's denial of its new trial motion regarding the marking requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 287(a) for lack of jurisdiction, holding that an amended or supplemental notice of appeal was required under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(4)(B)(ii) to challenge the order disposing of the motion for new trial.

The court reversed and vacated the lost profits award and remanded for a new trial on the issue of lost profits because the district court erred in excluding evidence of noninfringing substitutes that Ninebot sought to introduce regarding the Panduit factors, despite Ninebot's proper preservation of this issue.

summary.holding: The court affirmed the summary judgment of noninfringement for second-generation products, dismissed the appeal of the new trial motion denial for lack of jurisdiction, and reversed the lost profits award on the basis that exclusion of noninfringing substitutes evidence was improper, requiring a new trial on damages.

cases.case_name: Hawk Technology Systems, LLC v. Castle Retail, LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Tennessee

segments.text: Hawk forfeited its argument that the district court abused its discretion by sealing nearly the entirety of the briefing and exhibits related to the attorney fees motion. Hawk failed to raise the sealing issue before the district court, having consented to sealing of certain documents and never opposed Castle's sealing motions, precluding appellate review absent exceptional circumstances.

The district court did not abuse its discretion in awarding attorney fees to Castle under 35 U.S.C. § 285 as an exceptional case. The court's determination rested on the totality of circumstances including Hawk's pattern of frivolous patent lawsuits, the '091 patent being demonstrably weak on its face despite the statutory presumption of validity, and Hawk's impolite and unprofessional settlement negotiation conduct—all supported by clear factual findings not constituting an abuse of discretion.

summary.holding: Affirmed the district court's award of attorney fees to Castle Retail, LLC under 35 U.S.C. § 285 on the ground that the case was exceptional, while declining to address Hawk's forfeited argument regarding improper sealing of the fee motion briefing.

segments.text: The petition for review was dismissed for failure to pay the filing fee, failure to file the Statement Concerning Discrimination under Federal Circuit Rule 15(c), and failure to file a Notice of Unrepresented Person Appearance under Federal Circuit Rule 47.3. The court found these procedural deficiencies to constitute failure to prosecute under Federal Circuit procedural rules.

summary.holding: Petition for review of MSPB decision dismissed due to petitioner's failure to comply with mandatory Federal Circuit filing requirements.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.case_name: Smartrend Manufacturing Group (Smg), Inc. v. Opti-Luxx Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Michigan

segments.text: Opti-Luxx forfeited its objection to Mr. York's expert testimony on the ordinary observer's perspective because it failed to object when Smartrend moved to admit him as an expert, despite having received Mr. York's expert report containing his ordinary observer analysis well before trial. Under Federal Circuit precedent, a party must timely object to expert qualifications before the district court rules on admission or forfeit the objection.

The district court erred in construing the term "transparency" in the D930 patent to encompass both "transparent" and "translucent," and a new trial is necessary. The court's construction requires reassessment on remand based on proper interpretation of the design patent's intrinsic evidence and the distinction between these terms.

JMOL should have been granted on the '491 patent because no reasonable jury could have found infringement under the doctrine of equivalents. The accused product's integrated frame performed only one of the multiple functions required by the patent specification (mounting to the school bus), and the failure to perform all disclosed functions is fatal to equivalents liability as a matter of law.

The permanent injunction is vacated as moot given the reversal of infringement on the '491 patent and remand for new trial on the D930 patent. No injunction may issue pending the outcome of the D930 patent retrial.

summary.holding: The decision clarifies that in design patent cases, an expert may testify to the ordinary observer's perspective despite possessing above-ordinary knowledge, applying utility patent principles by analogy, though parties must timely object to avoid forfeiture. More significantly, the court holds that under the doctrine of equivalents, when a patent specification discloses multiple functions for a claim element, the accused product must perform all such functions to satisfy equivalents liability—it is insufficient to perform only a subset of those functions. This represents a meaningful articulation of the functional analysis required under modern equivalents doctrine for design and utility patents alike.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the appeal for failure to file the required brief within the time permitted by Federal Circuit Rule 31(a). Appellant's failure to comply with the procedural rules resulted in automatic dismissal of the notice of appeal.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for failure to prosecute.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the petition for review under Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) because the petitioner failed to pay the required docketing fee and failed to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination. Dismissal was entered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit Rules.

The Board's rejection of Jackson's second VEOA complaint as untimely under the 60-day filing deadline in 5 U.S.C. § 3330a(a)(2)(A) is affirmed. Jackson first became aware of the alleged violation in July 2022, filed a timely first complaint that same month, voluntarily withdrew it three days later, and did not refile until February 2023, well outside the statutory period.

Equitable tolling does not apply to Jackson's late-filed complaint because he failed to demonstrate reasonable diligence, which is a necessary condition under the two-prong test established in Pace v. DiGuglielmo. Jackson's voluntary withdrawal followed by inactivity until refiling demonstrated lack of diligence that acts as an absolute bar to equitable tolling, regardless of any extraordinary circumstances.

The Court does not address the underlying merits of Jackson's VEOA claim, including allegations that DHS removed veterans' preference materials from his applications or violated his preference rights, because Jackson failed to meet the statutory filing deadline and equitable tolling does not apply.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision denying Jackson's request for corrective action under the VEOA, holding that his second complaint was untimely under the 60-day statutory filing period and that equitable tolling does not apply due to his lack of reasonable diligence.

cases.case_name: Cloudofchange, LLC v. Lightspeed Commerce Inc.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in six inter partes review proceedings (IPR2022-00779, IPR2022-00997, IPR2022-01143, IPR2023-00232, IPR2023-00287, IPR2023-00288) brought by Lightspeed Commerce and Clover Network against Cloudofchange's patents. The affirmance was entered under Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating a nonprecedential disposition without opinion.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's patentability determinations across all six IPR proceedings, rejecting Cloudofchange's appellate challenges to the Board's findings.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's determination that Ms. Rough failed to establish by preponderant evidence that she made a protected disclosure under the Whistleblower Protection Act, 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)(A). The Board's finding was supported by substantial evidence, including the absence of corroboration from the alleged recipient of the disclosure (union representative Jose Ortiz) and Ms. Rough's uncorroborated statements, such that the Board properly concluded Ms. Rough did not meet her burden of proof.

summary.holding: The Board's denial of Ms. Rough's request for corrective action under the Whistleblower Protection Act was affirmed as supported by substantial evidence that Ms. Rough failed to prove she made a protected disclosure.

cases.case_name: Arena Ip, LLC v. New England Patriots LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Massachusetts

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's judgment in its entirety pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating the decision was rendered nonprecedential and without written explanation of the underlying merits.

summary.holding: The district court's judgment against Arena IP, LLC in favor of the New England Patriots LLC was affirmed on appeal.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims' decision in its entirety, upholding the Veterans Affairs' determination regarding claimant Atilano's benefits claim. The court issued a nonprecedential summary affirmance under Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating no reversible error in the lower court's application of veterans benefits law.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims' decision upholding the VA's benefits determination.

cases.case_name: Canatex Completion Solutions, Inc. v. Wellmatics, LLC

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's holding that asserted claims 1, 4–13, and 15–19 are invalid for indefiniteness due to lack of antecedent basis for the phrase "the connection profile of the second part." The court held that the intrinsic evidence clearly establishes that a skilled artisan would recognize "second" contains an evident error with an evident simple correction to "first," and therefore the phrase is not indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b).

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit clarifies that courts may correct obvious claim-language errors under a demanding standard when intrinsic evidence clearly establishes that a skilled artisan would recognize both that an error exists and that only one reasonable correction is possible. Here, the pervasiveness of the "second/first" error throughout the patent, combined with the logical flow of the claim structure, the specification, and the figures, satisfied this narrow exception to the rule against judicial claim rewriting.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded to clarify whether the final judgment rests solely on the jury's noninfringement verdict or also incorporates the jury's verdicts of anticipation and obviousness under 35 U.S.C. §§ 102 and 103. The record was unclear whether the district court's final judgment constituted a judgment of invalidity in addition to noninfringement, necessitating an amended final judgment to resolve this ambiguity before appellate review could proceed.

summary.holding: The case is remanded for the district court to enter an amended final judgment clarifying the disposition of the jury's invalidity verdicts and whether the judgment rests solely on noninfringement or also incorporates findings of anticipation and obviousness; the panel retains jurisdiction and will decide the appeal on the existing briefs following entry of the clarified judgment.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's dismissal of Warne's individual right of action appeal as untimely filed. Under 5 U.S.C. § 1214(a)(3)(A)(ii) and 5 C.F.R. § 1209.5(a)(1), an IRA appeal must be filed within 65 days after the Office of Special Counsel notifies the complainant of termination of investigation; the relevant date is when the notice is delivered, not when the recipient reads it, and Warne's email lockout did not delay the start of the filing period.

The court held that the statutory timing requirement for IRA appeals cannot be waived for good cause, citing MacDonald v. Department of Justice, 105 M.S.P.R. 83 (2007), and therefore Warne's dyscalculia could not excuse his late filing.

The court affirmed that equitable tolling is limited to extraordinary circumstances where a litigant has pursued rights diligently but cannot bring a timely action, and held that neither Warne's dyscalculia nor his parallel pursuit of an Equal Employment Opportunity complaint met this standard under Lozano v. Montoya Alvarez, 572 U.S. 1 (2014).

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's dismissal of Warne's individual right of action appeal as untimely, holding that the 65-day filing deadline is statutory and cannot be waived for good cause or equitable tolling based on dyscalculia or pursuit of a parallel EEO complaint.

cases.case_name: Cpc Patent Technologies Pty Ltd. v. Assa Abloy Ab
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office, Patent Trial and Appeal Board

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed both PTAB final written decisions holding claims 3–18 of the '039 patent unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103, finding the Board's obviousness analysis lacked substantial evidence. The Board erred in treating Hsu's disclosure of "associating" card information with biometric data as equivalent to the claim requirement that card information "define" or "establish" the memory location of biometric data, without meaningful explanation of how association accomplishes that control function.

The court limited its review to claims 3–18 because a separate appeal in CPC v. Apple affirmed the unpatentability of claims 1–2 and 19–20 based on different prior art, and the court declined to review those claims to avoid inconsistent outcomes on the same claims across separate proceedings.

summary.holding: Both PTAB decisions are reversed and remanded for consideration of unpatentability grounds not reached by the Board.

summary.holding: The PTAB's IPR decision was affirmed in its entirety.

cases.case_name: Lbt Ip II LLC v. Uber Technologies, Inc.

summary.holding: The PTAB's decision in the inter partes review proceeding was affirmed in its entirety.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's dismissal of Rivers's appeal as untimely filed. Rivers filed his appeal to the Board 11 days after the 30-calendar-day deadline prescribed in 5 C.F.R. § 1201.22(c), and the Board did not abuse its discretion in determining that his reasons—delayed procurement of medical records, electronic filing difficulties, and non-receipt of the administrative judge's order—did not constitute good cause for the late filing under the abuse-of-discretion standard.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board did not abuse its discretion in dismissing Rivers's appeal as untimely filed and in rejecting his good-cause arguments for the delay.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Richardson's notice of appeal was untimely filed. Under 28 U.S.C. § 2522 and § 2107(b), a non-governmental party must file a notice of appeal within 60 days after the Court of Federal Claims enters judgment; here, judgment was entered December 20, 2023, making the deadline February 20, 2024, but Richardson did not mail her notice until March 1, 2024, and it was received and filed March 5, 2024. The timely filing of a notice of appeal is a jurisdictional requirement that cannot be waived and is not subject to equitable tolling.

The court declined Richardson's request to transfer the case to the United States District Court for the Northern District of Georgia because that court was not one in which the action could have been brought at the time the claim was filed, and because the appeal was untimely. Transfer under applicable law requires that the receiving court be one in which the action could have been originally brought.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely notice of appeal; transfer request denied.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board

segments.text: The Board did not abuse its discretion in admitting the Draft Notes and other exhibits over hearsay and authentication objections. Under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c) and Federal Circuit precedent, hearsay evidence is permissible in Board proceedings and procedural evidentiary matters fall within the sound discretion of the Board and its administrative judges, which is reviewable only for clear and harmful abuse.

Raiszadeh's arguments challenging the Draft Notes' admission were directed to the weight of the evidence rather than admissibility, and the court declines to reweigh evidence on appeal. The court held it is not its role to second-guess the Board's assessment of how much probative weight to accord hearsay evidence under the Borninkhof factors.

Even assuming the AJ erred in admitting the Draft Notes, any such error was harmless under Curtin v. Off. of Pers. Mgmt. because the Draft Notes were merely cumulative of other independent evidence of employee complaints and management concerns about Raiszadeh's performance, and Raiszadeh cannot show the error affected the outcome.

Hearsay evidence may constitute substantial evidence in an administrative proceeding if it has circumstances giving it credibility and probative value to a reasonable mind. The Draft Notes satisfied this standard under Sanders v. U.S. Postal Service because they were corroborated by other record evidence and independently confirmed by management testimony.

Under the Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8) and § 1221(e)(1)), to establish prima facie retaliation an employee must show she made a protected disclosure and that it contributed to an adverse personnel action. The Board found Raiszadeh satisfied this burden by establishing both elements.

An agency may rebut a prima facie WPA retaliation case by proving with clear and convincing evidence, under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e), that it would have taken the same adverse action absent the disclosure. The Board affirmed the AJ's finding that DHS met this burden.

Applying the first Carr factor (strength of agency's evidence supporting the personnel action), the AJ found strong evidence of Raiszadeh's managerial deficiencies through numerous employee complaints describing her as abrasive, overbearing, and causing significant disintegration of team cohesion, which constitutes substantial evidence supporting termination during probation.

Under the second Carr factor (existence and strength of retaliatory motive), the AJ found DHS's motive to retaliate was weak because Dibbins, the deciding official, was unaware of Raiszadeh's OIG disclosure until 2011 or 2012, years after the 2008 termination decision.

The Board's finding that DHS would have terminated Raiszadeh regardless of her protected disclosure was supported by substantial evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c), defined as relevant evidence a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to support the conclusion. The court affirmed the entire decision of the Merit Systems Protection Board.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision denying Raiszadeh's whistleblower retaliation complaint, holding that DHS proved by clear and convincing evidence that it would have terminated her for performance deficiencies during her probationary period regardless of her protected disclosure to the Office of Inspector General, and that the Board did not abuse its discretion in admitting hearsay evidence that was cumulative, corroborated, and probative.

summary.holding: The petition for writ of mandamus is denied because the PTAB's discretionary decision to deny IPR institution based on the progress of parallel district court litigation does not present cognizable constitutional or statutory grounds for extraordinary relief, and reliance on rescinded interim guidance does not establish a due process or APA violation.

segments.text: The Court of Federal Claims lacked subject matter jurisdiction over Miles' claims for multiple independent reasons: (1) it could not exercise jurisdiction over claims against individual federal judges and prosecutors, only against the United States, under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1); (2) Miles had a pending parallel action in district court challenging the same arrest and conviction, which deprived the Court of Federal Claims of jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1500; and (3) Miles failed to identify a money-mandating source of law required for jurisdiction under Fisher v. United States, 402 F.3d 1167 (Fed. Cir. 2005). The court rejected Miles' arguments that equity could expand the court's statutory jurisdiction or that he could grant jurisdiction by designating the court as his trustee.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction, holding that the court properly lacked jurisdiction over claims against individual federal officials, that a pending parallel action in district court divested jurisdiction under the Tucker Act, and that Miles failed to invoke a money-mandating source of law necessary to establish the court's jurisdiction.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the petition for review because the petitioner failed to pay the docketing fee required by Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) within the time permitted by the rules. The dismissal was based on failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's procedural rules.

The court affirmed the Board's denial of Ms. Woodroof's petition to enforce the 2016 settlement agreement's confidentiality provision. The Board found no material breach because the settlement agreement expressly permitted disclosures to the MSPB, and Ms. Woodroof voluntarily testified as a witness about her PIP in another employee's case, meaning the agency's cross-examination questions did not constitute a breach of the confidentiality clause.

The court affirmed the administrative judge's discretionary denial of Ms. Woodroof's requests for discovery and a status conference. Under Federal Circuit precedent, procedural matters regarding discovery and evidentiary issues fall within the sound discretion of the Board, and Ms. Woodroof failed to demonstrate that the denial caused substantial harm or prejudice warranting reversal.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of Ms. Woodroof's petition to enforce the settlement agreement and the denial of her requests for discovery and a status conference.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeals in IPR2024-00537 and IPR2024-00538 pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) following the parties' agreement to settle. The dismissal was entered as the court's order on November 6, 2025.
Each party bears its own costs in the dismissed appeals, with no allocation of litigation expenses to either side.

Boyd's petition for review was filed approximately nine years after the Merit Systems Protection Board's final decision in September 2015, violating the 60-day deadline requirement of 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1). The court dismissed the appeal as untimely, holding that even if equitable tolling were available under that statute, Boyd failed to demonstrate either diligent pursuit of her rights or extraordinary circumstances warranting tolling.

The court acknowledged that the Supreme Court in Harrow v. Department of Defense (2024) determined section 7703(b)(1)'s deadline is non-jurisdictional but left unresolved whether equitable tolling applies to it. The Federal Circuit expressly declined to resolve this question, assuming arguendo that equitable tolling might be available but finding Boyd's arguments insufficient to satisfy the two-element test for tolling.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed Boyd's petition for review as untimely filed under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1), which requires petitions to be filed within 60 days of the Board's notice of its final decision, without reaching the merits of her challenge to the MSPB's affirmance of her termination based on an alleged breach of a Last Chance Agreement.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied SAP's petition for a writ of mandamus challenging the PTAB's denial of institution of inter partes review. Under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d), institution decisions are final and nonappealable, and mandamus is ordinarily unavailable to review such decisions, including those based on parallel civil litigation standards, absent colorable constitutional claims or certain statutory challenges—neither of which SAP properly raised before the agency.

summary.holding: The PTAB's discretionary denial of institution of inter partes review based on parallel civil proceedings is generally unreviewable by mandamus under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d), and SAP failed to preserve any colorable exceptions by raising its challenges before the agency.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court held that mandamus is ordinarily unavailable for review of IPR institution decisions because Congress committed such decisions to the Director's discretion under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a) and made them final and nonappealable under § 314(d). The court noted possible exceptions for colorable constitutional claims or certain statutory challenges, but found none present here.

The court rejected Motorola's claim that the Vidal Memorandum created a constitutionally protected property interest in having IPR petitions considered without regard to discretionary Fintiv factors. Under Board of Regents v. Roth, when a statute leaves a benefit to an official's discretion, no protected property interest arises, and the Director's discretion to institute or deinstitute IPR is committed by statute.

The court found no violation of the Administrative Procedure Act in the Acting Director's rescission of the Vidal Memorandum or its application to pending cases. The rescission was not retroactively applied because no final institution determination had been made on the challenged petitions when the rescission took effect, and Motorola was afforded opportunity to request additional briefing but declined to do so.

summary.holding: This decision confirms that IPR institution decisions rest within the Director's unreviewable discretion under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d) and are generally immune from mandamus review absent extraordinary circumstances such as colorable constitutional claims—which the court found absent here. The decision establishes that interim guidance on discretionary factors like Fintiv does not create a constitutionally protected entitlement that constrains the Director's statutory authority to rescind such guidance and reallocate weight among discretionary considerations. The ruling is fact-bound to these specific circumstances but clarifies the limited scope of judicial review over institution decisions and administrative guidance modifications.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) by agreement of the parties, with each side bearing their own costs.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1), the Claims Court has limited jurisdiction over certain claims against the United States, and lacks jurisdiction over claims against state and local government officials or institutions, as well as challenges to state court decisions. Rodriguez's complaint, which primarily alleged wrongdoing by state and local officials arising from dismissal of her Florida Supreme Court mandamus petition, fell outside this jurisdiction.

The Court affirmed that Rodriguez failed to identify a money-mandating statute required under the Tucker Act. To invoke the Claims Court's jurisdiction, a plaintiff must identify a separate source of law that 'can fairly be interpreted as mandating compensation by the Federal Government,' but Rodriguez's complaint cited only the Federal Rules of Evidence, Federal Rules of Civil Procedure, 28 U.S.C. § 2006, and 21 U.S.C. § 848(e)—none of which qualify as money-mandating statutes.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's dismissal of Rodriguez's complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction on two independent grounds: (1) many of her claims arose from state and local government wrongdoing over which the Claims Court lacks jurisdiction, and (2) to the extent her claims targeted the United States, she failed to identify a money-mandating statute required under the Tucker Act.

segments.text: The Board affirmed the administrative judge's findings that Ms. Howard's complaints about meal breaks constituted protected disclosures under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8) and were a contributing factor in the decision to terminate her employment under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e)(1). The Board found Ms. Howard satisfied the knowledge-and-timing test for establishing a prima facie case of whistleblower retaliation.

The Board found that the agency proved by clear and convincing evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e)(2) that it would have terminated Ms. Howard's employment even absent her protected disclosures. The Board applied the Carr factors and determined that the strength of the agency's evidence regarding insubordination, deficient performance, and patient safety risks outweighed the limited motive to retaliate and lack of similarly situated comparators.

The court held that an Individual Right of Action appeal is narrowly limited to merits of Whistleblower Protection Act violations under 5 U.S.C. § 2302, and rejected Ms. Howard's arguments regarding negligent supervision and authority to terminate as falling outside the scope of IRA review. The court noted such arguments might constitute affirmative defenses in different contexts but are not cognizable in an IRA appeal under 5 C.F.R. § 1209.2(c).

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's decision denying Ms. Howard's Individual Right of Action appeal for whistleblower retaliation is affirmed because, although her protected disclosures regarding meal breaks were a contributing factor in her termination, the agency proved by clear and convincing evidence it would have terminated her for documented performance deficiencies and conduct issues independent of the protected disclosures.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the appeal based on the parties' joint stipulation of voluntary dismissal pursuant to Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b). Each side was ordered to bear its own costs.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed by voluntary stipulation of the parties with each side bearing its own costs.

segments.text: The Board lacked jurisdiction over Ms. Demery's non-selection appeal. Non-selection claims generally cannot be appealed to the Board under 5 U.S.C. § 7512, and Ms. Demery's receipt of an unofficial, tentative job offer that was rescinded still constitutes non-selection rather than an appealable adverse action, so errors during the selection process alone do not confer jurisdiction.

The Board properly rejected Ms. Demery's employment practices claim as a basis for jurisdiction. To establish jurisdiction under an employment practices appeal, a petitioner must show both that the actions constitute employment practices and that OPM is significantly involved in administering them; Ms. Demery failed on both prongs—her challenge to application of the rule of three was distinct from the Lackhouse precedents she cited, and she presented no facts showing OPM's significant involvement in the selection process.

segments.issue: Procedural Error Claims Without Appealable Action
segments.text: The Board correctly found it lacked jurisdiction over Ms. Demery's allegations of improper personnel practices and procedural error. Allegations of prohibited personnel practices are not an independent source of the Board's jurisdiction absent an otherwise appealable adverse action, and since non-selection is not an appealable action, these claims could not proceed.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board did not err in dismissing Ms. Demery's appeal for lack of jurisdiction, as her claims arising from non-selection for a Management Analyst position and her failure to establish an exception based on OPM employment practices left the Board without jurisdiction to hear the matter.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision in the underlying employment dispute. The court applied Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating a summary affirmance without detailed opinion where the lower tribunal's decision was correct as a matter of law.

summary.holding: The MSPB decision in No. AT-1221-15-0157-B-1 was affirmed.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's construction of 'background noise level' to encompass background noise levels in a subset of frequencies (e.g., a single frequency subband), rather than only a single overall background noise level. The Board's construction was supported by intrinsic evidence and expert testimony, and the court reviewed it without deference under the standard set forth in Intel Corp. v. Qualcomm Inc.

The court affirmed the Board's interpretation that adjustments to an internal sound signal are 'based on' a background noise level even when made to a noise-reduced ambient signal, because the noise-reduced signal serves as a control input for the adjustment. The Board's reasoning that the combination of noise reduction and adaptive equalization constitutes an adjustment based on background noise level was supported by the intrinsic record.

The court affirmed the Board's determinations that claims 1, 6–7, 12–14, and 17 are unpatentable for anticipation by the Alves reference, and that claims 2–3, 9–11, and 18–20 are unpatentable for obviousness over Alves combined with other prior art. These holdings rested upon the claim constructions upheld on appeal.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's determination that the patent's claims are unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 102 (anticipation) and § 103 (obviousness).

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's finding that the VA established by clear and convincing evidence it would have terminated Dr. Barrette regardless of his whistleblower activity. Under the Carr factor test for federal employee retaliation claims, the court held that substantial evidence supported the administrative judge's conclusions on the second and third Carr factors, and the court declined to reweigh evidence on appeal.

segments.issue: Motive to Retaliate – Second Carr Factor
segments.text: The court affirmed the administrative judge's conclusion that none of the VA officials involved in Dr. Barrette's removal had a strong motive to retaliate. The court held that although Dr. Fowler and Dr. Antoine were aware of whistleblowing activity, the record did not establish fabrication of evidence or impropriety, and any animus was based on prior conduct and complaints rather than protected disclosures.

segments.issue: Similarly Situated Comparators – Third Carr Factor
segments.text: The court affirmed that other physicians at the facility were not similarly situated to Dr. Barrette for purposes of the third Carr factor. The court held that differences in the number and severity of misconduct grounds, and differences in probationary status, properly distinguished comparator employees, and Dr. Barrette's bare appellate allegations regarding Dr. Bolling lacked record citation and support.

The court rejected Dr. Barrette's challenge to the administrative judge's partial grant of discovery requests and denial of sanctions against the VA. The court found no clear abuse of discretion in the AJ's evidentiary rulings, applying the deferential standard of review for such MSPB procedural matters.

segments.issue: Issue Preservation – SRB Bias and Due Process
segments.text: The court declined to consider Dr. Barrette's arguments regarding Summary Review Board bias, failure to interview relevant individuals, and due process deprivation because he failed to raise these issues before the administrative judge and only presented them for the first time in his petition for review to the Board, violating the requirement to preserve issues in administrative proceedings.

The court confirmed jurisdiction to review the Board's decision under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A) and 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), applying the arbitrary and capricious standard along with review for substantial evidence support.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's final decision upholding Dr. Barrette's termination from the VA during his probationary period, finding that he established a prima facie case of whistleblower retaliation but that the VA sustained its affirmative defense under the Carr factor test by demonstrating clear and convincing evidence that it would have terminated him regardless of his protected disclosures.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's determination that Demery's Veterans Employment Opportunity Act complaint filed with the Department of Labor on May 7, 2019 was untimely under 5 U.S.C. § 3330(a)(2)(A), which requires filing within 60 days of the alleged violation. The Board properly found that Demery failed to explain the eleven-month delay between her discovery of allegedly fraudulent concealment on June 12, 2018 and her actual filing date, and that neither a fraud-specific discovery rule nor equitable tolling excused her untimeliness.

The court rejected Demery's argument that a fraud-specific discovery rule—a distinct equitable doctrine separate from traditional equitable tolling—excused her deadline miss. Even assuming such a rule could apply under federal law, Demery failed to explain why she waited eleven months after discovering the alleged fraud to file her complaint, making the exemption unavailable.

The court affirmed the Board's rejection of equitable tolling for the 60-day VEOA filing deadline, which is otherwise subject to tolling under Kirkendall v. Department of Army. The Board correctly found that Demery presented no circumstances showing she was induced or tricked by adversary misconduct into missing the deadline, as equitable tolling requires.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of corrective action under the Veterans Employment Opportunity Act based on Demery's untimely filing of her complaint with the Department of Labor, rejecting both fraud-specific discovery rule and equitable tolling arguments.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's dismissal of Courtney's IRA appeal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the Board lacked jurisdiction because Courtney failed to exhaust OSC remedies with respect to the new allegations (injury, being chased, touching, cursing) that were not included in her original March 2, 2023 grievance submitted to OSC, and the Board's jurisdiction over an IRA appeal is limited to issues previously raised with OSC under 5 U.S.C. §§ 1214(a)(3), 1221(a), (b).

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's finding that Courtney's March 2, 2023 grievance did not constitute a protected disclosure under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8) because her allegations of insufficient training and disagreements over supervisory feedback did not evidence a violation of law, rule, or regulation, nor did they rise to the level of gross mismanagement, gross waste of funds, abuse of authority, or substantial danger to public health and safety as required for Board jurisdiction over whistleblower claims.

The Federal Circuit affirmed that Courtney's act of filing a grievance does not establish Board jurisdiction under the IRA because although grievance-filing may be protected activity, the Board lacks jurisdiction in IRA appeals concerning grievances unless the grievance seeks to remedy a violation of 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), which Courtney's grievance did not do.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the MSPB's final order dismissing Courtney's IRA appeal for lack of jurisdiction because she failed to exhaust OSC remedies as to new allegations beyond her original grievance, and her original grievance did not contain protected disclosures or constitute protected activity qualifying for Board jurisdiction under the whistleblower provisions of 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8).

cases.case_name: Merck Serono S.A. v. Twi Pharmaceuticals, Inc.

segments.text: The Board correctly applied the complete-identity-of-inventive-entity rule from In re Land when holding that Bodor was prior art despite having some overlapping inventors with the patent-in-suit. Because Bodor's authors (Dr. Bodor and Dr. Dandiker) differed from the named inventors of the patents (Drs. De Luca, Ythier, Munafo, and Lopez-Bresnahan), Bodor constituted disclosure "by another" under 35 U.S.C. § 102(a), and the patentee failed to provide credible and corroborated evidence that each named inventor contributed to Bodor's seven-line disclosure.

The Board correctly held claims 36, 38, 39, and 41–48 of the '947 patent and claims 17, 19–20, and 22–29 of the '903 patent unpatentable as obvious over Bodor in combination with Rice. The Board identified adequate motivation to combine the references based on MS symptoms' propensity to relapse, and substantial evidence supported a reasonable likelihood of success because an ordinary artisan would logically repeat Bodor's induction dosing and follow treatment phases with cladribine-free periods to manage drug toxicity.

The Court affirmed the Board's final written decision holding all challenged claims unpatentable as obvious, finding no legal or factual errors in the Board's analysis and rejecting Merck's arguments regarding the proper inventive-entity standard and the sufficiency of the motivations to combine.

summary.holding: Affirmed: The Board correctly determined that Bodor was prior art as disclosure "by another" under the complete-inventive-entity rule, and that all challenged claims were unpatentable as obvious over Bodor in combination with Rice.

cases.case_name: Merck Serono S.A. v. Hopewell Pharma Ventures, Inc.

segments.text: The Board held claims 36, 38, 39, and 41–46 of the '947 patent and claims 17, 19, 20, and 22–27 of the '903 patent unpatentable as obvious over a combination of Bodor and Stelmasiak. The Board found that Bodor's disclosed six-line dosing regimen, combined with Stelmasiak's teaching of oral cladribine efficacy, rendered the claimed oral cladribine regimen obvious to a person skilled in the art. The court affirmed the Board's unpatentability determination, finding no legal or factual errors in the analysis.

segments.issue: Bodor Reference as Prior Art—Overlapping Inventors
segments.text: The court clarified the interpretation of "by others" or "by another" under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a), (e) when a reference and the patent-at-issue identify overlapping inventors. The Board held that despite Bodor being authored by Drs. Bodor and Dandiker (who worked at Ivax in partnership with Serono), the reference qualified as prior art because there was no facial overlap in named inventors or assignees, and Merck failed to prove that all named inventors of the '947 patent contributed to Bodor's disclosure. The court affirmed this holding and clarified that a reference disclosing an invention of a subset of inventors is not automatically disqualified as prior art, and co-inventors of a reference's applied portions who made significant contributions (under the Duncan Parking standard) may render that reference available as "by another" prior art.

The court affirmed the Board's factual finding that Merck failed to produce credible and corroborated evidence establishing that inventor De Luca provided an inventive contribution to Bodor's six-line dosing regimen, thus failing to meet its burden of production to rebut the prima facie case that Bodor was prior art. Although De Luca attended the August 2003 Amsterdam Minutes meeting where formulation progress was discussed, the evidence was insufficient to corroborate that De Luca contributed to the specific disclosure appearing in Bodor.

In the alternative, the court affirmed the Board's holding that Drs. Bodor and Dandiker qualify as at least co-inventors of the applied portions of Bodor under the Duncan Parking standard because they provided sufficiently significant contributions to the disclosure. Therefore, even if all named inventors had contributed to Bodor's six-line disclosure, it would remain available as prior art "by another" under the pre-AIA statute.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies Federal Circuit precedent on the interpretation of "by others" or "by another" under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. §§ 102(a), (e) in cases involving overlapping inventors between a reference and a patent-at-issue. The court confirms that facial absence of inventor or assignee overlap does not automatically render a reference prior art; rather, a patentee must affirmatively prove inventive contribution by all named patent inventors to the reference's disclosure. However, if one or more co-inventors of the reference made sufficiently significant contributions under the Duncan Parking test, the reference remains available as prior art "by another," even if some patent inventors contributed to the reference. The decision is primarily fact-bound to the specific circumstances of Merck's partnership with Ivax and does not fundamentally alter patent law doctrine.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed Wright's appeal for lack of jurisdiction. The Court held that it lacks jurisdiction to review the Veterans Court's denial of a petition for extraordinary relief under the All Writs Act when the underlying Board decision was merely a remand (not a final grant or denial of benefits), citing Kirkpatrick v. Nicholson, 417 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2005), which establishes that remand orders are not appealable to the Veterans Court.

segments.issue: No Right to Substantive Relief Without Remand
segments.text: The Court held that a veteran has no colorable legal claim to substantive relief from the Veterans Court (or through mandamus petition) without remand back to the Regional Office for further development. The Court reaffirmed its precedent in Ravin v. McDonough, 107 F.4th 1357 (Fed. Cir. 2024), which forecloses any argument that a veteran is entitled to a decision on the merits without administrative remand.

The Court held that the Veterans Court's jurisdictional bar against reviewing Board remand orders cannot be circumvented by filing a mandamus petition under the All Writs Act. The Court agreed with the Veterans Court's reliance on Gardner-Dickson v. Wilkie, 33 Vet. App. 50 (2020), holding that just as a remand order is not appealable, there is no colorable claim to a writ of mandamus in the same circumstance.
The Court held that Wright's request for contempt sanctions against the Chair of the Board lacked colorable merit and was not pursued on appeal, requiring no further analysis of that claim.

summary.holding: The decision clarifies that the Federal Circuit has no jurisdiction over appeals from the Veterans Court involving Board remand orders, whether presented as direct appeals or disguised as All Writs Act mandamus petitions, and confirms that veterans have no enforceable right to substantive relief without administrative remand—principles that foreclose attempted end-runs around the jurisdictional limitations established in Kirkpatrick and reaffirmed in Ravin.
