Ms. Chisum failed to state a claim for breach of contract because, even accepting as true her allegation that the government agreed not to retaliate if she voluntarily dismissed her 2022 complaint, she breached that alleged agreement by failing to voluntarily dismiss and instead opposing dismissal. No error was shown in the Court of Federal Claims' determination that she "cannot prevail on her claim because by her own terms she breached the agreement."

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of the entire complaint for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction as to most claims and failure to state a claim as to the remaining breach-of-contract claim.

summary.holding: The Court of Federal Claims correctly dismissed Ms. Chisum's complaint under the Tucker Act because the court lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over claims against non-federal actors and over tort and non-money-mandating constitutional claims, her medical-care and SSDI claims were time-barred under the six-year statute of limitations, and her breach-of-contract claim failed as a matter of law because she herself breached the alleged agreement by failing to voluntarily dismiss her prior complaint.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit granted Berthiaume's motion for summary affirmance without opinion pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 36(a), affirming the Veterans Court's decision in the underlying case.

summary.holding: The Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims decision is affirmed.

segments.text: The Board's finding that Ms. Young failed to prove a reasonable belief in the truth of her alleged protected disclosures is supported by substantial evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c). The Administrative Judge determined Ms. Young's allegations were 'wholly without merit and detached from reality,' and the Board affirmed this determination on review.

The Board correctly determined that Ms. Young failed to prove her protected disclosures were a contributing factor to her termination under the Whistleblower Protection Act, 5 U.S.C. § 2302. The record showed termination procedures were initiated one month before service of the Temporary Peace Order, and Ms. Young did not dispute that the deciding official lacked knowledge of her disclosures.

The Board correctly ruled that post-termination personnel actions fall outside the scope of 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), which covers only actions 'with respect to any employee or applicant for employment.' Ms. Young cannot seek corrective action for alleged retaliation occurring after her termination based on the plain language of the statute.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's final decision denying corrective action in Ms. Young's individual right of action appeal under the Whistleblower Protection Act is affirmed as supported by substantial evidence and consistent with applicable law.

cases.case_name: Ag Der Dillinger Huttenwerke v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed Commerce's rejection of Dillinger's proposed quality codes (759 and 771) for sour service steel products. Commerce permissibly declined to split product categories based on physical characteristics under 19 U.S.C. § 1677(16) and the model-match methodology, and the Trade Court correctly upheld this determination as timely and substantively sound.

The court vacated Commerce's use of likely selling price as facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e(a) to fill gaps in Dillinger's non-prime plate cost of production data. While Commerce permissibly invoked facts otherwise available, using selling price to substitute for actual cost of production is unreasonable because these are distinct metrics, and the court remanded for Commerce to identify an appropriate alternative factual basis or reconsider its approach.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that although Commerce has broad authority to use facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e(a) when information is not available on the record, it cannot mechanically substitute selling price for cost of production absent a reasoned explanation for why that proxy accurately reflects the actual cost metric. The holding narrows Commerce's discretion in choosing among available facts and reinforces the distinction between cost-based and price-based methodologies in antidumping investigations.

cases.case_name: Rasmussen Instruments, LLC v. Depuy Synthes Products, Inc.

segments.text: Rasmussen lacked standing to sue for patent infringement under Article III because it did not own either asserted patent at the time it filed suit in October 2020. Under 35 U.S.C. § 261, a valid assignment requires an instrument in writing that transfers the entire exclusive patent right or an undivided interest, and the court found Rasmussen failed to meet this requirement, triggering a threshold jurisdictional defect.

The court determined that Rasmussen's purported assignment of the patents from Dr. Rasmussen in 2020 was invalid under Utah and Tennessee contract law because the 2006 Agreement with Wright assigned all intellectual property rights to Wright, the 2013 Settlement Agreement did not reconvey any rights back to Dr. Rasmussen, and no written instrument effectuated a valid transfer to the LLC. The court reviewed this question of law de novo.

The district court erred in denying DePuy's motion for judgment as a matter of law on the ownership issue and in denying DePuy's request that the jury verdict form include a question on ownership, since the lack of valid patent assignment presented a legal issue that should not have been submitted to the jury.

The Federal Circuit vacated the entire final judgment, including the jury's verdict of infringement of the '180 patent, the denial of DePuy's JMOL motions, and the awards of prejudgment interest and permanent injunction, and remanded for the district court to dismiss the action for lack of subject matter jurisdiction.

summary.holding: A plaintiff lacks constitutional standing to sue for patent infringement under Article III when it does not own the patents at the time of filing suit, presenting a threshold jurisdictional issue that bars all relief regardless of the merits of infringement claims.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Columbia

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's dismissal for lack of standing, holding that appellants failed to demonstrate that at least one member of their organizations would have suffered a non-speculative, concrete injury in fact from the PTO's denial of the petition for rulemaking. The alleged injury—risk of patent cancellation due to IPR/PGR institution—was too speculative because it depended on an extended chain of hypothetical future events involving independent third-party actors (PTAB and district courts), which cannot serve as the basis for Article III standing under D.C. Circuit precedent. The court emphasized that a procedural right alone, such as the right to petition for rulemaking, cannot establish standing unless it protects a threatened concrete interest, and that predictions of future events, especially actions by third parties, must be rejected as speculative.

summary.holding: This decision affirms established standing doctrine under Article III and D.C. Circuit law as applied to administrative petitions, clarifying that organizational plaintiffs cannot establish associational standing based on speculative chains of hypothetical future conduct by independent third parties, even when challenging alleged statutory or procedural violations by a federal agency. The decision does not break new legal ground but confirms the application of rigorous injury-in-fact requirements to rulemaking petitions.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court reviewed the Board's claim constructions de novo and affirmed them on cross-appeal, finding no error in the Board's interpretation of the limitations at issue, including the Tensile Transfer Limitations and Bridge Limitation.

The court reversed the Board's finding that Slater did not anticipate the independent claims, concluding that substantial evidence does not support the Board's determination and that Slater discloses all elements of the independent claims arranged as recited, including the transfixation screw hole, trajectory, and bridge portion.

The court vacated and remanded for the Board to evaluate whether the dependent claims are similarly anticipated by Slater and the other cited prior art grounds, as the reversal on the independent claims necessarily impacts the validity analysis for dependent claims.

summary.holding: Reversed in part and vacated in part regarding the Board's findings on the Tensile Transfer Limitations and independent claims under the Slater anticipation ground; affirmed the Board's claim constructions on cross-appeal.

cases.case_name: Intercurrency Software LLC v. Askeladden L.L.C.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeals by stipulated agreement of the parties pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b), which permits dismissal when the parties so agree. Each side bears its own costs.

cases.case_name: Rex Medical, L.P. v. Intuitive Surgical, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: The district court excluded Rex's damages expert's reliance on a Covidien license agreement under Daubert gatekeeping because the expert failed to adequately apportion the contribution of the '650 patent versus other patents in the portfolio covered by the $10 million lump-sum settlement. The Federal Circuit affirmed, holding that where a comparable license covers multiple patents, the party must reliably apportion the value attributable to the asserted patent alone.

The district court reduced the jury's $10 million damages award to $1 nominal damages, and the Federal Circuit affirmed because Rex presented no reliable damages evidence at trial—its expert was excluded and only Rex's president testified about the Covidien negotiation without expert analysis. Without admissible damages proof, the jury's award lacked evidentiary support under 35 U.S.C. § 284.

The district court found substantial evidence supported the jury's verdict that Intuitive directly infringed claim 6 of the '650 patent, and the Federal Circuit affirmed this finding on cross-appeal. The claim construction at issue—permitting a jury factual determination whether the accused product's material extended beyond the lower portion—was applied consistently with the evidence.

segments.issue: Invalidity for Lack of Written Description
segments.text: The district court upheld the jury's finding that Intuitive failed to prove by clear and convincing evidence that claim 6 was invalid for lack of written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112, and the Federal Circuit affirmed. The specification's detailed description of the beam structure and its function satisfied the written description requirement.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that under Daubert and Federal Circuit precedent, when a damages expert relies on a comparable license agreement to establish reasonable royalty damages, the expert must reliably apportion the value of that license as between the asserted patent and any other patents or subject matter included in the multi-patent settlement, or the testimony must be excluded. Without such apportionment or alternative reliable damages evidence, a party cannot support a jury damages award and the trial court properly may reduce it to nominal damages. The decision does not materially change existing law but reinforces strict application of apportionment requirements to multi-patent license comparables.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for failure to prosecute pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 30(a)(5), finding that the appellant failed to submit a compliant appendix after receiving a July 14, 2025 Notice of Non-Compliance.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for failure to prosecute due to non-compliance with appendix requirements.

cases.case_name: Electrical Welfare Trust Fund v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims

segments.text: The court affirmed summary judgment against plaintiffs because they failed to establish a cognizable property interest in the funds used to satisfy Transitional Reinsurance Program (TRP) contributions. Under established precedent, money is fungible and the mere obligation to pay money does not constitute a Fifth Amendment taking; the fact that payments came from trust accounts did not transform the monetary obligation into an appropriation of specific funds.

segments.issue: Monetary Obligation vs. Specific Fund Taking
segments.text: The court held that the requirement to pay TRP contributions was a mere obligation to pay a sum of money annually calculated, not an appropriation of specific, identifiable funds. Following Commonwealth Edison Co. v. United States, the court confirmed that regulatory actions requiring payment of money are not compensable takings under the Fifth Amendment, regardless of the source account from which payment is made.

summary.holding: The decision affirms that imposing monetary obligations through legislation—even when funds must come from trust accounts established by federal law—does not trigger Fifth Amendment takings liability because money is fungible and lacks the specific identifiability required for takings claims. This clarifies that trust status or statutory source requirements do not elevate a payment obligation into a cognizable property taking.

Each party was ordered to bear its own costs of the appeal, consistent with the standard allocation when an appeal is dismissed by stipulation under Fed. R. App. P. 42(b).

cases.case_name: Snap Inc. v. You Map, Inc.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's determination that substitute claims 21–40 satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112, finding adequate support in the '727 patent specification for the "combined ranking" step and other limitations present in the substitute claims.

The court affirmed the Board's finding that Feldman does not disclose a request containing a "current zoom level" (as opposed to a "radius"), since the two achieve the same result through different mechanisms, but vacated and remanded the Board's determination that adding "current zoom level" to Feldman would not have been obvious, holding the Board's reasoning inconsistent with KSR's standard and the substantial evidence presented by Snap's expert.

summary.holding: Affirmed in part, vacated in part, and remanded for further proceedings regarding whether substitute claims adding a "current zoom level" limitation would have been obvious over Feldman in light of KSR standards, while affirming compliance with the written description requirement.

cases.case_name: Focus Products Group International, LLC v. Kartri Sales Co., Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York

segments.text: The district court denied appellants' motion to transfer venue as untimely under TC Heartland because appellants failed to raise the objection seasonably, formally submitted to the cause, and actively conducted litigation in the Southern District of New York after TC Heartland was decided. The Federal Circuit affirmed this denial, holding that venue objections may be forfeited through waiver and active litigation participation.

The district court denied appellants' unclean hands affirmative defense as improperly raised on the eve of trial. The Federal Circuit affirmed this denial, confirming that defenses raised too late in litigation may be excluded under rules of civil procedure.

The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's finding of patent infringement by Marquis Mills for the '248 and '609 patents and vacated the '088 patent infringement finding as to Marquis, disagreeing with the district court's claim constructions and infringement analysis on the merits.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that Kartri Sales Co. infringed the '248, '609, and '088 patents based on the district court's claim constructions and infringement determinations.

The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's finding of infringement of Focus's EZ ON trademark mark, determining that the evidence did not support a likelihood of confusion or other trademark infringement liability.
The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's finding that Kartri infringed Focus's HOOKLESS® trademark, requiring further proceedings on remand.
The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's trade dress infringement finding, determining that the shower curtain trade dress claim required further factual or legal development on remand.

The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's determination that appellants' infringement was willful, requiring reconsideration in light of the reversals and vacaturs of specific infringement findings.
The Federal Circuit vacated the award of attorneys' fees to appellees, which was contingent upon the willfulness finding and other infringement determinations that were reversed or vacated.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that venue objections under TC Heartland may be forfeited through delay, formal submission, and active litigation participation, and confirms that affirmative defenses raised too late may be excluded. The decision also demonstrates fact-bound claim construction analysis regarding shower curtain ring designs; the reversals of Marquis's patent infringement (while affirming Kartri's) reflect differing factual findings about which defendant's products actually satisfied the asserted claims' technical limitations. The vacation of willfulness and fees is contingent upon the infringement vacaturs and reversals, showing these remedies depend on underlying infringement liability.

cases.case_name: Underwood v. Bank of America Corporation

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because the case involves only trademark and unfair competition claims, which fall outside the court's limited jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1) and related provisions. The plaintiff's assertion that a pending Trademark Trial and Appeal Board matter was "intertwined" with the district court action was insufficient to establish jurisdiction, and the court declined to transfer the appeal despite the availability of 28 U.S.C. § 1631.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over this appeal and therefore dismissed it, directing the plaintiff to pursue relief in the appropriate regional circuit court (the Tenth Circuit), where the notice of appeal was already docketed.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a). The court held that a habeas corpus petition arising from a district court transfer is outside the Federal Circuit's limited jurisdiction, which extends only to patent cases, PTO review cases, and certain damages claims against the United States not exceeding $10,000.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction; the Federal Circuit lacks authority to hear habeas corpus appeals that do not fall within its statutory subject-matter jurisdictional grants under 28 U.S.C. § 1295.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks subject matter jurisdiction over this appeal because the case involves § 1983 claims against state entities, which fall outside the court's limited appellate jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a). The court's jurisdiction is confined to patent cases, appeals from USPTO proceedings, and certain small damages claims against the United States, none of which apply here.

The court declined to transfer the appeal to another circuit court under 28 U.S.C. § 1631 because no court of appeals would have jurisdiction, as the case remains pending in the district court with no final appealable judgment entered pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1291 and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(b).
The appeal is dismissed, and each party shall bear its own costs.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and declined to transfer it, finding the case involved non-patent § 1983 claims outside the court's statutory authority and that no final appealable judgment had yet been entered in the underlying district court proceeding.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over this appeal because the damages claim exceeds $10,000 and does not arise under patent law or from PTAB review. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1)–(2), the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction is limited to patent cases and certain small damages claims against the United States not exceeding $10,000.

summary.holding: Appeal transferred to the United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1631 due to lack of Federal Circuit jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: In Re VELCRO IP HOLDINGS LLC
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court granted the Acting Director's unopposed motion for remand, conceding that the Patent Trial and Appeal Board erred in its analysis affirming the examiner's rejection of certain claims as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103. The case was remanded to the USPTO for further consideration consistent with the motion and court order.
Each side was ordered to bear its own costs in the appeal.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit granted the USPTO's unopposed motion for remand and vacated the Board's obviousness rejection, requiring reconsideration before the Board.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal as untimely under 28 U.S.C. § 2107 and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(4)(A). Because appellants' "motion for clarification" was not a post-judgment motion that tolled the appeal deadline, their second notice of appeal filed July 9, 2025 fell outside the 60-day window from the Court of Federal Claims' April 8, 2025 order denying reconsideration, and timely filing is a non-waivable jurisdictional requirement.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely notice of appeal.

cases.case_name: Exeltis USA, Inc. v. Lupin Ltd.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit granted the parties' joint motion to dismiss the appeal and remanded to the district court to rule on the parties' motion to amend the final judgment consistent with the district court's August 29, 2025 indicative ruling, following settlement of all claims. The court left the amendment decision to the district court's discretion under Ohio Willow Wood Co. v. Thermo-Ply, Inc., 629 F.3d 1374 (Fed. Cir. 2011).
Each party shall bear its own costs, with no award of costs to either party.

summary.holding: Upon settlement resolving all claims, the Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal and remanded for the district court to rule on amending the judgment, while requiring each party to bear its own costs.

cases.case_name: Warren v. American Broadcasting Companies, Inc.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks subject-matter jurisdiction over this appeal because the underlying trademark, copyright, and breach-of-contract claims do not arise under the patent laws, do not involve review from the USPTO, and do not qualify as certain damages claims against the United States under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a). Pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 3(d)(1), which mandates that a notice of appeal be sent to the court of appeals named in the notice, the appeal is transferred to the Sixth Circuit.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit transferred the appeal to the Sixth Circuit for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: Stewart v. Alfred A. Arraj United States Courthouse

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Mr. Stewart's notice of appeal filed on April 15, 2025 was more than three years late from the district court's January 24, 2022 dismissal order. Under Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), timely filing of a notice of appeal is a jurisdictional requirement in civil cases, and the court and any other appellate court lack jurisdiction over an untimely appeal.

The court dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Stewart's notice of appeal, filed on April 15, 2025, was untimely under the requirement that a notice of appeal in a civil case must be filed within the prescribed period following entry of judgment. The timely filing of a notice of appeal is a jurisdictional requirement under Bowles v. Russell, 551 U.S. 205 (2007), and the notice here was filed more than five months after the November 24, 2024 district court judgment, depriving the Federal Circuit and any other appellate court of jurisdiction.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely notice of appeal.

segments.issue: Appeal Dismissal for Failure to Prosecute
segments.text: The Court of Appeals dismissed the appeal because appellant failed to file the required brief within the time permitted by Federal Circuit Rule 31(a). The dismissal was ordered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit Rules.

cases.case_name: Rideshare Displays, Inc. v. Lyft, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's determination that claims 1–9 and 11–20 of U.S. Patent No. 9,892,637; claims 1, 2, 4, and 6–8 of U.S. Patent No. 10,169,987; claim 1 of U.S. Patent No. 10,395,525; claims 1 and 2 of U.S. Patent No. 10,599,199; and claims 1–5 of U.S. Patent No. 10,748,417 are unpatentable for obviousness. The Board found the claims obvious over prior art references including Kalanick, Lalancette, and Kemler, either alone or in combination.

The Federal Circuit reversed the Board's partial grant of Rideshare's motions to amend substitute claims 29, 31, and 32 of the '637 patent and claims 3 and 4 of the '199 patent, which the Board had previously allowed during the inter partes review proceedings. Lyft's cross-appeal challenging the Board's allowance of these amendments was successful.

summary.holding: The court affirmed the Board's unpatentability findings on all challenged original claims but reversed the Board's allowance of the proposed substitute claims.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Utah

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied petitions for writs of mandamus filed by Nazir Khan and Iftikhar Khan, applying the three-part test from Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 542 U.S. 367, 380–81 (2004) requiring: (1) a clear and indisputable right to relief; (2) no adequate alternative avenue for relief; and (3) that mandamus is appropriate under the circumstances. The court held that to the extent the petitioners sought to relitigate earlier final judgments on patent infringement claims already affirmed on appeal, mandamus does not provide a second opportunity to challenge those judgments, and to the extent they challenged subsequent rulings, they failed to demonstrate that a timely direct appeal would be inadequate.

summary.holding: Petitions for writs of mandamus denied; mandamus is not an appropriate vehicle for relitigating final judgments already affirmed on appeal or for challenging post-judgment rulings when direct appeal remains available.

cases.case_name: Dashti Sanat Logistics and General Contracting v. Army

segments.text: The court lacks jurisdiction to review the Acting Enterprise Head's letter because the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals has not issued a final decision from which an appeal may be taken, petitioner has not sought or demonstrated entitlement to interlocutory review, and petitioner has not established jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295 for a direct appeal from the letter. The court affirmed that 28 U.S.C. § 1631 permits transfer only to another court, not to an administrative tribunal, making petitioner's request for transfer to the Board procedurally improper.

The petition for review is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction and because petitioner failed to establish a viable alternative basis for this court's review or to identify a permissible forum with jurisdiction over its claims. Each party bears its own costs.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over a petition challenging a letter from the Department of the Army's Acting Enterprise Head where the underlying matter remains pending before the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals without a final decision, and the court cannot transfer the case to an administrative tribunal under § 1631.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Chowdhury failed to file his notice of appeal within the 60-day deadline prescribed by 28 U.S.C. §§ 2107(b) and 2522. Timely filing is a non-waivable jurisdictional requirement that is not subject to equitable tolling, and Chowdhury's notice filed 100 days after judgment was untimely.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely notice of appeal.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Chowdhury filed his notice of appeal 274 days after the Court of Federal Claims entered judgment, exceeding the 60-day deadline under 28 U.S.C. §§ 2107(b), 2522 and Fed. R. App. P. 4(a)(1)(B). Timely filing is a non-waivable jurisdictional requirement not subject to equitable tolling under Marandola v. United States, 518 F.3d 913 (Fed. Cir. 2008).

The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a). The court held that federal tax-related claims do not fall within the Federal Circuit's limited jurisdiction, which extends only to patent cases, USPTO review cases, and certain damages claims against the United States not exceeding $10,000. The Tenth Circuit was the proper appellate forum, and dismissal was appropriate because an appeal from the same judgment was already pending there.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over this federal tax dispute and therefore dismissed the appeal.

cases.case_name: Interactive Communications International, Inc. v. Blackhawk Network, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal of InComm's appeal for lack of standing under Article III. InComm failed to demonstrate a concrete and particularized injury-in-fact because Blackhawk's covenants not to sue encompassed all past infringing activity InComm identified, InComm ceased the relevant product sales by March 2025 with no plans for future activity, and InComm presented no evidence of concrete plans for future activity creating a substantial risk of infringement.

The court rejected InComm's argument that alleged collateral and statutory estoppel effects from the Board's decision conferred standing, holding that potential collateral consequences or estoppel implications cannot, on their own, provide a sufficient basis for Article III standing.

The court granted Blackhawk's motion to file a sur-sur-reply, reasoning that because the filing responded to new arguments in a court-directed filing and InComm had an opportunity to respond, consideration of the sur-sur-reply was appropriate.

summary.holding: Blackhawk's motion to dismiss for lack of standing is granted, and the appeal is dismissed because InComm failed to establish Article III standing, as covenants not to sue eliminated any injury-in-fact from past activities and InComm demonstrated no concrete plans for future infringing activity.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Louisiana

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied mandamus relief requiring a hearing on Williams's motion to appear pro hac vice, holding that Evans v. Fifth Circuit (which required a hearing on pre-trial pro hac vice motions) does not extend to post-trial admissions sought by an attorney who testified at trial and whom the district court found engaged in inequitable conduct. The court found Williams lacked a clear and indisputable right to the requested relief under the circumstances.

The court held that Williams has an adequate alternative remedy through appeal following entry of final judgment, satisfying the requirement under Cheney v. U.S. District Court for D.C. that a petitioner show no other adequate avenue for relief exists before mandamus will issue. The court noted that ordinary procedure allows a party to raise denial of pro hac vice admission in an appeal from final judgment.

summary.holding: The petition for a writ of mandamus is denied because Williams failed to satisfy the requirements for mandamus relief, including demonstrating a clear and indisputable right to a hearing on his pro hac vice motion and establishing the absence of an adequate alternative remedy through appeal.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The Federal Circuit vacated the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims' decision and remanded with instructions to dismiss based on mootness. The Secretary's amendment to the regulation at issue gave Hambidge the relief he sought, mooting the appeal under the standard from United States v. Munsingwear, Inc., 340 U.S. 36 (1950).
The court ordered each party to bear its own costs, departing from a default rule that might award costs to the prevailing party.

cases.case_name: Cascades Branding Innovation LLC v. Aldi, Inc.

segments.text: The court affirmed the district court's determination that all claims of the three asserted patents (the '395, '766, and '504 patents) are patent-ineligible abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and the Alice two-step framework. At Alice step one, the claims are directed to the abstract idea of collecting geographic information about device location and nearby stores and displaying that information; at step two, the claims lack an inventive concept because they recite only generic functional steps using conventional computer technology such as GPS and touchscreen displays, with no technological details or improvements over existing mapping systems.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of leave to amend and dismissal with prejudice under Fed. R. Civ. P. 12(b)(6) and 15(a)(2). The court held that amendment would be futile as a matter of law because the patent-eligibility defect under § 101 cannot be cured by additional allegations of fact from the specification, prosecution history, expert declarations, or evidence of licensing success, given the abstract nature of the claimed invention.

The Board sustained the charge of failure to safeguard Personally Identifiable Information because Mr. Spyropoulos conceded to making "four or five inadvertent PII violations" and sent at least nine emails containing claimant information outside of SSA custody. Under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c), proof of one or more supporting specifications is sufficient to sustain a charge, and substantial evidence supports the finding.

The Board sustained the lack of candor charge under Ludlum v. Department of Justice, 278 F.3d 1280 (Fed. Cir. 2002), finding that Mr. Spyropoulos knowingly made misrepresentations or omissions regarding his email practices. Substantial evidence supported the determination that he made false statements about ceasing to send work-related emails outside of SSA custody when he continued to do so from April through May 2015.

The Board sustained the charge of misuse of position, finding that Mr. Spyropoulos leveraged nonpublic information learned in his employment regarding how to successfully prosecute disability claims and shared it with a third-party attorney in exchange for assistance with his application for a family-court position.

The Board sustained the charge of misuse of government property based on Mr. Spyropoulos's sending emails from his work account containing a confidentiality agreement and material transfer agreement related to his personal business to outside email accounts, thereby using his work account to further personal business interests.

The Board vacated the portion of the initial decision addressing whether the agency would have removed Mr. Spyropoulos absent protected disclosures because the administrative judge found that Mr. Spyropoulos failed to establish that he made any "protected disclosure" within the meaning of 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8), thereby eliminating the need to address the alternative causation analysis.

The Board affirmed that removal was the appropriate penalty under the Douglas v. Veterans Administration factors, finding the disciplinary action reasonable given the sustained charges involving security violations and lack of candor.

The Federal Circuit reaffirmed that it reviews Board conclusions of law de novo, findings of fact for substantial evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c), and that the petitioner bears the burden of establishing error in the Board's decision.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision sustaining Mr. Spyropoulos's removal from employment at the Social Security Administration for failure to safeguard Personally Identifiable Information, lack of candor, misuse of position, and misuse of government property, as each charge was supported by substantial evidence and at least one specification under applicable law.

segments.issue: Appeal Dismissal for Failure to Prosecute
segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for failure to comply with Federal Circuit Rule 31(a), which requires timely filing of an appellant's brief. The court exercised its authority to dismiss appeals where the appellant fails to prosecute in accordance with the rules of appellate procedure.

The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review the MSPB's dismissal because it was not a final order. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(9), this court may only review final decisions of the Board; dismissal without prejudice allowing refiling is an intermediate order that does not satisfy the finality requirement, following Strausbaugh v. Merit Systems Protection Board, 401 F. App'x 524, 526 (Fed. Cir. 2010).

summary.holding: The petition for review is dismissed for lack of jurisdiction, and each party bears its own costs.

segments.text: The court determined that even if Mr. Seda raised a discrimination claim constituting a "mixed case" under 5 U.S.C. § 7702, district courts—not the Federal Circuit—have jurisdiction over such cases pursuant to 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2). The court noted it need not definitively resolve whether a mixed case was presented because the petition was untimely regardless.

The court dismissed the petition as untimely because Mr. Seda filed more than 600 days after the Merit Systems Protection Board's final decision, far exceeding the 30 or 60-day filing deadline under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)–(2). The court found Mr. Seda failed to demonstrate the prerequisites for equitable tolling—diligent pursuit of rights and an extraordinary circumstance—as required under Pace v. DiGuglielmo.
The court denied Mr. Seda's motion to transfer the case to district court under 28 U.S.C. § 1631, rendering the transfer request moot given the dismissal on timeliness grounds.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the petition for review as untimely filed, exceeding the statutory deadline by over 600 days without sufficient basis for equitable tolling.

cases.case_name: Hmtx Industries LLC v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed USTR's authority to modify its original Section 301 action by imposing escalatory tariffs on List 3 and List 4A under Section 307(a)(1)(C), which permits modification of discretionary actions that are no longer appropriate. The court declined to address whether Section 307(a)(1)(B)'s "increased or decreased" burden standard independently authorized the modifications, finding Section 307(a)(1)(C) as the dispositive statutory basis.

The court affirmed that USTR's remand redetermination, produced after the trial court ordered further explanation of how USTR considered significant public comments, satisfied the Administrative Procedure Act's requirements for notice-and-comment rulemaking and supplied the necessary clarification regarding the modified tariff actions. The court upheld the trial court's remand order as lawful and USTR's compliance with it as adequate.

summary.holding: The decision clarifies that Section 307(a)(1)(C) of the Trade Act of 1974—permitting modification of discretionary Section 301 actions when they are "no longer appropriate"—provides independent statutory authority for USTR to escalate tariff actions in response to changed circumstances, and that supplemental explanations on remand can cure APA deficiencies in original agency determinations regarding trade actions. This precedent may influence future trade remedy litigation involving statutory interpretation of modification authority under Section 307.

cases.case_name: Apex Bank v. Cc Serve Corp.

segments.text: The Board's finding that the parties' services are highly similar, even partially legally identical, was affirmed because the Board properly analyzed credit card services against banking and financing services and substantial evidence supports that the services are related such that they could emanate from a single source under one mark.

The Board erred by narrowing the relevant universe of third-party marks to only those for credit card services while excluding marks for other banking and financing services, when the Board's own second-factor analysis had found the services highly similar; the court vacated and remanded for reconsideration of the appropriate scope of similar marks eligible for consideration.

The Board's analysis of mark similarity in appearance, sound, connotation and commercial impression was vacated and remanded for reconsideration because the Board's reassessment of the sixth DuPont factor—which relates to commercial strength—may alter the overall commercial impression analysis under the first factor.

summary.holding: The decision confirms that DuPont factor analysis requires internal consistency: when the Board determines services are highly similar under the second factor, it must apply the same scope of similarity when evaluating third-party marks under the sixth factor, rather than imposing a narrower definition that contradicts its earlier findings. This establishes that trademark weakness analysis cannot artificially restrict the relevant market based on service subcategories when the Board has already determined broader similarity.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's denial of judgment as a matter of law (JMOL) and held that Finesse failed to prove the accused radios sample a passband containing both "signals of interest" and "interference generating signals" as required by limitation 1(a) of claim 1 of the '134 patent. The infringement expert's testimony was confusing and self-contradictory, first mapping the claimed signals to the DL(TX) reference and modeled PIM path, then attempting to pivot to x1 and x2 without clear explanation, and substantial evidence does not support the jury's infringement verdict under these circumstances.

The Federal Circuit vacated the jury's damages award of $166,303,391 in lump-sum damages as a consequence of reversing the infringement verdict on the '134 patent and the asserted claims of the '775 patent, which were dependent on a finding of infringement.

summary.holding: This decision reinforces that a party bearing the burden of proving infringement must establish through clear, non-contradictory expert testimony how an accused product's components map onto claimed limitations, and self-contradictory or confusing expert testimony that shifts its theory under cross-examination cannot support an infringement verdict. The case does not establish new legal doctrine but applies existing substantial evidence and JMOL standards rigorously to fact-intensive infringement analysis.

cases.case_name: Bayer Pharma Aktiengesellschaft v. Mylan Pharmaceuticals Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court held that "clinically proven effective" is a functionally unrelated limitation that cannot rescue an otherwise anticipated claim, even if the phrase is construed as limiting and requires clinical proof of efficacy. Applying the functional-relationship test from King Pharmaceuticals, the court reasoned that clinical proof of efficacy does not transform the underlying method of administering specified dosages, and thus cannot claw back an anticipated treatment method from the public domain merely by referencing subsequent trial results.

The court reversed the Board's construction that "first product comprising rivaroxaban and aspirin" could encompass separate dosage forms, holding instead that the plain language requires a single dosage form containing both drugs. The court concluded that the Board's reading violated the basic principle of giving effect to all terms in the claim and was inconsistent with the specification, which distinguishes between combination therapy using separate dosage forms and the claimed "first product."

The court vacated and remanded the Board's anticipation finding as to claims 1–2 based on Foley, concluding that because the Board improperly construed "first product" to encompass separate dosage forms and failed to properly address the functionally unrelated nature of "clinically proven effective," the factual findings underlying the anticipation rejection could not stand and required reconsideration.

The court vacated the Board's obviousness rejections of claims 1–8 over Foley and Plosker and remanded for reconsideration, finding that the Board's reasoning relied on flawed claim constructions and did not adequately articulate why a skilled artisan would have had a reasonable expectation of success in combining the references or whether clinical efficacy constituted an unexpected result.

summary.holding: The decision clarifies that functional-relationship analysis, established in King Pharmaceuticals for instructional limitations, extends to result-oriented limitations such as "clinically proven effective" in method-of-treatment claims, preventing patentees from reclaiming anticipated methods by adding novel but functionally unrelated descriptors. The court also confirms that claim language containing a noun of art (here, "product") must be given its plain, ordinary meaning, requiring a single dosage form rather than multiple components, and established that when claim construction errors pervade the Board's underlying factual findings, those findings cannot stand on appeal.

cases.case_name: Lambeth Magnetic Structures, LLC v. Seagate Technology (Us) Holdings Inc.

segments.text: The court held that the district court erred in construing "uniaxial symmetry broken structure" as "a structure that is uniaxial as a result of the structure being symmetry broken." summary.holding: The district court's judgment of noninfringement was vacated due to erroneous claim construction; Seagate's cross-appeal was dismissed as improper for lack of jurisdiction; and the case was remanded for a new trial on both infringement and enablement under the correct claim construction.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's rejection of claims 1–15 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) for lack of adequate written description support for the negative limitation "free of germanium." The specification must reasonably convey to skilled artisans that the inventor possessed the claimed subject matter, and for negative limitations, there must be something in the specification describing a reason to exclude the relevant element; silence generally is not sufficient disclosure.

summary.holding: Affirmed. The Board correctly applied the written description standard and its conclusion that the original disclosure lacked adequate support for the "germanium-free" negative limitation was supported by substantial evidence, as the specification contained only a cursory reference to germanium in a comparative alloy and failed to distinguish germanium as an alternative element or suggest the inventor intended to exclude it from the claimed composition.

cases.case_name: Ng LLC v. Createdhair Designs, LLC

segments.text: The court affirmed the district court's construction of "the wig grip apparatus terminates at the forward periphery" to mean that the forward periphery of the mesh element is the most forward portion of the wig grip apparatus. The court applied de novo review of claim construction based on intrinsic evidence (Phillips standard) and found that the plain claim language, specification, and prosecution history all supported this construction, rendering NG's broader alternative interpretation meaningless.

The court affirmed application of prosecution history estoppel to bar NG's doctrine of equivalents argument. The narrowing amendment was added during prosecution to overcome prior art rejections by emphasizing "the extension of the middle mesh section of the instant invention to the forward edge of the wig grip apparatus" as a distinguishing feature, making the rebuttal claim that the amendment was only tangentially related to the accused infringement unpersuasive under Festo.

The court affirmed summary judgment of non-infringement as to the asserted claims of U.S. Patent Nos. 10,945,477 and 10,881,159. Because NG conceded no literal infringement under the correct claim construction and prosecution history estoppel barred the doctrine of equivalents, no infringement theory remained viable.

summary.holding: Affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment of non-infringement.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit granted Foto Electric's motion to dismiss its own appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), finding it no longer necessary based on Marut Enterprises' continued inaction. Each party was ordered to bear its own costs.

The court affirmed the Board's determination that Edwards's reconsideration request was untimely filed. Edwards argued for the first time on appeal that she had timely faxed the request on August 24, 2020, but the court held that because she never raised this fax argument before the administrative judge and provided no supporting evidence, the Board properly declined to consider it under 5 C.F.R. § 1201.114(a)(4), which prohibits new evidence after the record closes unless it is new, material, and not readily available beforehand.

The court affirmed OPM's and the Board's denial of Edwards's request to waive the 30-day reconsideration deadline. Under the two-step standard in Azarkhish v. OPM, 915 F.2d 675, Edwards bore the burden to prove by preponderance of evidence that she either lacked notice of the deadline or was prevented by circumstances beyond her control from filing timely. The court held that the Board's finding that COVID-19 restrictions and Edwards's illnesses did not prevent her from accessing the post office—evidenced by her successful visits on August 5 and August 24—was supported by substantial evidence under the deferential standard of 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c).

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's affirmance of OPM's dismissal of Edwards's untimely and unwaived reconsideration request for disability retirement was affirmed, as the reconsideration request postmarked August 24 and received August 27, 2020 fell outside the 30-day deadline, Edwards failed to present her fax argument before the administrative judge, and she failed to meet her burden of proving circumstances beyond her control prevented timely filing.

cases.case_name: Motorola Mobility LLC v. Largan Precision Co., Ltd.

segments.text: The Board found insufficient motivation for a skilled artisan to combine Chung's lens system with Sekine's R1/f teaching based on multiple factual grounds: significant differences in lens polarity between the systems, Sekine's disclosure of an inferior lens system with poorer image quality and field of view, and the inapplicability of Sekine's track-length teachings to Chung's embodiments. The Federal Circuit affirmed, finding these factual findings were supported by substantial evidence and that the Board's comparison of embodiment differences directly addressed Motorola's asserted balancing motivation.

summary.holding: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision upholding claims 1–27 of U.S. Patent No. 9,696,519 is affirmed; Motorola failed to prove the claims unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over the cited references because it did not establish a motivation to combine Chung with Sekine's teachings.

segments.text: The Board's finding that Ms. Russell failed to establish she made protected whistleblowing disclosures is supported by substantial evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c). The administrative judge's credibility determinations—that Ms. McGovern did not recall an oral disclosure and that the email disclosure was vague and lacked supporting documentation—are virtually unreviewable on appeal, and Ms. Russell failed to meet the high burden of showing the testimony was inherently improbable or contradicted by undisputed evidence.

Ms. Russell's challenge to a purported gap in the hearing testimony recording is rejected because she failed to demonstrate a significant gap existed or that she was prejudiced by any missing information. Under the standard articulated in Harp v. Department of Army, 791 F.2d 161 (Fed. Cir. 1986), speculative assertions of prejudice without identification of specific testimony are insufficient to overturn the Board's findings.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's final order denying Ms. Russell's request for corrective action in her individual right of action whistleblower appeal is affirmed because the Board's decision was in accordance with law and supported by substantial evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c).

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the petition for lack of jurisdiction, holding that it lacks authority over mixed cases (cases involving both MSPB and non-MSPB claims). cases.case_name: Dynamite Marketing, Inc. v. the Wowline, Inc.

segments.text: Sherman lacked standing to appeal Cooper's inventorship counterclaim because Sherman was not a party to that claim before the district court and Cooper, the losing counterclaim-plaintiff, did not appeal. Under the general rule, only parties to a judgment may appeal, and an assignment of patent rights does not confer independent appellate rights over claims to which the assignee was not a party. The court dismissed this portion of the appeal for lack of jurisdiction.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of Sherman's post-verdict motion challenging the jury's finding that the D877 Patent was not obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103. The jury's determination that the patent was valid was supported by substantial evidence, and Sherman failed to demonstrate clear error in the district court's evidentiary rulings or instructions.

The court affirmed the jury's and district court's determinations that the D877 Patent was not invalid as a primarily functional design. Sherman's arguments that the design's elements were merely functional rather than ornamental were rejected on the merits by the jury and upheld by the district court.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of Sherman's post-verdict motion on non-infringement and affirmed the jury's finding of willful infringement of the D877 Patent. Sherman's Original TOL4 products clearly infringed, and the Redesigned TOL4 products also infringed despite the minor design modifications made after receiving cease-and-desist letters.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of remittitur or a new trial on the jury's lost profit damages award of $1,850,000. The damages award was supported by substantial evidence and fell within the range of reasonable verdicts given the record evidence of Sherman's infringement and sales.

The court affirmed the district court's grant of attorney's fees to Dynamite in the amount of $1,536,644.27, plus prejudgment interest of $148,673.06, for a total of $3,535,317.33. The district court properly exercised its discretion under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in awarding fees as part of an exceptional case involving willful infringement.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed Sherman's appeal regarding the inventorship counterclaim for lack of jurisdiction but affirmed all other rulings: the validity of the D877 Patent, the finding of willful infringement, the damages award, and the attorney's fees award.

The court declined to consider arguments Faris raised for the first time on appeal rather than before the administrative judge, including his claim of unknowing and involuntary entry into the LCA and his challenge to the USPS time-conversion methodology for calculating AWOL hours, consistent with the requirement that MSPB issues be raised before the administrative judge to be preserved for appeal.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's two final orders dismissing Faris's appeals for lack of jurisdiction were affirmed in their entirety.

The court declined to address whether transfer was also appropriate under 28 U.S.C. § 1406(a), as it had already determined VirtaMove lacked a right to mandamus relief under § 1404(a) and therefore reached no need to consider the alternative statutory ground.

cases.case_name: Future Link Systems, LLC v. Realtek Semiconductor Corporation
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas

segments.text: The court held that Realtek is a prevailing party under 35 U.S.C. § 285, entitling it to recover attorney fees, because the district court's conversion of Future Link's voluntary dismissal into a dismissal with prejudice constitutes a judicially sanctioned material alteration of the legal relationship between the parties. Following Highway Equipment, Raniere, B.E. Technology, and United Cannabis, a defendant prevails when it rebuffs plaintiff's claim, regardless of whether judgment is rendered on the merits, so long as the dismissal is with prejudice.

The court held that the district court erred in failing to address Realtek's request for costs under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1) in the 363 case, as the court must award costs to the prevailing party unless a federal statute, rule, or court order provides otherwise. Because Realtek qualifies as the prevailing party, it is entitled to recover costs on remand absent statutory or rule-based exception.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of Rule 11 sanctions, holding that the district court did not err in refusing to award such sanctions against Future Link despite the objectively baseless nature of the litigation.
The court affirmed the district court's denial of attorney fees under 28 U.S.C. § 1927 in both cases, holding that the court did not err in refusing this alternative basis for fee recovery.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of Realtek's discovery requests regarding confidentiality designations and protective order relief, noting that most of Realtek's requests were rendered irrelevant on appeal and the sole remaining relevant request was properly denied.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies Federal Circuit precedent that a defendant qualifies as a 'prevailing party' under 35 U.S.C. § 285 and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 54(d)(1) when it obtains a dismissal with prejudice, even absent a judgment on the merits, so long as it has effectively rebuffed the plaintiff's attempt to materially alter their legal relationship. The holding reaffirms and applies settled law established in Highway Equipment, Raniere, B.E. Technology, and United Cannabis, confirming that the touchstone is material alteration and that a favorable ruling on the merits is not prerequisite for prevailing party status.

segments.text: Commerce properly rejected Corinth's submitted cost data and employed facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e based on multiple deficiencies across three questionnaire responses. Corinth failed to provide a single, complete reconciliation of its cost of manufacture to its accounting system as requested, instead submitting incomplete and fragmented reconciliations with double-counted costs and unexplained methodology, justifying Commerce's reliance on adverse inferences rather than the submitted information.

Commerce properly applied an adverse inference in reaching its final determination by assigning Corinth a significantly higher dumping margin after rejecting the submitted data. Under the antidumping statute, when a respondent fails to comply with Commerce's information requests despite multiple opportunities and supplemental questionnaires, Commerce may use an adverse inference as part of its facts-otherwise-available determination.

segments.issue: Standard of Review for Commerce Determinations
segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of International Trade's decision sustaining Commerce's final determination, applying the standard of review requiring affirmance unless Commerce's action was unsupported by substantial evidence or violated the Administrative Procedure Act. The court found substantial evidence supported Commerce's factual findings regarding deficiencies in Corinth's responses and the unreliability of the submitted cost data.

summary.holding: This decision confirms that Commerce has substantial discretion under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e to reject cost data submitted by respondents in antidumping administrative reviews when the data is incomplete, inadequately reconciled to accounting records, or contains methodological deficiencies, even when the respondent has made multiple submission attempts. The opinion clarifies that Commerce need not accept voluminous, fragmented worksheets lacking clear methodology or adequate explanation as reliable cost information, and may properly employ an adverse inference in such circumstances without violating the Administrative Procedure Act or the antidumping statute.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; the Federal Circuit may only review challenges to the validity or interpretation of statutes and regulations, and constitutional issues, but not factual determinations or application of law to the particular facts of a case.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

The court dismissed appellants' request for a patent term adjustment as beyond its jurisdiction, holding that patent term adjustments apply only to issued patents under 35 U.S.C. § 154(b), and that any challenge to such an adjustment must be brought in the Eastern District of Virginia. Since no patent had issued from the application, the Federal Circuit lacked subject-matter jurisdiction over this claim.

The court dismissed as moot appellants' request for a ruling that a notice of abandonment was improper, finding that the Patent Office subsequently granted appellants' petition to revive the application, eliminating the need for judicial review of the abandonment notice.

The court denied appellants' request for costs associated with filing a petition to revive their application, holding that the request was forfeited because appellants cited no legal authority supporting an entitlement to such costs and had not requested costs from either the Patent Office or the Board.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's rejection of patent application claims over prior-art references, holding that applicants failed to satisfy statutory and regulatory requirements for claiming priority by omitting application numbers from their Application Data Sheets and missing the deadline to cure the deficiency. The court dismissed as moot and beyond its jurisdiction requests for relief concerning notice of abandonment and patent term adjustment, and denied a request for costs as forfeited.

The court rejected Gladden's argument that the government and Board improperly considered a previous sexual harassment charge and resulting settlement in the removal decision. Substantial evidence from government decisionmaker testimony supported the Board's finding that the removal decision was not based on the prior charge and settlement.

The court rejected Gladden's claim that he failed to meet his burden of proof due to psychological distress or lack of opportunity to present his defense, noting that Gladden himself conceded he "simply did not meet [his] burden of proof" and the record showed he was given full opportunity to present evidence both to the government and the Board.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in four inter partes review proceedings (IPR2022-00847, IPR2023-00123, IPR2023-00129, and IPR2022-00848). The court applied Federal Circuit Rule 36, which permits affirmance of PTAB decisions without opinion when no judge requests oral argument or written explanation.

summary.holding: The PTAB's inter partes review decisions are affirmed in all respects.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the district court's denial of plaintiffs' Rule 60(b) motion seeking relief from a previously affirmed sanctions award of $213,765. The mandate rule barred reconsideration of the sanctions award because it was explicitly affirmed on appeal despite the court's subsequent finding that Spota LLC had standing, since the affirmance rested on no clear error in the district court's findings of bad faith conduct including failure to timely disclose ownership documents and misrepresentation of patent status in the amended complaint.

The court rejected plaintiffs' argument that the sanctionable misconduct was harmless because the defendants could have obtained summary judgment on standing grounds had disclosure been timely. The district court's sanctions were properly based on a course of bad faith conduct—including failure to satisfy discovery obligations regarding the December 2021 patent assignment, denials of document existence, and blatant misrepresentation in the Fourth Amended Complaint—regardless of whether the ultimate outcome on standing would have changed, as the misconduct affected the posture and timing of the case.

The Federal Circuit denied defendants' motion for additional sanctions under Fed. R. App. P. 38, finding that although the appeal lacked merit, it was not so wholly frivolous as to warrant further sanctions.
The court awarded costs but not attorney fees to the defendants-appellees.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the district court's denial of Rule 60(b) relief from a sanctions award previously affirmed on appeal, holding that the mandate rule precluded reconsideration and that the sanctions were properly grounded in findings of bad faith conduct independent of the ultimate standing determination.

segments.issue: Removal for Failure to Satisfy Condition of Employment

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's final decision sustaining Ms. Rose's removal from her Air Force IT specialist position for failure to meet a condition of employment (IA Certification) was supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law, and the Board properly conducted an independent Douglas-factor analysis where the agency failed to consider such factors prior to the adverse action.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court reversed the Board's rejection of claims 10-18 as ineligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, holding that apparatus and system claims reciting a computer system running software fall within a statutorily provided category (machine) and therefore require application of the full Alice/Mayo two-step framework rather than categorical exclusion for lacking structure. The specification's disclosure of a computer system with hardware (CPUs, servers, processors) and software constitutes sufficient tangible structure for § 101 threshold purposes, and the alleged generic nature of such structure does not render it nonexistent for this inquiry.

The court vacated and remanded the Board's rejection of claims 10-17 as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b), rejecting the application of IPXL Holdings' prohibition on single claims covering both apparatus and method of use based on the court's reconsideration of that precedent in light of modern claim-drafting practices and the statutory framework for means-plus-function claims under § 112(f).

The court held that claims 10-18 invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f) means-plus-function treatment despite lacking the word 'means,' because the term 'subsystem' is a nonce word devoid of particular structure followed by functional language, and the specification discloses corresponding structure in the form of a computer system with specified hardware components and software executing a decision matrix. This structural correspondence supports the § 101 eligibility analysis and undermines the indefiniteness rejection.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit reversed in part, vacated in part, and remanded patent application claims 10-18, holding that they are not categorically barred under § 101 as ineligible software, and remanding for Alice/Mayo analysis on the merits, while also vacating the § 112(b) indefiniteness rejection based on IPXL Holdings and the applicability of § 112(f) means-plus-function interpretation.

segments.issue: Jurisdiction to Review Veterans Court Decision
segments.text: The court dismissed the appeal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction. Under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(c)-(d), the Federal Circuit may only review challenges to the validity of statutes or regulations, and may not review factual determinations or application of law to particular facts unless a colorable constitutional question is presented; Mr. Miller's arguments challenged factual matters (whether he received certain documents) and application of law to facts, and his vague constitutional claim was not colorably presented.

The court affirmed the Veterans Court's upholding of the Board's assignment of an effective date of March 9, 1994. The Board properly determined that Mr. Miller could not obtain an earlier effective date because he failed to appeal the 1976 denial, the 1978 Board decision became final, and he did not respond to the 1980 letter requesting new and material evidence to reopen his claim.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction, as Mr. Miller's arguments presented only factual challenges and application-of-law claims beyond the court's statutory authority to review, and his constitutional argument was not colorably presented.

cases.case_name: Dasso International, Inc. v. MOSO North America, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. The Claims Court lacks jurisdiction over claims against entities other than the United States, over tort claims, and over claims based on the Fourth Amendment, Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment, or Thirteenth Amendment, pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1491. Appellant's complaint primarily challenged actions by New York state officials and asserted only tort and constitutional claims without identifying a money-mandating source of law against the United States.

summary.holding: The Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed for lack of jurisdiction where the complaint's primary allegations targeted state officials rather than the United States and where the asserted claims—including tort claims and those based on non-money-mandating constitutional provisions—fall outside the Claims Court's limited jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1491.

cases.case_name: Largan Precision Co., Ltd. v. Motorola Mobility LLC
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision in IPR2022-01156. The court's affirmance was entered summarily pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 36, indicating the decision was not precedential and the issues lacked substantial question.

summary.holding: The Board's IPR decision was affirmed without precedential effect.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's finding that although Mr. Stenson engaged in protected disclosures and activities under 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)–(b)(9), the Department of Justice presented clear and convincing evidence under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e)(2) that it would have taken the same personnel actions absent those protected activities. The Board's application of the Carr factors—evaluating the strength of the agency's evidence, motive to retaliate, and consistency with treatment of similarly situated non-whistleblowers—was supported by substantial evidence of Mr. Stenson's unprofessional conduct.

The court rejected Mr. Stenson's requests to reweigh the evidence and confirmed that under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c), the Board's factual findings need only be supported by substantial evidence—relevant evidence that a reasonable mind might accept as adequate—not by the strongest evidence or only one reasonable conclusion. The court found no basis to overturn the Board's findings regarding Mr. Stenson's reckless accusations, unprofessional conduct, and the contributing-factor analysis.

The court upheld the administrative judge's discretionary admission of hearsay evidence from supervisors regarding Mr. Stenson's workplace conduct, finding no legal error and noting that hearsay is long-settled as admissible in administrative proceedings and that procedural evidentiary matters fall within the sound discretion of the Board. Mr. Stenson did not demonstrate an abuse of that discretion under the particular circumstances.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's decision denying Mr. Stenson's Individual Right of Action appeal for whistleblower retaliation was affirmed because, although Mr. Stenson made protected disclosures and engaged in protected activity under the Whistleblower Protection Act, 5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)–(b)(9), the agency presented clear and convincing evidence that it would have taken the same personnel actions based on his documented unprofessional conduct, independent of any retaliatory motive.

cases.case_name: Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd. v. Power2b, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the Board's construction of "detector assembly" as requiring "two or more detector elements." Under claim differentiation doctrine, since dependent claims expressly require plural detector elements while independent claims do not, the independent claims require only at least one detector element. The specification's description of preferred embodiments with multiple detector elements does not justify narrowing the independent claims without clear intent to limit scope.

The Board's implied construction requiring detector assembly to be arranged at "one edge" was upheld as part of the proper claim interpretation. The claims contain express language requiring arrangement at "at least one edge" or "an edge," which the Board correctly applied to determine whether prior art references satisfied the edge limitation.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's finding that detector assembly claims 15–18, 21, 22, 26 and 30 of the '850 patent and claims 26, 29, 36–38, 44–46, 48, 49, and 56–58 of the '093 patent were not shown to be unpatentable. With the corrected claim construction, the asserted Reime prior art was found insufficient to disclose a detector assembly arranged at a single edge as required by the claims.

The Board construed claims directed to object position sensing to include responsiveness to an object's touch and found these claims disclosed by prior art. Power2B's cross-appeal argument that these claims should exclude touching and that the Board's obviousness findings lacked substantial evidence required review on the merits.

The Federal Circuit reversed the Board and found claims 31 and 41 of the '850 patent and claims 1, 5, 8, and 12–13 of the '093 patent were unpatentable, as cross-appealed by Power2B. The decision was remanded for further proceedings consistent with the revised claim constructions and legal standards applied.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed-in-part, reversed-in-part, vacated-in-part, and remanded the Board's inter partes review decision. The Court reversed the Board's construction of "detector assembly" to require only at least one detector element, not two or more, based on claim differentiation doctrine. The Court affirmed that detector assembly claims were not shown unpatentable under the corrected construction. The Court reversed the Board's holdings of unpatentability for certain object position sensing claims.
