segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the entire appeal pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) based on the parties' agreement to dismiss the proceeding. The dismissal was entered as a nonprecedential order with each party bearing its own costs.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's rejection of claims 77–83 and 85–94 under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a) for failing to provide adequate written description. The court held that although claim 77 recites a specific amino acid sequence for CDR3, it imposes no comparable structural limitations on CDR1 and CDR2 regions, making the claimed VHH antigen-binding protein genus broad, while the specification discloses only one protein meeting all claim limitations and no common structural features across the genus, falling short of the written description requirement established in Ariad Pharms., Inc. v. Eli Lilly & Co.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's rejection of claims 77–83 and 85–94 of U.S. Patent Application 16/282,082 for lack of adequate written description under 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), finding the specification fails to convey possession of the broad genus of VHH antigen-binding proteins claimed.

segments.text: The Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over McCrory's claim because 26 U.S.C. § 7623(a) and its implementing regulations at 26 C.F.R. § 301.7623-1–4 are discretionary, not money-mandating. A statute or regulation is money-mandating for jurisdictional purposes only if it can fairly be interpreted as mandating compensation for damages sustained as a result of breach of duties it imposes, and § 7623(a) grants the Secretary discretionary authority to pay awards with no statutory entitlement to monetary damages.

The 2014 promulgation of regulations at 26 C.F.R. § 301.7623-1–4 did not transform the discretionary nature of § 7623(a) into a money-mandating provision. The regulation's language providing for the WBO to "pay all awards" under § 7623(a)—as opposed to "determine and pay" under the mandatory § 7623(b)—reflects and reinforces the differing legal treatment between discretionary and mandatory award schemes and does not create an enforceable statutory entitlement.

Section 7623's specific statutory scheme, which provides for judicial review in Tax Court for certain claims meeting the § 7623(b) threshold, excludes relief under the general terms of the Tucker Act. The fact that § 7623(a) claimants may lack recourse to judicial review if they fail to satisfy the § 7623(b)(5) thresholds does not prevent this preemption, as Congress contemplated this result.

summary.holding: Affirmed the dismissal for lack of jurisdiction because § 7623(a) and its implementing regulations are discretionary rather than money-mandating, and thus the Court of Federal Claims has no jurisdiction to review whistleblower awards under the Tucker Act.

cases.case_name: Tau-Ken Temir LLP v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The Court vacated Commerce's rejection of Tau-Ken's September 16 submission as untimely filed 1 hour 41 minutes past the 8:30 a.m. deadline. Commerce had not decided Tau-Ken's timely-filed one-day-extension request before the deadline, triggering an automatic extension policy under 19 U.S.C. § 1671b and Commerce's established procedures, which entitled Tau-Ken to rely on that automatic extension.

The Court addressed Commerce's use of adverse inference in applying facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e(b) based on the rejected submission. Because the underlying basis for rejection (untimeliness) was vacated, the propriety of the adverse inference determination and resulting 160% countervailable subsidy rate required reconsideration by Commerce on remand.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that Commerce's deadline procedures must account for its own extension policies, including automatic extensions triggered by untimely extension requests made before the deadline. When Commerce fails to decide an extension request before a 5:00 p.m. deadline, the automatic extension to 8:30 a.m. the next day applies, and parties may rely on that extended deadline. The decision does not establish broad precedent but rather enforces procedural requirements against Commerce's own prior determinations and administrative law principles regarding fairness in deadline enforcement.

cases.case_name: Kroy Ip Holdings, LLC v. Groupon, Inc.

segments.issue: Collateral Estoppel and Burden of Proof
segments.text: The panel held that collateral estoppel does not apply when a prior PTAB proceeding uses a preponderance-of-the-evidence standard while a subsequent district court proceeding requires clear-and-convincing evidence, because the differing burden of proof materially alters the question of invalidity. The court relied on B & B Hardware and Grogan v. Garner to support the proposition that collateral estoppel is unavailable when the legal standard differs between proceedings, rejecting patent-specific departures from well-established common-law principles.

The Federal Circuit denied both the petition for panel rehearing and the petition for rehearing en banc filed by Groupon. The court conducted a poll on the en banc petition, which failed to secure the necessary votes for rehearing.

summary.holding: The decision confirms that traditional collateral estoppel doctrine, including the burden-of-proof exception, applies uniformly across patent and non-patent contexts without patent-specific modifications, even where PTAB and district court proceedings involve different standards of proof. This clarifies that the differing burdens between IPR (preponderance) and district court invalidity challenges (clear and convincing) prevent issue preclusion under settled collateral estoppel law, rejecting arguments that the AIA's efficiency goals warrant departing from common-law preclusion principles.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas

segments.text: The court denied Fintiv's petition for a writ of mandamus seeking to postpone trial and its motion to stay. The court applied the exceptional-case standard requiring clear abuse of discretion or usurpation of judicial power, finding Fintiv failed to demonstrate it had no adequate alternative remedy (such as appeal after final judgment) or a clear and indisputable right to relief, particularly since Fintiv had indicated willingness to proceed and the scheduling conflict was ameliorated by the other court's rescheduling.

summary.holding: A mandamus petition to postpone trial does not meet the exceptional-circumstances standard when the petitioner has indicated ability to proceed and has an adequate alternative remedy through post-judgment appeal, even where counsel faces a scheduling conflict with another proceeding.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The court held that 38 U.S.C. § 3562(2) permanently bars a disabled veteran from receiving additional compensation under § 1115(1)(F) once the veteran's child elects to receive DEA benefits, regardless of whether the child later exhausts those benefits. The statutory language "additional amounts, of compensation" in § 3562(2) encompasses all monthly payments under § 1115 that the veteran would otherwise receive, not merely future increases to an existing benefit level.

The court's holding was supported by interpreting § 3562(1) and § 3562(2) as having a common scope and purpose, despite their textual differences, because both provisions implement the same nonduplication policy for children of disabled and deceased veterans respectively. The legislative history showed that Congress expanded the DEA program to children of disabled veterans in 1964 with the same nonduplication intent as applied to children of deceased veterans.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that the nonduplication provision of 38 U.S.C. § 3562 operates as a permanent bar to § 1115 dependent compensation once a child elects DEA benefits, even after those DEA benefits are exhausted, establishing that the two statutory subsections operate in parallel despite textual variations. The holding confirms that identical statutory terms receive consistent meanings across related provisions and rejects the interpretation that "additional amounts" refers only to future rate increases rather than the underlying monthly payments themselves.

cases.case_name: Bright Data Ltd. v. Code200, Uab
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board's role-based constructions of "client device" and "second server" are affirmed. Both terms refer to the functional role a communication device plays in the network (client, peer, or agent) rather than to fixed hardware structures, as the specification teaches that structurally identical devices toggle between roles via software modules depending on network requirements. Bright Data's narrower hardware-based constructions requiring specific device types are rejected.

The Board's finding that the Crowds reference anticipated the challenged claims is affirmed as supported by substantial evidence. Crowds proposes a system for web transactions allowing users to join a crowd that collectively issues requests, and this system is found to disclose all elements of the claimed patents.

The Board's determination that the claims would have been obvious over the Crowds reference is affirmed as a matter of law. The ultimate question of obviousness is reviewed de novo, and the underlying factual findings regarding what Crowds discloses and the motivation to combine references are reviewed for substantial evidence, with the Board's conclusions supported by the record.

The Board's rejection of Bright Data's evidence of secondary considerations of non-obviousness is affirmed. Bright Data failed to demonstrate the requisite nexus between its proffered evidence and the claims at issue, rendering such evidence lacking in probative value under the Graham factors.

summary.holding: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions finding the challenged claims of four Bright Data patents unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 102 and § 103 are affirmed in their entirety.

cases.case_name: Fmc Corporation v. Sharda USA, LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Pennsylvania

segments.text: The district court erred in construing the term "composition" to limit claims to stable compositions only, relying on stability disclosures in the earlier provisional application and related patent that were deliberately deleted from the asserted patents' specification. Under DDR Holdings precedent, a skilled artisan would understand that deletion of textual references to stability from the provisional application to the final patent indicates an evolution in the applicant's intended meaning, and therefore "composition" should not be limited to stable formulations based on disclosures that do not appear in the asserted patents themselves.

The Federal Circuit reviews preliminary injunction decisions under Third Circuit law for abuse of discretion, but gives dominant effect to Federal Circuit patent-specific precedent; an abuse of discretion occurs when the district court made a clear error of judgment in weighing factors, exercised discretion based on an error of law, or relied on clearly erroneous factual findings.

Because the district court's claim construction was erroneous, its rejection of Sharda's anticipation and obviousness defenses based on the McKenzie reference was necessarily erroneous, as the reference may disclose unstable compositions that would fall within the properly construed term "composition" and thus raise a substantial invalidity question.

summary.holding: The decision confirms that Federal Circuit precedent, particularly DDR Holdings, requires courts to treat deliberate deletions from a provisional application to a final patent specification as significant evidence of narrowed or redefined claim scope, and such deletions override reliance on disclosures in earlier filings when construing claim terms. This precedent rejects importing limitations from abandoned provisional application language into granted claims.

cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' determination that it possessed subject matter jurisdiction over plaintiffs' Fifth Amendment takings claim under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1), rejecting the Government's argument that PROMESA implicitly displaced Tucker Act jurisdiction. The court found no clear congressional intent in PROMESA to displace the Claims Court's traditional jurisdiction over constitutional takings claims, and the Tucker Act's waiver of sovereign immunity extends to Fifth Amendment takings claims.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the dismissal for failure to state a claim, holding that plaintiffs could not establish a taking effected by the United States because Congress's enactment of PROMESA alone did not constitute sufficient federal government action to support a takings claim under the framework established in A & D Auto Sales, Inc. v. United States, 748 F.3d 1142 (Fed. Cir. 2014). The court concluded that plaintiffs could not establish either an agency relationship or coercion between the Government and the independent actors (the Oversight Board and Title III court) whose actions directly caused the diminution in bond value.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's denial of plaintiffs' request to amend their complaint, finding no abuse of discretion where the amended allegations would still fail to state a claim for a taking under established law regarding the necessity of federal government action.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that Fifth Amendment takings claims based on federal legislation are subject to Tucker Act jurisdiction in the Court of Federal Claims, but confirms that plaintiffs must still allege direct federal government action—not merely legislative authorization of third-party conduct—to state a viable takings claim. The decision does not significantly advance takings jurisprudence beyond applying existing A & D Auto Sales precedent to the specific factual circumstances of PROMESA's debt restructuring scheme.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The court issued an errata correcting a citation on page 2, line 31, from 35 U.S.C. § 503 to 38 U.S.C. § 503 in the underlying opinion.

A petitioner seeking compensation for an off-Table vaccine injury under 42 U.S.C. § 300aa-13(a)(1) must prove causation by a preponderance of the evidence using the three-prong Althen test: (1) a medical theory causally connecting vaccination and injury, (2) a logical sequence of cause and effect showing vaccination was the reason for injury, and (3) a proximate temporal relationship between vaccination and injury. All three prongs must be proven by preponderance of the evidence.

The special master and Court of Federal Claims properly found that petitioner failed to meet his burden of proof on the first Althen prong regarding molecular mimicry as a causation theory. While molecular mimicry has general scientific basis, the expert's opinion lacked the specific evidence needed to support its application to ulcerative colitis in this particular case, and temporal factors (81-day delay between vaccination and symptom onset) undermined the causal connection.

The court affirmed the special master's finding that the timing of symptom progression, as documented in medical records, weighed against petitioner's causation theory. The respondent's expert credibly testified that no gastrointestinal bleeding was recorded until February 13, 2016—over four months after the October 2015 vaccination—and that self-reported decreased stamina in November 2015 was speculative, supporting the conclusion that vaccines did not cause the ulcerative colitis.

On appeal from the Court of Federal Claims in Vaccine Act cases, the Federal Circuit conducts de novo review of the special master's legal rulings while applying the arbitrary and capricious standard to factual findings. The court performs independent review without deference to the lower court, though it pays close attention to the Court of Federal Claims' careful analysis.

Petitioner's claimed vaccine-induced ulcerative colitis constitutes an off-Table injury under the Vaccine Act because it does not fall within any designated Table injury (42 U.S.C. §§ 300aa-11(c), 300aa-14). In off-Table cases, the presumption of causation does not apply, and petitioner bears the full burden of proving causation by preponderance of the evidence rather than merely triggering a rebuttable presumption.

summary.holding: This decision affirms well-established Federal Circuit precedent on Vaccine Act off-Table injury claims, confirming that petitioners must satisfy all three Althen prongs by preponderance of the evidence and that general scientific theories like molecular mimicry, without specific evidentiary support, cannot meet the causation standard. The opinion does not materially change existing law but demonstrates the continued rigorous application of Althen's requirements to speculative immunological causation theories lacking adequate factual grounding.

cases.case_name: Habas Sinai Ve Tibbi Gazlar Istihsal Endustrisi v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed Commerce's use of lira-denominated sales values rather than dollar values to calculate normal value for Habaş's home-market sales under the Tariff Act of 1930, 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(a)(1)(B)(i). Commerce's decision was supported by substantial evidence because Habaş could only reconcile its lira prices to its audited financial records and could not provide payment dates or exchange rates linking its dollar invoice prices to actual payments, thereby failing to demonstrate that dollar prices controlled the transaction.

The court held that Commerce did not deviate from its prior precedent in similar Turkish steel cases by using lira values instead of dollars. Unlike prior respondents who successfully reconciled dollar prices through payment documentation showing the USD price controlled, Habaş failed to demonstrate that its dollar invoice prices controlled the amounts actually paid, making the cases factually distinguishable under the reconciliation requirement.

summary.holding: Affirmed Commerce's final antidumping determination using lira-denominated sales values to calculate a 24.32 percent dumping margin, finding the methodology complied with statutory obligations and was supported by substantial evidence.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal because the Veterans Court issued a non-final remand order, which is generally not reviewable under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 absent narrow exceptions. The court held that finality is a jurisdictional requirement and that remand orders are categorically non-final for purposes of Federal Circuit review.

The court held that Jenkins failed to satisfy all three conditions of the Williams v. Principi exception to the finality requirement because: (1) the Veterans Court made no definitive legal ruling separate from the remand proceedings; (2) Jenkins was not adversely affected by the remand order, which favored him by requiring better reasons; and (3) there was no substantial risk his legal arguments about the presumption of soundness would be mooted on remand. 275 F.3d 1361 (Fed. Cir. 2002).

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed Jenkins's appeal from the Veterans Court's non-final remand order because neither the general finality requirement nor the narrow Williams exception permitted review.

cases.case_name: Jilin Forest Industry Jinqiao Flooring Group Co. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.issue: NME presumption and country-wide rate legality
segments.text: The court held that Commerce lawfully applied the rebuttable presumption of government control to exporters in nonmarket economy countries and assigned a single country-wide antidumping duty rate to Jilin, which failed to rebut the presumption despite cooperating with the investigation. The Tariff Act recognizes a close correlation between nonmarket economy status and government control of prices, output, and resource allocation, and Sigma Corp. v. United States, 117 F.3d 1401 (Fed. Cir. 1997), established that Commerce has broad authority to employ such presumptions and place the burden on exporters to demonstrate independence from government control.

summary.holding: This decision confirms, consistent with Sigma and subsequent Federal Circuit precedent, that Commerce may lawfully apply a rebuttable presumption of government control and assign a single country-wide rate to exporters in nonmarket economy countries that fail to rebut the presumption, even when they cooperate fully with the investigation. The decision affirms that this practice is authorized by the Tariff Act and does not require Commerce to calculate individual rates for each exporter simply because it failed to demonstrate independence.

cases.case_name: Jiaxing Super Lighting Electric Appliance, Co. v. Ch Lighting Technology Co., Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas

segments.text: The district court erred in granting judgment as a matter of law on the on-sale bar defense for the '125 and '540 patents because it improperly excluded evidence offered by CH Lighting to demonstrate that prior art tubes embodying the claimed inventions were on sale before the patents' 2015 effective filing dates. Although the invalidity expert's testimony alone might have been insufficient, excluding the evidence altogether deprived the jury of material factual evidence necessary to adjudicate the AIA on-sale bar defense and therefore violated CH Lighting's right to present its validity defense.

The JMOL of non-invalidity on the on-sale bar for the '125 and '540 patents is reversed and vacated, and a new trial is required on the validity of these patents. The district court was required to permit CH Lighting to present admissible evidence of prior sales to allow the jury to determine whether the on-sale bar under 35 U.S.C. § 102(b)(1)(A) applied.

Substantial evidence supports the jury's verdicts that CH Lighting infringed the '140 patent and that the patent was not invalid. The district court's findings and the jury verdict regarding the '140 patent are affirmed on the infringement and invalidity issues, though damages are vacated pending reassessment of expert testimony.

The district court must reassess the reliability of Ms. Kindler's damages testimony consistent with the Federal Circuit's en banc decision in EcoFactor and under Federal Rule of Evidence 702. The prior admission of her testimony over Daubert objection requires reconsideration under the updated standard, necessitating a new trial as to damages for all three patents.

The damages award and the district court's grant of enhanced damages are vacated. A new trial on damages is required for all three asserted patents, conditioned upon proper Daubert review of the damages expert's testimony and reassessment of the on-sale bar validity defense for the tube patents.

summary.holding: The decision clarifies that in patent infringement cases, district courts may not grant JMOL on invalidity defenses by excluding evidence altogether, even when expert testimony standing alone might be insufficient; parties have a right to present material evidence supporting affirmative defenses that would allow a jury to evaluate them. The opinion also reinforces the application of EcoFactor's en banc standard to expert testimony reliability determinations, requiring renewed Daubert scrutiny when such objections are raised on appeal. The judgment is largely fact-bound but establishes that procedural exclusion of evidence supporting validity defenses violates due process principles in patent trials.

cases.case_name: Wherevertv, Inc. v. Comcast Cable Communications, LLC

segments.text: The court affirmed the district court's plain and ordinary meaning construction of the "adding or deleting" limitation and held that WhereverTV failed to present evidence that X1 users could subscribe to new channels not already on the IPG or remove apps entirely, requiring reversal of the JMOL because the evidence could support a different interpretation of whether user subscription management constitutes the claimed functionality.

The court vacated the JMOL on the "IPG application installed on the device" limitation, holding that the district court erred in finding uncontested evidence that the XRE receiver (on the set-top box device) does not constitute an IPG application, as the specification and Figures did not definitively resolve whether a thin-client receiver could perform the claimed IPG functions.

The court affirmed the district court's construction that "distinct" in the server limitation means "functionally distinct," rejecting Comcast's alternative interpretation based on ownership or control, and held this construction was supported by intrinsic evidence and the patent's goal of shifting control to users rather than MSOs.

The court affirmed the district court's rejection of Comcast's challenge under 35 U.S.C. § 112 to the term "only or virtually entirely streaming video programming," finding that the language is not indefinite because persons skilled in the art could understand it, as evidenced by Comcast's own proposed construction of the related limitation.

The court vacated the district court's judgment as a matter of law of noninfringement and remanded for further proceedings, holding that WhereverTV presented sufficient evidence on the "adding or deleting" and "IPG application" limitations to survive Comcast's Rule 50(a) motion and proceed to or return to the jury.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit vacated the district court's judgment as a matter of law of noninfringement on U.S. Patent No. 8,656,431 claim 1, reversing the erroneous claim constructions and rejecting Comcast's indefiniteness challenge, and remanded the case for proceedings consistent with the proper constructions of the "adding or deleting" limitation and "IPG application" limitation, which require functional rather than ownership-based distinctness of the server.

cases.case_name: SSI Technologies, LLC v. Dongguan Zhengyang Electronic Mechanical Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Wisconsin
United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board was not required to resolve the parties' express dispute over whether the "target" and "first" protocols must be different or can be identical, because the Board determined that Duncan disclosed the "translating" claim limitation under either party's proposed construction. Under the principle that the Board need only construe claim terms that are in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve that controversy, the Board did not commit legal error by abstaining from the disputed construction.

The Board's finding that Duncan's protocol converters taught the claimed "translating" limitation is supported by substantial evidence. Duncan discloses protocol converters that convert data from one protocol to a target protocol, and DocuSign's expert testified that Duncan contemplates conversion to a different protocol in appropriate circumstances, rendering the translating limitation obvious by a preponderance of the evidence.

The Board's final determination that claims 1 of the '066 patent, claims 1–3 of the '957 patent, and claim 1 of the '214 patent were unpatentable as obvious in light of Duncan alone or in combination with other prior art is affirmed, as Dr. Clark conceded that all claim limitations other than the "translating" limitation were obvious.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decisions in all three inter partes review proceedings, holding that the challenged patents were obvious in light of prior art, particularly Duncan's protocol converter technology.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed Evans's appeal for lack of jurisdiction. Under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over challenges to a law or regulation as applied to the facts of a particular case, and Evans's argument that the Veterans Court erred in applying the Rice v. Shinseki standard to his facts fell within this jurisdictional bar.

cases.case_name: Acorda Therapeutics, Inc. v. Alkermes Plc
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Southern District of New York

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks appellate jurisdiction over Acorda's petition to modify the arbitral award on manifest-disregard grounds. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1), the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction extends to appeals from district court decisions on patent matters, but review of arbitration awards for manifest disregard of law falls outside this statutory grant and instead belongs to the regional circuit court of appeals.

The district court's confirmation of the arbitration tribunal's award—including the tribunal's holding that Brulotte renders royalty provisions unenforceable upon patent expiration and the award of $16.5 million for protested post-expiration payments under the License Agreement—was affirmed, as the tribunal's application of the New York Voluntary Pay Doctrine and requirement of written protest was not manifestly disregarded under applicable law.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies the jurisdictional boundaries between the Federal Circuit and regional circuits in reviewing arbitration awards: manifest-disregard challenges to arbitral awards, even when they involve patent law arguments, fall within the appellate jurisdiction of regional circuit courts of appeals under 9 U.S.C. chapters 1 and 2, not the Federal Circuit under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1). The opinion does not substantively alter patent or arbitration law but rather reaffirms the jurisdictional allocation framework for appellate review of arbitration matters.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board

segments.text: The Board erred by failing to apply fundamental corrective remedy principles when determining reinstatement relief for a whistleblower. Under the Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 1221(g)(1)(A)(i)), an employee must be restored "as nearly as possible" to the position they would have occupied but for the wrongful personnel action, and the Board failed to address whether the employee would have chosen disability retirement absent the removal.

The Board's denial of back pay was based on an incomplete analysis that did not address causation between the wrongful removal and the employee's disability retirement or his inability to work. Under principles applied to Back Pay Act cases, denying back pay for a period of disability without examining whether that disability resulted from the unlawful discharge is unreasonable and contrary to the make-whole purpose of remedies.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's final order denying reinstatement and back pay is vacated and remanded because the Board failed to apply proper remedial principles under the Whistleblower Protection Act by not addressing whether the employee would have pursued disability retirement absent the wrongful removal, and failed to conduct proper causation analysis regarding the employee's eligibility for back pay.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the petition for review because petitioner failed to file the required Entry of Appearance form by an attorney admitted to the bar of the Federal Circuit, in violation of the Federal Circuit's procedural rules. Dismissal was entered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules.

summary.holding: Petition for review of an MSPB decision dismissed due to petitioner's failure to comply with the Federal Circuit's procedural requirement of filing an Entry of Appearance by an admitted attorney.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the petition for review of the Merit Systems Protection Board decision for failure to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination in accordance with the Federal Circuit's rules. The dismissal was entered as a sanction for failure to prosecute.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board correctly construed the claim limitation "determining whether the received response matches the expected response" to require only a single determination of whether the received response matches the expected response, without requiring an explicit disclosure or possibility of an unexpected response. The claims do not recite an unexpected response, the specification never mentions an "unexpected response," and Xerox's proposed substitute claims (which explicitly addressed expected versus unexpected responses) demonstrate that the original claims lack this limitation.

All claims of the '599 patent are unpatentable as obvious under the prior art cited by Snap, given the Board's claim construction. The parties stipulated that if the claim construction were affirmed, the Board's decision holding all claims unpatentable under Snap's IPR could be affirmed.

The Board's determination that Xerox's substitute claims (claims 26-40) are unpatentable as obvious and patent-ineligible is not challenged on appeal and therefore remains undisturbed. Xerox limited its appeal to the Board's decision on the original claims only.

summary.holding: Affirmed. The Board's claim construction is correct, and therefore all claims of the '599 patent are properly held unpatentable as obvious under the prior art.

cases.case_name: Sunkist Growers, Inc. v. Intrastate Distributors, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board's finding that the KIST and SUNKIST marks have different commercial impressions lacks substantial evidence. The Board relied on a lips image in isolated marketing materials to conclude IDI markets KIST to reference a kiss, but that image was not part of the registered mark itself, appeared in only some marketing materials, and was not the focus of those materials. Similarly, the Board overly relied on SUNKIST design marks containing a sun when the majority of Sunkist's registrations and products use the standard character form without that design.

The Board's overall likelihood-of-confusion analysis is reversed. With four DuPont factors favoring likelihood of confusion (similarity of goods, trade channels, conditions of sale, and strength of opposer's mark) and the similarity-of-marks factor no longer supporting a finding of no confusion, actual confusion alone cannot outweigh the combined weight of the other factors. The absence of reported actual confusion is not dispositive, and doubts about likelihood of confusion must be resolved against the newcomer under 15 U.S.C. § 1052(d).

summary.holding: The court clarifies that in likelihood-of-confusion analysis under the Lanham Act, actual confusion is not a dispositive factor that can alone outweigh multiple other DuPont factors favoring confusion, and that commercial-impression analysis must rest on substantial evidence of how marks are actually presented to and perceived by consumers, not isolated or non-dominant design elements in marketing materials. This reinforces that Federal Circuit precedent requires weighing all relevant DuPont factors de novo while resolving doubts against the mark applicant.

cases.case_name: Sme Steel Contractors, Inc. v. Seismic Bracing Company, LLC

segments.text: The district court construed the claimed 'air gap' as 'an empty or unfilled space or interval' and 'positioned between' or 'formed between' as 'spans the distance between' the core member and bearing members. On appeal, the Federal Circuit affirmed this construction and found no error in the district court's interpretation of the patent's requirements for independent movement of the steel core.

The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment of no infringement under the literal terms of the patent claims. Seismic Bracing's use of corrugated cardboard affixed to the steel core, rather than an air gap that spans the distance between the core and bearing members, did not infringe the asserted claims of the '680 patent.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's determination that SME Steel lacked standing for its false advertising and false association claims under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(A), (B) because SME Steel failed to demonstrate that alleged misrepresentations in the Design Manual were the proximate cause of its injury, rejecting any presumption of injury.

segments.issue: Lanham Act—No Literal Falsity or Intent to Deceive
segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment on Lanham Act claims, finding no genuine issue of material fact that Seismic Bracing made literally false statements or acted with intent to deceive consumers based on the representations in the Design Manual.

The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment on Utah Truth in Advertising Act claims under Utah Code § 13-11a-3(b), (c), concluding there was no genuine issue of material fact as to the likelihood of confusion element required for those claims.

segments.issue: Copyright Infringement—No Causal Connection to Damages
segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment for Seismic Bracing on copyright infringement claims, holding that SME Steel failed to present sufficient evidence of a causal connection between the use of copyrighted technical drawings and Seismic Bracing's profits.
The Federal Circuit affirmed summary judgment on SME Steel's unfair competition claim under Utah Code § 13-5a-103, which the parties agreed rose and fell with the patent infringement claim.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed in full the district court's grant of summary judgment to Seismic Bracing on all claims, including patent infringement, Lanham Act false advertising and false association, copyright infringement, and related state law unfair competition and deceptive trade practice claims.

cases.case_name: Williams Building Company, Inc. v. Secretary of State

segments.text: The court affirmed that modification-7 and modification-8 contained clear, broad releases barring Williams' cardinal change claim under Count I. The releases expressly covered "any and all liability" for facts or circumstances giving rise to the document substitution, and modification-20 did not vitiate or waive those earlier releases.

The court affirmed that the majority of Williams' Count II claims for breach of implied duty based on OBO's delayed responses to RFIs and submittals were barred by the releases in modification-7 and modification-8, as those delays were associated with the circumstances of the document substitution expressly covered by those modifications.

The court affirmed the Board's exclusion of evidence for Count III (breach based on alleged interference with subcontractor Huashi) because Williams failed to properly identify associated costs within the discovery cutoff and scheduling order; evidence first submitted in response to summary judgment was barred from consideration.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Civilian Board of Contract Appeals' grant of summary judgment in favor of the Department of State on all three counts, finding that prior bilateral contract modifications and releases barred recovery for the cardinal change and delayed response claims, and that Williams failed to properly identify damages for the subcontractor interference claim.

cases.case_name: Touchmusic Entertainment LLC v. Netflix, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Northern District of Illinois

segments.text: The court affirmed that Mr. Pace failed to establish clear and unmistakable error (CUE) in the April 2006 VA rating decision. To prove CUE, a claimant must show either that correct facts known at the time were not before the adjudicator or that statutory/regulatory provisions were incorrectly applied, that the error is undebatable, and that it would have manifestly changed the outcome—with the analysis based on law as it existed at the time of the original decision.

The court rejected Mr. Pace's contention that the Veterans Court misinterpreted regulations governing disability rating reductions by holding that the VA may reduce a total disability rating based on a single showing of sustained material improvement across the entire medical record. The court found that the Veterans Court's interpretation was consistent with Collier v. Derwinski (1992), which predated the April 2006 decision and established the contemporary understanding of those regulations, and that no CUE arose from a legal-based misapplication as understood in April 2006.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's decision that the VA's April 3, 2006 rating decision reducing Mr. Pace's disability rating from 100% to 50% did not contain clear and unmistakable error, as the VA's review of the full medical record to demonstrate sustained material improvement was consistent with the applicable regulatory interpretation at that time.

segments.text: The Court held that the PTO Director's decision not to apply interference estoppel under 37 C.F.R. § 41.127(a)(1) to bar Zynga's IPR petition falls within the general rule of unreviewability established by 35 U.S.C. § 314(d), which precludes judicial review of decisions to institute inter partes review. The Court noted that even under the narrow "shenanigans" exception articulated in Cuozzo Speed Technologies, LLC v. Lee, 579 U.S. 261, 275 (2016), no legal error occurred here.

The Court concluded that the PTO had sound reasons for declining to apply interference estoppel, affirming the Director's determination on the merits. Although the Board had dismissed Zynga's obviousness motion as moot during the prior interference proceeding when it terminated on the threshold issue of inadequate written-description support, the PTO reasonably determined that interference estoppel did not bar Zynga from raising a different obviousness theory based on different prior-art references in the subsequent IPR.

The Court affirmed the Board's final written decision that claims 28–29, 31–33, 47–50, 84–86, 90–92, and 99–100 of the '089 patent were unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103 based on the combination of Goldberg and Olden references, rejecting IGT's procedural and substantive challenges to that finding on appeal.

summary.holding: This decision confirms that decisions to institute inter partes review, including those declining to apply interference estoppel, are generally unreviewable under 35 U.S.C. § 314(d), with only a narrow exception for conduct not in accordance with law ("shenanigans"). The opinion clarifies that interference estoppel does not necessarily bar a party from raising a different obviousness theory supported by different prior-art references in a subsequent IPR, even when the party raised an earlier obviousness motion in the interference that was dismissed as moot on a threshold basis.

cases.case_name: Buergofol Gmbh v. Omega Liner Company, Inc.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied Buergofol's petition for a writ of mandamus seeking to vacate the district court's order compelling production of trade-secret documents regarding film composition and manufacture. Under the mandamus standard, the court would disturb a discovery order only upon finding exceptional circumstances amounting to a clear abuse of discretion, and Buergofol failed to demonstrate such abuse where the district court reasonably found need for the information and adequate protection under the existing attorney's-eyes-only protective order.

summary.holding: Mandamus petition denied; district court's discovery compulsion order affirmed on the ground that trade-secret information is discoverable upon showing of relevance and need, discretionary balancing favors production where the patent plaintiff has placed the product at issue and the defendant asserts prior-art counterclaims, and the existing protective order adequately safeguards the trade secrets.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the petition for review of the Merit Systems Protection Board decision for failure to prosecute in accordance with Federal Circuit rules, specifically the petitioner's failure to pay the required docketing fee under Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) and failure to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination.

cases.case_name: Largan Precision Co., Ltd. v. Motorola Mobility LLC
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.issue: Jurisdictional Scope of Federal Circuit Review
segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review Davis's challenge to the Veterans Court's application of the constructive-possession standard to the facts of his case. Under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), appeals from Veterans Court decisions may not include challenges to the application of law to the facts of a particular case, which is precisely what Davis attempted to raise on appeal.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

cases.case_name: Fba Operating Co. v. Etn Capital, LLC

segments.text: The Court granted the parties' joint motion to remand the case to the district court to allow ETN Capital to withdraw its pending motion for attorneys' fees and permit the parties to request vacatur of the district court's dismissal orders. The Court took no position on whether the district court should grant the vacatur request, leaving that determination to the district court's discretion.
Each party shall bear its own costs on appeal, consistent with the settlement agreement reached by the parties.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Southern District of Texas

segments.text: The Federal Circuit recalled its prior mandate issued June 27, 2024, reinstated the appeal, and vacated its own February 12, 2024 opinion and judgment following the Supreme Court's reversal and remand in No. 24-320, consistent with the Supreme Court's directive for further proceedings.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Final Judgment of the district court and remanded the case for further proceedings in accordance with the Supreme Court's decision, with the mandate to issue 14 days from the order date.

The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) based on the parties' agreement to dismiss the proceeding. This was a consensual dismissal in which both parties agreed to terminate the appeal from the PTAB's decisions in IPR2022-00921 and IPR2022-00922.

Each party was ordered to bear its own costs in the appeal. This allocation reflected the mutual agreement between the parties to dismiss the proceeding without shifting any litigation expenses to either side.

summary.holding: The appeal was dismissed by agreement of the parties, with each party bearing its own costs.

cases.case_name: P2i Ltd. v. Jiangsu Favored Nanotechnology Co., Ltd.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the notice of appeal for failure to comply with Federal Circuit Rules, specifically for failing to pay the required docketing fee under Rule 52(a)(1) and failing to file the required Entry of Appearance form by an admitted attorney within the prescribed time. The dismissal was for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for procedural noncompliance.

segments.text: The Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 2501 is affirmed. A contract breach claim accrues when the plaintiff knew or should have known of the breach, not when the full extent of damages becomes apparent; the Murrays' claim accrued in 2010-2013 when snowmobile activity first materially interfered with Spout Springs operations, well before the June 21, 2021 filing, placing the claim outside the six-year limitations period.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the lower court's characterization of the government's Rule 12(b)(1) motion as a factual (rather than facial) attack on jurisdiction, permitting fact-finding based on deposition testimony. The Murrays did not lack notice or discovery opportunity, so no error occurred in allowing the Court of Federal Claims to make jurisdictional findings of fact reviewed for clear error.

summary.holding: Affirmed. The six-year statute of limitations on claims in the Court of Federal Claims is jurisdictional and cannot be equitably tolled; the Murrays' breach of contract claim accrued when they knew or reasonably should have known of material snowmobile interference with their ski resort operations in 2010-2013, rendering their 2021 filing untimely.

cases.origin: Merit Systems Protection Board

segments.text: The court held that mandamus is an extraordinary remedy available only when the petitioner demonstrates a clear and indisputable right to relief and lacks adequate alternative means to obtain it. The writ may not be used as a substitute for the regular appeals process. Love v. McDonough, 100 F.4th 1388 (Fed. Cir. 2024); Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C., 542 U.S. 367 (2004).

The court denied Jackson's petition for mandamus seeking to reassign his MSPB appeals, vacate rulings, and obtain other relief. Jackson has adequate alternative remedies: he may raise challenges to jurisdictional and disqualification orders before the Board after an initial decision or before the Federal Circuit after a final decision, rendering mandamus unavailable.

The court rejected Jackson's argument that mandamus was justified due to an alleged Board quorum deficiency. The appeals are proceeding toward disposition with a hearing scheduled, and once the administrative judge issues initial decisions, they become final Board decisions 35 days after issuance absent a petition for Board review, at which point Jackson may seek Federal Circuit review. 5 C.F.R. § 1201.113(a); 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1)(A).

summary.holding: Petition for writ of mandamus denied; petitioner's challenges to administrative judge orders regarding jurisdiction and disqualification are reviewable through normal appellate procedures.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied Micron's petition for a writ of mandamus, holding that Micron failed to satisfy the demanding three-part test from Cheney v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for D.C.—requiring no other adequate means to obtain relief, clear and indisputable entitlement to the writ, and appropriateness under the circumstances. Micron could not demonstrate a clear and indisputable right to have the district judge rule on the transfer motion before the magistrate judge conducted the claim construction hearing, nor could it show that expedited review of objections to the magistrate judge's order would be inadequate.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit denied Micron's petition for a writ of mandamus seeking to compel the district court to rule on its motion to transfer under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a) before proceeding with claim construction, finding Micron failed to meet the demanding mandamus standard and that expedited appellate review of objections would provide an adequate remedy.

cases.case_name: Colibri Heart Valve LLC v. Medtronic Corevalve, LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Central District of California

segments.text: The court held that prosecution history estoppel bars Colibri from asserting the doctrine of equivalents to cover the "retraction" method of partial deployment after Colibri cancelled a claim explicitly reciting retraction during prosecution due to a lack of written description rejection under 35 U.S.C. § 112. The court found that Colibri's own recognition of the close linkage between the cancelled and retained claims regarding the alternative deployment methods triggered estoppel to prevent extending the surviving "pushing" claim to cover the accused "retracting" method.

The court reversed the district court's denial of judgment as a matter of law (JMOL) on noninfringement, holding that because the doctrine of equivalents was barred by prosecution history estoppel and Colibri had abandoned literal infringement at trial, Medtronic could not have induced infringement of the '294 patent as a matter of law under 35 U.S.C. § 271(b).

As a consequence of reversing on infringement, the court vacated the jury's verdict awarding more than $106 million in damages to Colibri, since that damages award was predicated on a finding of induced infringement that the court determined was improper as a matter of law.

summary.holding: This decision confirms that prosecution history estoppel applies when a patentee cancels a claim reciting an alternative limitation during prosecution and subsequently seeks to use the doctrine of equivalents to capture that same alternative in a surviving claim, preventing unjust reliance on the estoppel doctrine to circumvent the examination process. The holding clarifies the interaction between prosecution history estoppel and the doctrine of equivalents in the context of abandoned claim alternatives, reinforcing that surrendered subject matter cannot be reclaimed through equivalency arguments.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the entire appeal pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) based on the parties' stipulated agreement to dismiss. Each side bears its own costs.

cases.case_name: Allen v. State of North Carolina

segments.text: The court dismissed the appeal for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a), the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction is limited to patent cases, USPTO review cases, and certain small claims against the United States; this case involving state and private entities fell outside all three categories and thus was not appealable to the Federal Circuit.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of subject-matter jurisdiction.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the notice of appeal was filed nearly four years after the April 2021 judgment, well beyond the 60-day deadline prescribed by 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a), 28 U.S.C. § 2107(b), and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 4(a)(1)(B). The court held that timely filing is a non-waivable jurisdictional requirement not subject to equitable exceptions, and that although Mr. King argued late receipt of notice, no applicable statute or rule authorized extension of the deadline absent a motion filed within 180 days of judgment or within 14 days of receipt of notice, whichever is earlier.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction due to untimely filing of the notice of appeal, holding that the 60-day deadline for appealing from the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims is a non-waivable jurisdictional requirement admitting no equitable exceptions, and that the appellant's failure to file within the statutory extension window precluded any relief based on delayed receipt of the underlying judgment.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the Veterans Court's orders denying suspension of agency action were non-final procedural decisions, not final decisions on the merits of Mr. Latham's claims. Under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 and the Williams v. Principi exception, the court held that interlocutory orders denying suspension requests do not meet the three-part test for review of non-final orders, as they resolve no legal issues separate from pending merits proceedings and present no substantial risk of mootness.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; the Federal Circuit cannot review non-final interlocutory orders from the Veterans Court denying requests to suspend agency action pending appeal.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(3), holding that it may only review final decisions of the Court of Federal Claims—those that end litigation on the merits and leave nothing for the court to do but execute the judgment. The Court of Federal Claims's rejection of appellant's response to a motion to dismiss does not constitute a final decision because it does not terminate the underlying litigation on the merits.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction; the order rejecting a response to a motion to dismiss is not a final decision appealable to the Federal Circuit.

cases.case_name: Top Brand LLC v. Cozy Comfort Company LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Arizona

segments.text: Top Brand did not waive its prosecution history disclaimer claim construction argument by failing to object at jury instructions, applying principles established in utility patent law to design patents. Where a party has previously argued a claim construction position to the district court and that court has rejected it, no renewed objection at jury instructions is required to preserve the position for appeal.

segments.issue: Prosecution History Disclaimer for Design Patents
segments.text: The doctrine of prosecution history disclaimer applies to design patents, permitting a patentee's statements during prosecution to disclaim certain features and limit claim scope. Although design patent claims present unique challenges compared to utility patents, prosecution history remains binding where the applicant made clear disavowals to the Patent Office to overcome rejections or obtain allowance.

Top Brand was entitled to judgment as a matter of law of noninfringement of the D788 design patent because the accused products fell within the scope of subject matter Cozy Comfort disclaimed during prosecution. The evidence, viewed most favorably to Cozy Comfort, established only one reasonable conclusion: noninfringement under the prosecution history disclaimer doctrine.

The jury's verdict of trademark infringement of the "THE COMFY" marks was reversed because substantial evidence did not support the verdict. The court concluded that the evidence, construed in the light most favorable to Cozy Comfort, did not permit the jury's finding of infringement under the Lanham Act.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that the prosecution history disclaimer doctrine, well-established for utility patents, extends to design patents and operates as a binding limit on design patent scope based on applicant statements during prosecution. Additionally, the court confirms that claim construction objections need not be reiterated at jury instructions if the position has been clearly made and rejected in prior proceedings—applying established utility patent preservation doctrine to the design patent context. The decision is significant as precedent establishing design patents are subject to the same prosecution history estoppel principles as utility patents.

cases.case_name: Canadian Solar International Limited v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

cases.case_name: Trina Solar Science & Technology (Thailand) Ltd. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The Board lacked jurisdiction over Ms. Muhleisen's involuntary retirement appeal because she was a registered nurse employed by the VA under 38 U.S.C. § 7401(1), which excludes such positions from the competitive service and thereby removes them from the definition of "employee" in 5 U.S.C. § 7511(b)(10), whose adverse action appeals are cognizable under 5 U.S.C. § 7513(d). The court affirmed the Board's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, applying de novo review to the jurisdictional determination.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board lacks jurisdiction to hear involuntary retirement appeals from registered nurses employed by the Department of Veterans Affairs under title 38, as such positions are excluded from the competitive service and thus fall outside the definition of "employee" entitled to appeal adverse actions to the Board.

cases.case_name: Wonderland Switzerland Ag v. Evenflo Company, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the entire proceeding pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) based on the parties' agreement, and each side bears its own costs.

The Court of Federal Claims lacked jurisdiction over Lopez's claims because they sound in tort and thus fall outside the Tucker Act's scope, 28 U.S.C. § 1491, which excludes tort claims and requires that substantive law "can fairly be interpreted as mandating compensation by the Federal Government." Additionally, Lopez's claims for harassment, stalking, interference with litigation, social security benefits, and criminal actions do not arise under any statute conferring Tucker Act jurisdiction.

Lopez's due process challenge to the trial judge's refusal to recuse failed because he did not establish the requisite "deep-seated favoritism or antagonism that would make fair judgment impossible," and his accusations remained purely speculative rather than substantiated.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit summarily affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of jurisdiction under the Tucker Act.

segments.text: The Court of Federal Claims lacked subject matter jurisdiction over claims alleging violations of criminal statutes, judicial conduct codes, and tort-based claims arising from alleged mishandling of documents by the Supreme Court's clerk's office. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1) and Federal Tort Claims Act principles, the court cannot adjudicate federal criminal code violations or tort claims, and lacks jurisdiction over the Supreme Court and its clerk.

Maddox forfeited his First Amendment claim by raising it for the first time on appeal without asserting it in his amended complaint before the Court of Federal Claims, violating the requirement that constitutional claims be presented to the trial court. See Allen v. United States, 88 F.4th 983, 986 (Fed. Cir. 2023).

The Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed Maddox's breach of contract claim for failure to state a claim because payment of a filing fee alone does not create a contract with the United States absent mutual intent to contract. A simple fee payment lacks the requisite contractual elements.

Maddox failed to state a viable Fifth Amendment Takings claim where he voluntarily provided documents to the court that were subsequently docketed; voluntary transfer of property does not support a Takings claim, and public docketing of filed documents does not constitute taking for public use within the Fifth Amendment. The Court of Federal Claims also lacked jurisdiction over Takings claims sounding in tort.
Maddox's motion to vacate the lower court's decision based on alleged fraud and obstruction by the clerk's office was denied as unpersuasive.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal for lack of subject matter jurisdiction over criminal and tort-based claims, dismissal for failure to state a claim on the contract and Takings theories, and forfeiture of the First Amendment argument.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because the Court of Federal Claims' transfer order under 28 U.S.C. § 1631 was not a final decision ending the litigation on the merits. Transfer orders are interlocutory and not immediately appealable absent certification under § 1292(d)(2), and § 1292(d)(4)(A) does not authorize Federal Circuit review of Court of Federal Claims transfer orders to district court.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction over a non-final § 1631 transfer order.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The court affirmed that 38 U.S.C. § 511 unambiguously denies the Board and CAVC judicial review authority over the Secretary's discretionary decisions to grant or deny equitable relief under 38 U.S.C. § 503. The court held that this jurisdictional bar results from traditional statutory construction rather than agency deference and is therefore unaffected by Loper Light Enterprises v. Raimondo.

segments.issue: Due Process Challenge to § 503 Review Restriction
segments.text: The court rejected the appellant's due process claim, holding that because equitable relief under § 503 is discretionary, the appellant cannot establish a protected entitlement triggering due process protections. The court found that due process was satisfied because the Board provided notice of the jurisdictional defect and afforded the appellant a fair opportunity to submit additional written argument and request a hearing.

The court held that 38 U.S.C. § 511 does not violate the Administrative Procedure Act, as 5 U.S.C. § 702 expressly preserves other statutory limitations on judicial review, including § 511's bar on review of the Secretary's § 503 decisions.

The court rejected the appellant's CUE claim, holding that the Board's earlier denials of benefits based on the 1972 claim were not erroneous merely because the Board ultimately granted benefits on appeal in 2021. A CUE is an error that 'had it not been made, would have manifestly changed the outcome,' and the change of position through the appeals process did not satisfy this standard.

summary.holding: Affirmed the United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims' dismissal for lack of jurisdiction, holding that the Board and CAVC lack authority to review the Secretary's discretionary decisions under 38 U.S.C. § 503, and that such restriction does not violate due process or the APA.

cases.case_name: Nespresso USA, Inc. v. K-Fee System Gmbh
BYD (H.K.) Co., Ltd. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's determination that Cunningham did not meet the legal requirements for disability retirement under FERS. The Board found that Cunningham failed to demonstrate by preponderant evidence that her medical conditions (migraine headaches and anxiety/depression) were incompatible with useful and efficient service or that they caused deficiencies in performance, attendance, or conduct under 5 C.F.R. § 831.1203(a)(2), because her medical documentation lacked work restrictions, her supervisor reported satisfactory performance, and Cunningham provided no evidence quantifying specific job duties she could not perform.

The court held that the Board did not abuse its discretion in accepting OPM's file submitted two days late, as Cunningham failed to object to its admission at the prehearing conference and excluding the file would have left almost no medical evidence in the record—thereby harming Cunningham's burden of proof. This did not constitute a substantial departure from important procedural rights under the deferential review standard applicable to FERS disability cases.

The court affirmed the Board's denial of Cunningham's request to submit additional documents and medical evidence for the first time on review, because Cunningham neither provided the evidence to the Board with her petition for review nor explained why it was not presented before the record closed, as required by 5 C.F.R. § 1201.114(b), constituting an abuse of discretion claim unsupported by the record.

The court affirmed the Board's conclusion that a mere diagnosis of depression or anxiety disorder, without functional limitations or evidence of incompatibility with work, is insufficient to establish entitlement to disability retirement benefits under FERS, rejecting Cunningham's reliance on diagnoses alone.

The court upheld the Board's holding that DVA and Social Security Administration disability determinations, while relevant, are not dispositive of FERS disability eligibility and cannot alone establish entitlement when other record evidence does not meet the applicable FERS criteria.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's denial of Cunningham's disability retirement application under FERS, finding she failed to prove by preponderant evidence that her medical conditions prevented her from performing her position or caused deficiencies in performance, attendance, or conduct, and that procedural objections regarding late evidence submission and the opportunity to file additional evidence lacked merit under the highly deferential review standard governing FERS disability determinations.

cases.case_name: WSOU Investments LLC v. Google LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas

cases.case_name: Netlist, Inc. v. Micron Technology Texas, LLC
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The Court affirmed the Board's rejection of Agboke's motion to disqualify the administrative judge. Adjudicators are afforded a presumption of honesty and integrity, and bare allegations of bias without evidence of actual partiality are insufficient to overcome this presumption.

The Court affirmed that the reprimand letter was properly considered in the removal decision. Although Agboke grieved the letter, the agency rejected his grievance, and Agboke failed to show the letter was improperly considered.

The Court held that any failure to conduct a 2018 performance assessment review was harmless error under 28 U.S.C. § 2111. The removal was based on Agboke's inappropriate conduct, failure to follow instructions, and failure to cooperate with investigation—not lack of technical competence—and Agboke failed to demonstrate prejudice from the missing review.

The Court dismissed Agboke's challenge to the denial and delay of his FOIA request for lack of jurisdiction. The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over FOIA actions under 28 U.S.C. § 1295; Congress has designated district courts as the proper forum under 5 U.S.C. § 552(a)(4)(B).

The Court affirmed the Board's final decision upholding Agboke's removal from his position as an auditor based on charges of inappropriate conduct, failure to follow instructions, and failure to cooperate with an investigation. The court held that any error in the administrative judge's consideration of the reprimand letter was harmless because the letter was reviewed only in assessing allegations of protected disclosure, and the Board's ultimate conclusion that no non-frivolous disclosure was alleged did not depend on its admission.

The court held that the administrative judge did not abuse her discretion in accepting the agency's one-day late filing of part of its response to the Jurisdiction Order because evidentiary matters are committed to the adjudicator's sound discretion, harmless errors need not be disregarded, and Agboke failed to demonstrate actual prejudice.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board permissibly relied on applicant-admitted prior art (AAPA) as evidence of general background knowledge of an ordinarily skilled artisan, rather than as a formal basis for the IPR petition under 35 U.S.C. § 311(b). Unlike Qualcomm II, where the petitioner expressly labeled AAPA as part of its "basis," CSI here used AAPA only to establish that over-the-wire angioplasty balloon catheters were well-known in the art, consistent with background knowledge permissible in obviousness analysis.

The Board's determination that claims 1–4 and 6–17 were shown to be unpatentable as obvious is affirmed. The Board properly combined Levy (a prior art reference describing laser-generated pulses to disintegrate plaque) with general background knowledge of standard over-the-wire balloon catheters, and substantial evidence supports the factual findings underlying the legal conclusion of obviousness.

The Board's determination that claim 5 was not shown to be unpatentable as obvious is reversed. Claim 5, which requires that electrodes be "disposed adjacent to and outside of the guide wire lumen," does not present the limitation distinction from dependent claims that the Board found sufficient to avoid obviousness, and the same motivation and background knowledge support obvious combination as to all dependent claims.

A petitioner's challenge to whether the Board properly found the petition met § 311(b) threshold requirements is appealable to this court as part of review of the Board's final written decision, not barred by § 314(d) as a procedural determination. This distinguishes such challenges from ordinary run-of-the-mill determinations about whether to institute an IPR.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that applicant-admitted prior art (AAPA) may serve as evidence of background knowledge in IPR obviousness analysis without violating § 311(b)'s requirement that only patents and printed publications form the "basis" of a petition, provided the petitioner does not expressly designate AAPA as its basis. The decision also confirms that § 311(b) compliance determinations embedded in final written decisions are appealable under the Qualcomm II framework, and it reaffirms that dependent claims must be evaluated independently under the same obviousness framework as independent claims.

segments.issue: Subject Matter Jurisdiction Under Tucker Act
segments.text: The Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed for lack of subject matter jurisdiction because Mr. Serp failed to describe the alleged contract with sufficient detail. Under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1491(a)(1), and Rule of the Court of Federal Claims 9(k), a plaintiff must identify either a copy of the contract or describe its substantive provisions, including when it was signed, who signed for the government, and other material terms. Mr. Serp relied only on vague assertions without identifying any contractual terms or provisions.

The Court of Federal Claims properly dismissed for failure to state a claim under the standard requiring allegations of facts sufficient to establish an express or implied-in-fact contract, entry by an authorized government agent, and breach. Mr. Serp's allegations were insufficient to meet this standard given his failure to provide details about the alleged contract with DHS.

The court rejected Mr. Serp's argument that he was denied his Sixth Amendment right to represent himself, finding no evidence that either the Court of Federal Claims or the Federal Circuit had prevented him from proceeding pro se; both courts had in fact permitted him to do so.

The court held that the Court of Federal Claims could not issue subpoenas for DHS agents because it lacked subject matter jurisdiction over the complaint, and Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 45(a)(2) requires that a subpoena issue from the court where the action is pending.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Court of Federal Claims' dismissal of the complaint for lack of subject matter jurisdiction and failure to state a claim.
