cases.case_name: Juniper Networks, Inc. v. Swarm Technology LLC
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's construction of the term "any communication" in the patent claims as including one-way messaging that does not require a response. The Board found support in the plain language of the claims, where the word "any" before communication precludes both two-way and one-way communication, and further support in the specification.

The court affirmed the Board's finding that Juniper failed to demonstrate that the challenged claims of the '275 patent were unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103, holding that the combination of Leong and AppleTalkBook references failed to teach accepting a co-processor into a system without any communication as required by the claims.

The court affirmed the Board's rejection of Juniper's zone-theory argument as a new argument raised for the first time in the reply brief, which is properly barred from consideration in IPR proceedings.

The court dismissed Juniper's appeal regarding the '004 patent as moot because a companion case (Swarm Tech. LLC v. Amazon.com, Inc.) decided by the same panel on the same day affirmed the Board's finding that all claims of the '004 patent were unpatentable, making the present appeal regarding that patent no longer justiciable.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's rejection of Juniper's IPR challenges to the '275 patent claims under 35 U.S.C. § 103, finding that the Board's construction of "any communication" as including one-way messaging was correct and that the prior art combination failed to render the claims obvious. The appeal regarding the '004 patent was dismissed as moot due to the outcome in a companion case.

cases.case_name: Eye Therapies, LLC v. Slayback Pharma LLC

segments.text: The court reversed the Board's construction of the phrase "consisting essentially of" in claims 1 and 3. Although "consisting essentially of" typically allows unlisted ingredients that do not materially affect basic and novel properties, the court held that the prosecution history here supports an atypical, narrower meaning precluding the use of active ingredients other than brimonidine, based on the applicant's explicit representations during prosecution that the claimed methods do not require any other active ingredients and the examiner's reliance on those representations in allowing the claims.

The court vacated the Board's obviousness determination and remanded for reconsideration. Because the Board's analysis materially relied on its erroneous claim construction allowing coadministration of additional active agents, the court could not affirm the unpatentability finding and vacated rather than affirmed the Board's decision.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that although "consisting essentially of" has a presumptive ordinary meaning permitting unlisted components, a patentee may establish an atypical, narrower meaning through explicit prosecution history arguments demonstrating that securing allowance depended on limiting claim scope—here, precluding additional active ingredients. The prosecution history, including the applicant's amendments and the examiner's acknowledgment of limiting representations, can inform claim construction even absent unmistakable disavowal.

cases.case_name: Swarm Technology LLC v. amazon.com, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board had substantial evidence to support its finding that the claim limitation 'agent configured to search the task pool' is disclosed by the combination of Lurie and Ethernet, where data frames in Lurie modified by Ethernet's frame structure would function as agents searching the task pool. The Board's factual findings regarding claim scope were reviewed for substantial evidence support.

The Board properly found that claims 2-12 of the '004 patent were rendered obvious by the combination of Lurie and Ethernet under 35 U.S.C. § 103, where a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine Lurie's task distribution system with Ethernet's data frame structure to create the claimed agent-based search functionality. Swarm's appeal of this obviousness determination was affirmed.

The Board properly denied Swarm's contingent motion to amend to add substitute claims 13 and 14 because the limitation of 'dynamically accepting an additional co-processor on a plug-and-play basis without communication with the controller' lacked support in the original application under 35 U.S.C. § 112. The Board additionally found the substitute claims directed to nonpatentable subject matter under 35 U.S.C. § 101.

The Board's construction of the term 'proactively' in the '275 patent claims, understood as periodic monitoring of the task pool by co-processors, was proper, and applying that construction, Amazon failed to prove unpatentability of any of the challenged claims 1-17 of the '275 patent. Swarm's cross-appeal challenging this finding was denied.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's Final Written Decisions in full, upholding the findings of unpatentability for certain claims of the '004 patent, the denial of the motion to amend, and the Board's conclusion that the '275 patent claims were not proven unpatentable.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's Final Written Decisions finding certain claims of the '004 patent obvious over Lurie and Ethernet under 35 U.S.C. § 103, denying Swarm's motion to amend to add substitute claims lacking written description support under 35 U.S.C. § 112, and finding that Amazon failed to prove the '275 patent claims unpatentable.

cases.case_name: Ball Metal Beverage Container Corporation v. Crown Packaging Technology, Inc.

segments.text: The court affirmed that 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b) requires the VA to assess whether evidence submitted during an appeal period is new and material before treating it as filed in connection with a prior claim, but the statute does not automatically entitle a claimant to an earlier effective date merely because the VA failed to make that assessment before granting benefits on a later claim. The proper remedy when the VA has not yet made a responsive determination is remand, not retroactive application of an earlier claim's effective date.

The court clarified that its prior decisions in Bond v. Shinseki and Beraud v. McDonald, which held that a claim remains "open" pending the VA's responsive determination under § 3.156(b), do not support a claimant's argument that an intervening grant of benefits must incorporate the date of application of the uncompleted prior claim. Bond and Beraud establish only that the VA must provide a responsive determination; they do not create a rule requiring retroactive effective dating based on the timing of that determination relative to subsequent benefit grants.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(b), a claimant is entitled to an earlier effective date corresponding to a prior claim only if the VA determines that new evidence is both new and material; a delay by the VA in making that determination does not itself alter the effective-dating analysis or require the VA to consider the earlier application date when granting benefits on a later claim. The holding distinguishes between a claim remaining "open" for purposes of requiring the VA to fulfill its assessment obligation and the legal consequences of that procedural incompleteness for purposes of retroactive benefit dating, establishing that the latter does not automatically flow from the former.

segments.text: The Board lacked jurisdiction to review the merits of FEHB and FEGLI premium charges, but properly exercised its limited jurisdiction to determine whether Ms. Lucas established grounds for waiver of collection and whether she received due process prior to offset. The Board's jurisdiction extended only to these two collateral matters under the applicable standard articulated in Miller v. Office of Personnel Management.

segments.issue: Law of the Case Doctrine Application
segments.text: The administrative judge properly applied law of the case doctrine to foreclose Ms. Lucas' arguments regarding waiver for overpayments attributable to insurance premium deductions, as this issue had already been decided adversely to her in the First Initial Decision and she had abandoned related due process claims in her prior petition for review.

Ms. Lucas failed to state a cognizable due process claim against OPM or the Board for failure to inform her of separate appeal rights in federal court under 5 U.S.C. § 8715, as neither entity misled her about her ability to challenge the merits before the Board, and no legal authority obligated them to advise of appeal rights in a different venue.

The Board properly found that it lacked jurisdiction to consider Ms. Lucas' statute of limitations argument regarding OPM's collection of overpayments attributable to insurance premiums, as this issue fell outside the Board's limited jurisdiction over debt collection matters.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's August 2024 final decision dismissing Ms. Lucas' appeal for lack of jurisdiction over the merits of insurance premium charges and properly rejecting her due process and statutory limitation defenses.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board properly exercised its limited jurisdiction in finding that Ms. Lucas was not eligible for waiver of overpayment attributable to FEHB and FEGLI premium deductions and correctly determined that it lacked jurisdiction to consider her arguments regarding notification obligations and statute of limitations, with the exception of the previously waived SSA benefits portion.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's rejection of claims 1 and 3–5 as indefinite under 35 U.S.C. § 112(b). The claims contain contradictory limitations requiring both a "one piece planar mirror surface" and "a bent tab incorporated within" that surface; because a bent tab cannot physically exist within a single plane, the claims fail to provide reasonable certainty of scope and thus lack the particularity required by the statute.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's finding that claims 1–4 are anticipated by the Anderson prior art reference under 35 U.S.C. § 102. Anderson discloses each limitation of the claims, including a mirror positionable in front of one eye; the presumptive enablement of prior art references applied, and Shafovaloff's bare assertion of nonenablement was insufficient to overcome it.

The Court rejected Shafovaloff's attempt to read the specification's description of a "bendable" tab as clarifying the plain claim language requiring a "bent" tab, holding that importing such limitations from the specification would impermissibly rewrite the claims rather than construe them in light of the specification.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision rejecting all claims in Application No. 15/173,604 on grounds of indefiniteness under § 112(b) and anticipation by the Anderson reference.

cases.case_name: Lyft, Inc. v. Quartz Auto Technologies LLC

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's construction of "defective operational conditions in said automobile" in the '871 patent as limited to automobile-based defects of the type typically addressed at a diagnostic and repair center. The court held that the specification decisively resolved the dispute by describing the invention as relating to defects requiring detection and correction by diagnostic and repair centers, and by providing examples limited to automobile operating systems, valves, gauges, and tire traction, thereby excluding external conditions unrelated to the automobile itself.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's construction of "alert" in the '215 patent as "notice indicating a problem with or in a managed IT device." Although the claim language did not explicitly require an alert to indicate a problem, the specification's characterization of the invention established that alerts must relate to problems with managed IT devices, supporting the adopted construction over Quartz's proposed broader construction of "a notice describing an event."

The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's construction of "the event" in the '215 patent claims 5, 14, and 16, though the opinion text was truncated and does not provide the full reasoning or specific construction adopted, limiting analysis to the fact that this term was among the three disputed terms at issue and was affirmed.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the final judgment of non-infringement entered by the district court for U.S. Patent Nos. 6,847,871 and 7,958,215 based on the parties' stipulation that under the district court's claim constructions, the accused instrumentalities do not infringe the asserted claims.
The Federal Circuit exercised jurisdiction over the appeal pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(1), which provides jurisdiction over appeals from final decisions of district courts in patent cases.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's claim constructions and the resulting judgment of non-infringement, holding that 'defective operational conditions in said automobile' refers only to automobile-based defects of the type addressed at diagnostic and repair centers, and that 'alert' means notice indicating a problem with a managed IT device, not merely any event notice.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacked jurisdiction over the appeal because 38 U.S.C. § 7292(a) requires a final decision from the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims before appeal to this court, and the Veterans Court had not yet issued a decision on the Yoons' mandamus petition. Appellants' attempt to invoke 28 U.S.C. § 1292(a)(1) analogies lacked statutory support in the veterans appeal context.

Even if the court considered the matter as a petition for a writ of mandamus under 28 U.S.C. § 1651, the Yoons failed to satisfy the three-part test requiring no other adequate means of relief, a clear and indisputable right, and that the writ be appropriate under the circumstances. The existence of pending appeals before the Board and Veterans Court, combined with the Secretary's concession of potential reimbursement rights, precluded mandamus relief.
The Secretary's motion to dismiss was granted, and the appeal was dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because no final decision had been entered by the Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims on the pending mandamus petition, and mandamus relief was inappropriate given the availability of other remedies and the Secretary's concession regarding potential reimbursement.

cases.case_name: Directpacket Research, Inc. v. Polycom, Inc.

segments.text: The court affirmed the district court's judgment on the pleadings that the '588 patent claims are directed to a patent-ineligible abstract idea under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Applying the Alice two-step framework, the court found that Claim 1 is directed to the abstract idea of language translation, and that the claims lack an inventive concept at step two sufficient to transform that abstract idea into patent-eligible subject matter.

The court affirmed the district court's treatment of Claim 1 as representative for the patent eligibility analysis. Under Cleveland Clinic and Berkheimer, independent Claim 1 is substantially similar to independent Claims 7, 11, and 18, and dependent Claims 2–4, 6, 12, 16, and 23 lack distinctive significance sufficient to alter the eligibility conclusion.

summary.holding: Affirmed the grant of judgment on the pleadings dismissing the complaint for patent ineligibility under 35 U.S.C. § 101; the '588 patent claims are directed to the abstract idea of language translation without sufficient inventive concept to qualify for patent protection.

cases.case_name: amatea/grimberg Jv v. Secretary of the Navy
cases.origin: Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's denial of AGJV's constructive acceleration claim, holding that AGJV failed to prove the first element—excusable delay on the critical path—because the evidence showed delays in non-critical work items (roof, HVAC, windows) rather than the ESS or fire sprinkler work AGJV blamed. The court rejected AGJV's argument that a contracting officer's grant of time extension creates a presumption of government fault for delay, reaffirming that such extensions carry no binding findings of fact in subsequent litigation under the Contract Disputes Act.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's denial of AGJV's breach-of-contract and implied covenant of good faith and fair dealing claims regarding the government's denial of requests to work outside regular hours. The court held that the contract's discretionary language—permitting the CO to "may approve" based on justification—authorized the CO's reasonable exercise of discretion, and that AGJV's blanket requests for Saturday work lacked sufficient specific justification beyond general project delay to overcome the CO's reasonable determination that such work would impose significant costs and not be well-used.

The Federal Circuit exercised jurisdiction over the appeal under 41 U.S.C. § 7107(a)(1) and 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(10), reviewing questions of law de novo and factual determinations under the substantial-evidence standard of 41 U.S.C. § 7107(b)(2).

summary.holding: Affirmed the Armed Services Board of Contract Appeals' denial of both the constructive acceleration claim and work hours claim, finding the Board applied correct legal standards and its factual findings were supported by substantial evidence.

segments.text: The Board's finding that Ms. Morris failed to prove by preponderant evidence that her nepotism allegations constituted protected disclosures under the Whistleblower Protection Act (5 U.S.C. § 2302(b)(8)(A)) is affirmed as supported by substantial evidence. The court applied the 'disinterested observer' standard to determine whether Ms. Morris had a reasonable belief that a violation of law occurred, and substantial evidence supported the Board's factual finding that she did not meet this threshold.

The Board's determination that the EPA proved by clear and convincing evidence it would have removed Ms. Morris for insubordination and misuse of supervisory authority even absent her protected disclosures regarding MD-715 reports is affirmed. Although Ms. Higginbotham had a substantial motive to retaliate, the strength of the agency's evidence under the Carr factors—including Ms. Morris's disrespectful, disruptive conduct and failure to follow directions—outweighed the retaliation motive.

The court affirms that credibility determinations by the administrative judge and Board are virtually unreviewable on appeal under the substantial evidence standard, and the court will not reweigh evidence or second-guess how the Board weighted witness credibility in reaching its clear-and-convincing-evidence finding.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's final order denying Ms. Morris's individual right of action appeal, concluding that substantial evidence supported the Board's findings that (1) her nepotism allegations were not protected disclosures under the Whistleblower Protection Act and (2) the EPA proved by clear and convincing evidence it would have removed her for insubordination and misuse of supervisory authority regardless of her protected disclosures regarding MD-715 reports.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Northern District of California

segments.text: The court affirmed dismissal of Golden's direct infringement allegations under Rule 12(b)(6), holding that each of his five infringement theories required post-sale modification of Google's smartphones (including third-party apps, NFC tags, microfluidic lenses, external sensors, or separate devices) and therefore failed to plausibly allege that Google itself made or sold products with the claimed detector/sensor functionality under the Iqbal/Twombly standard.

The court affirmed dismissal of indirect and willful infringement claims, holding that because Golden failed to adequately plead direct infringement by Google, he could not establish the prerequisite direct infringement required for indirect infringement or willful infringement liability.

The court affirmed dismissal of the joint infringement claim against Google and third parties (Draper Laboratory Inc. and DoD/DTRA), holding that Golden failed to plead sufficient factual allegations regarding either direction or control by Google over the other entities or facts establishing a joint enterprise.

segments.issue: Preclusive Effect of Prior Apple Decision
segments.text: The court held that its prior decision in Golden v. Apple Inc. finding Golden's complaint "not facially frivolous" had no preclusive effect under the doctrine of issue preclusion, as the earlier opinion explicitly stated it did not preclude subsequent motions to dismiss for failure to state a claim.

The court affirmed the district court's denial of leave to amend, which was based on futility of amendment, as all of Golden's infringement theories were fundamentally deficient in alleging that Google's unmodified products performed the claimed functionality.

summary.holding: The court affirmed the district court's dismissal of Golden's amended patent infringement complaint under Rule 12(b)(6) for failure to state a claim, finding that all direct infringement theories required post-sale modification of Google's smartphones and that indirect, willful, and joint infringement claims necessarily failed absent adequate direct infringement pleading.

segments.text: The Board's finding that claims 1 and 10 of the '987 patent were unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103 over a combination of Biderman and Gigliotti is affirmed. The Court rejected DivX's argument that a skilled artisan would not have been motivated to apply Gigliotti's buffer-state-aware adaptive bitrate scheme only during the post-startup portion of playback, and found that Gigliotti itself disclosed the concept of using different stream selection methods at different playback stages, supported by substantial evidence in the record.

summary.holding: The Board's final written decision finding claims 1 and 10 of U.S. Patent No. 10,326,987 unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as obvious over Biderman and Gigliotti is affirmed.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over this appeal because the case involves constitutional claims arising from military discharge and does not fall within the court's limited appellate jurisdiction over patent matters, PTO cases, or certain damages claims under $10,000. The court transferred the appeal to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1631.

summary.holding: Appeal transferred to the D.C. Circuit for lack of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over non-patent constitutional claims.

segments.text: The Court affirmed that Simpkins was ineligible to redeposit his refunded FERS retirement contributions because he separated from federal service on April 16, 2009, prior to the October 28, 2009 statutory cutoff date. Substantial evidence supported the Board's finding that the effective resignation date in the settlement agreement controlled, regardless of when the agreement was later executed.

The Court affirmed that Simpkins's effective resignation date was April 16, 2009, as specified in the settlement agreement, not the later date when the agreement was fully executed. The agreement explicitly required resignation "no later than April 16, 2009," and this contractual language established the operative date for retirement eligibility purposes.

The Court affirmed the Board's exclusion of Simpkins's untimely emails from his union representative, finding no abuse of discretion. Simpkins failed to demonstrate due diligence or unavailability of the evidence, and his vague assertions of recent receipt were insufficient to warrant reopening the record.

The Court declined to consider arguments raised for the first time in Simpkins's reply brief concerning settlement agreement voidness and discrimination claims, as reply briefs are not the proper place to raise new issues. The Court also rejected as inadequately developed Simpkins's conclusory references to prior EEOC activity and FAA claims without substantive explanation of their relevance.

summary.holding: The Merit Systems Protection Board's decision affirming OPM's determination that Simpkins's refunded retirement contributions from 1987–1996 were not creditable and he was ineligible to redeposit them was affirmed, as Simpkins separated from service before the October 28, 2009 redeposit eligibility date.

cases.origin: United States District Court for the Western District of Texas

segments.text: The Federal Circuit denied Qualcomm and Apple's petition for mandamus challenging the district court's denial of their motion to transfer the case from the Western District of Texas to the Northern District of California under 28 U.S.C. § 1404(a). Applying Fifth Circuit law and reviewing for clear abuse of discretion, the court upheld the district court's finding that the petitioners failed to clearly establish that transfer was for the convenience of parties and witnesses, as both venues contained relevant witnesses and events giving rise to the suit occurred in both forums.
The Federal Circuit granted Apple Inc.'s motion to join Qualcomm's petition for mandamus, allowing Apple to participate as a co-petitioner in the appeal.

summary.holding: The district court did not abuse its discretion in denying the motion to transfer venue under § 1404(a), as the petitioners failed to clearly demonstrate that the Northern District of California was a clearly more convenient forum when both venues contained relevant witnesses and evidence.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's decision upholding Mr. Ruiz's removal from his position as a Customs and Border Protection Officer based on charges of conduct unbecoming and lack of candor. The Board's findings were supported by substantial evidence, including police photographs, contemporaneous police reports, and Officer Rivas' testimony, and the administrative judge's credibility determinations are virtually unreviewable on appeal under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(c).

summary.holding: The Board's decision was in accordance with law and supported by substantial evidence, and the removal was affirmed.

cases.case_name: Keyes Helium Company, LLC v. United States

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the Claims Court's dismissal of Keyes' breach of contract claim, holding that the Contract imposed a clear obligation on BLM to deliver helium-gas mixture containing not less than 50% helium by volume under Section 2.3(a), and that Keyes plausibly alleged BLM breached this obligation through at least two off-spec delivery events in December 2020 and February 2021. The court rejected the Claims Court's reversed analytical framework, which improperly began with alleged harm and worked backward to find a contractual duty, instead confirming that breach analysis must first identify the duty, then determine whether it was breached, and finally assess causation and damages.

segments.issue: Implied Duty of Good Faith and Fair Dealing
segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the Claims Court's dismissal of Keyes' implied duty of good faith and fair dealing claim, holding that Keyes adequately pleaded facts showing BLM's delivery of damaging levels of contaminants destroyed Keyes' ability to achieve the benefit of the bargain under the contract. The court determined the claim survived the motion to dismiss standard and should proceed on remand.

The Federal Circuit reversed the Claims Court's dismissal of Keyes' alternative tort claims, finding that the Claims Court erred in its analysis infected by the same faulty breach of contract reasoning, though the specific basis for reversal on the tort claims tracks the contractual analysis and requires further development on remand.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Claims Court's dismissal of Keyes' Fifth Amendment takings claim under the Tucker Act, 28 U.S.C. § 1491, holding that Keyes failed to state a plausible takings claim based on the alleged loss of helium and its reallocation to other companies on the BLM helium system.

The Federal Circuit applied de novo review to the Claims Court's Rule 12(b)(6) dismissal for failure to state a claim, requiring that all plausible factual allegations be accepted as true and construed in the light most favorable to the non-moving party, with contract interpretation as a legal question freely reviewable by the appellate court.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed in part, reversed in part, vacated in part, and remanded, reversing the dismissal of Keyes' breach of contract and implied duty of good faith and fair dealing claims because Keyes plausibly alleged BLM breached its contractual obligation to deliver helium-gas mixture containing not less than 50% helium by volume, while affirming the dismissal of the Fifth Amendment takings claim as failing to state a plausible cause of action.

cases.case_name: Msn Laboratories Private Ltd. v. Bausch Health Ireland Ltd.

segments.text: The Board's conclusion that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have selected uroguanylin as a lead compound for modification was supported by substantial evidence under 35 U.S.C. § 103. Although uroguanylin suffered from topoisomerism and lower cGMP production than bacterial ST peptide, the Board reasonably found that a POSITA would select uroguanylin over the pathogenic bacterial ST peptide, which was dangerous for human administration.

The Board's determination that Bausch's experiments demonstrated unexpected results sufficient to outweigh a prima facie case of obviousness was vacated and remanded for further explanation. The court found the Board's reasoning regarding topoisomerism and the experiments' evidentiary support was insufficiently detailed to enable meaningful judicial review under the Administrative Procedure Act, 5 U.S.C. § 706(2)(A), (E).

summary.holding: Vacated and remanded the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision that claims 1–6 of U.S. Patent 7,041,786 were not obvious, finding the Board's unexpected results analysis lacked adequate reasoned explanation under the Administrative Procedure Act, though the lead compound selection and motivation to modify findings were supported by substantial evidence.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over discrimination cases under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2) when an allegation involves both an action appealable to the Merit Systems Protection Board and a basis of covered discrimination. Because Smith alleged her removal was based partly on disability discrimination and retaliation for prior EEO activity—both covered grounds—jurisdiction belongs in federal district court, not the Federal Circuit.

The case was transferred to the United States District Court for the District of Columbia pursuant to 28 U.S.C. § 1631, as the employment action appeared to have occurred in that jurisdiction. The district court may consider, among other matters, the agency's timeliness arguments.

summary.holding: Petition for review dismissed and transferred to district court due to lack of Federal Circuit jurisdiction over discrimination allegations under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2).

The remand was necessary to allow the agency to reconsider those rejections in compliance with notice requirements.

summary.holding: Case remanded to the USPTO for reconsideration of Board rejections that were not properly designated as new grounds of rejection.

segments.text: The Board's finding that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine Al-Shaykh and Qureshey to meet claim 1's "one or more first cloud servers" limitation is supported by substantial evidence. Al-Shaykh and Qureshey are analogous art in the same field addressing similar networked playback problems, and a skilled artisan would recognize that Qureshey's disclosed server functionality would improve Al-Shaykh's system in the same manner.

segments.issue: Prior Art Teaching of Specific Server Functionality
segments.text: Substantial evidence supports the Board's finding that a skilled artisan would have incorporated Qureshey's IPAN server into Al-Shaykh's system. Although Al-Shaykh discloses only general capability for rendering devices to obtain media content from the Internet, Qureshey provides the detailed back-end server functionality and URL management mechanisms that a skilled artisan would have recognized as an improvement to Al-Shaykh's incomplete disclosure.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision that all challenged claims 1–2, 6–14, 18–25, and 27–29 of U.S. Patent No. 9,967,615 are unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103 based on combinations of Al-Shaykh, Qureshey, and Phillips. Sonos's challenges to the Board's factual findings regarding motivation to combine and prior art teachings lack substantial evidence support, and the Board's obviousness determination is affirmed.

summary.holding: The Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision that claims 1–2, 6–14, 18–25, and 27–29 of U.S. Patent No. 9,967,615 are unpatentable as obvious under 35 U.S.C. § 103 is affirmed.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the petition for review of the Merit Systems Protection Board for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules, specifically because petitioner failed to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination.

summary.holding: Petition for review dismissed due to petitioner's failure to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination.

cases.case_name: National Organization of Veterans' Advocates, Inc. v. Secretary of Veterans Affairs
cases.origin: Department of Veterans Affairs

segments.text: The proceeding was dismissed pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) following agreement by the parties, terminating the petition for review under 38 U.S.C. Section 502.
Each party was ordered to bear its own costs, precluding any award of appellate costs to either side.

summary.holding: The case was dismissed on stipulation with each party bearing its own costs.

cases.case_name: Avago Technologies International Sales Pte. Ltd. v. Netflix, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court affirmed the PTAB's finding that claims 1, 3–5, 7, 9–10, 12, 14–16, and 18–20 of the '014 patent are unpatentable as obvious over Baldwin. Substantial evidence supported the Board's factual findings that Baldwin teaches the receiving of multiple video streams and the identification of which stream would result in lower latency, and the court rejected Avago's challenges to those findings.

The court found no error in the PTAB's refusal to reach Avago's proposed sequential-order claim construction requiring limitation [1c] to be performed before limitation [1d]. Because the Board found that Baldwin teaches the steps in the proposed sequential order, the court determined the construction issue need not be decided.

The court vacated and remanded the PTAB's findings that dependent claims 6, 8, 11, and 17 are not unpatentable, holding that the Board failed adequately to address Netflix's argument that a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine Cooper and Baldwin to render those dependent claims obvious. The Board's conclusory rejection without clear explanation of how the combination would satisfy specific claim limitations was error.

summary.holding: Affirmed as to independent claims 1, 3–5, 7, 9–10, 12, 14–16, and 18–20 (unpatentable); vacated and remanded as to dependent claims 6, 8, 11, and 17 for reconsideration of the motivation-to-combine defense.

cases.case_name: Ancora Technologies, Inc. v. Roku, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board did not clearly err in finding claim 1 would have been obvious in light of the Hellman/Chou combination. The combination was operable and the Board's analysis of the motivation to combine was supported by substantial evidence under 35 U.S.C. § 103.

The Board's finding that Ancora did not link its AMI press release and commercialization agreements directed to BIOS-based security products to the challenged claims was supported by substantial evidence. The Board did not clearly err in distinguishing Ancora's own commercialization efforts from the specific technological limitations recited in the asserted claims.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's obviousness rejection of claim 1 and rejection of Ancora's arguments that the claimed invention was publicly disclosed or commercialized prior to the critical date.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review the ITC's denial of Realtek's sanctions motion. Under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(6) and 19 U.S.C. § 1337(c), the Federal Circuit has exclusive jurisdiction only over 'final determinations' relating to unfair practices in import trade, which the court interprets as decisions affecting the exclusion or non-exclusion of articles from entry. Because the Commission's sanctions decision has no effect on article entry, it does not constitute a reviewable final determination.

Section 1337(c)'s reference to review of sanctions determinations under subsection (h) 'in accordance with section 706 of title 5' does not confer Federal Circuit jurisdiction over non-entry-related sanctions orders. The statutory structure shows Congress did not include subsection (h) in the list of subsections giving rise to appealable final determinations, and historical amendments to the statute support the inference that sanctions review was not intended to be within the Federal Circuit's exclusive jurisdiction when disconnected from a final determination under subsections (d), (e), (f), or (g).

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that Federal Circuit jurisdiction under 28 U.S.C. § 1295(a)(6) extends only to ITC final determinations that affect the exclusion or non-exclusion of articles from entry. Sanctions decisions and other ancillary orders that do not impact article entry fall outside the Federal Circuit's exclusive jurisdiction, even when nominally labeled as final administrative decisions. The ruling establishes that statutory references to Administrative Procedure Act review in 19 U.S.C. § 1337(c) do not automatically confer Federal Circuit jurisdiction absent a nexus to the core entry-related determinations Congress explicitly enumerated.

cases.case_name: Xerox Corporation v. Meta Platforms, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The court dismissed the appeal as moot because a concomitant decision in Xerox Corp. v. X Corp., 23-1913, had already affirmed a Patent Trial and Appeal Board decision holding all claims 1–18 of U.S. Patent No. 7,043,475 unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103, encompassing the subset of claims at issue here (1–3, 5, 7, 10–12, and 15–16). Following the reasoning in Apple Inc. v. Voip-Pal.com, Inc., 976 F.3d 1316 (Fed. Cir. 2020), the court determined that the intervening judgment rendered further review of this appeal unnecessary.

cases.case_name: Express Mobile, Inc. v. Meta Platforms, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board applied an erroneous construction of the claim term "style" by implicitly construing the disjunctive "or" in Express Mobile's proposed construction to mean alternative choices rather than capabilities. Under the correct construction, "style" must be defined separately from any single object but capable of being associated with one or more objects—not merely associated with a single object—and the prior art combination failed to teach this requirement, warranting vacatur and remand.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's dismissal for lack of jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a). The Board's May 14, 2021 order constituted a remand for further factual development on whether the discharge barred benefits for the second service period, not a decision granting or denying benefits, and therefore fell outside the Veterans Court's exclusive appellate jurisdiction over Board decisions.

summary.holding: The Veterans Court properly lacked jurisdiction to review a Board remand order that did not grant or deny benefits on any claim, even where the Board had previously made favorable findings on a separate service period, because a remand for further development is not a 'decision' within the meaning of 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a).

cases.case_name: Ag Der Dillinger Huttenwerke v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The court held that Commerce reasonably resorted to facts otherwise available under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e when Salzgitter failed to provide complete manufacturer information for 28,000 reseller sales due to the manual burden involved. Commerce was entitled to fill an information gap in the record where Salzgitter could not supply the missing data after an extended back-and-forth with five supplemental questionnaires.

segments.issue: Failure to Cooperate and Adverse Inference
segments.text: Although Commerce's information request imposed an unreasonable burden on Salzgitter (estimated at 5,000 hours), the court affirmed that Commerce could still apply an adverse inference under 19 U.S.C. § 1677e(b) because Salzgitter failed to propose reasonable alternative forms of the missing information as required by statute. Salzgitter's three proposed alternatives were not deemed reasonable by either the Trade Court or the Federal Circuit.

The court sustained Commerce's use of the highest non-aberrational net price among Salzgitter's downstream market sales to fill the information gap as a reasonable application of adverse facts available. Commerce's methodology was justified given the size of the information gap and the need to deter noncooperation in future proceedings.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that under the antidumping duty statutes, an exporter's failure to propose reasonable alternative forms of missing information is dispositive to sustain an adverse inference, even where Commerce's original information request imposed an unreasonable burden. The holding does not meaningfully change Federal Circuit doctrine but rather applies established adverse facts available principles to confirm that statutory cooperation requirements focus on the exporter's proposal of alternatives, not solely on the burden placed by Commerce's request.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's conclusion that it lacked jurisdiction over Mrs. Shaw's new Clear and Unmistakable Error and finality claims raised for the first time on appeal to the Veterans Court. Under 38 U.S.C. § 7252(a), the Veterans Court's jurisdiction is limited to decisions of the Board, and a CUE claim must subsume a specific allegation of error previously decided by the Board; a new CUE claim not addressed by the Board cannot be adjudicated on appeal.

The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal as to the Veterans Court's holding that Mrs. Shaw abandoned any challenge to the Board's decision denying Mr. Shaw's February 2020 CUE motion because such a finding constitutes a factual determination and application of law to fact, which are barred from Federal Circuit review under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2).

The Federal Circuit affirmed that finality cannot be raised as a freestanding threshold issue after the period for direct appeal has expired; under Knowles v. Shinseki, any challenge to finality of a prior Regional Office decision must be raised through statutory or regulatory exceptions to finality, not through a collateral CUE claim.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed-in-part and dismissed-in-part the Veterans Court's judgment, upholding the denial of jurisdiction over new claims raised for the first time on appeal while dismissing review of the forfeiture finding as beyond Federal Circuit jurisdiction.

cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's construction of "determining proximal information" as meaning "finding words in text near or within a link within content portions associated with the user path." The court rejected Xerox's arguments that the construction was overly broad, conflated proximal information with multi-modal information, or failed to require characterization and association, finding the Board's construction more consistent with the patent specification.

The court affirmed the Board's finding that a person of ordinary skill in the art would have been motivated to combine Chen with Chi's teaching of proximal information, based on the substantial evidence that both references shared similar goals of recommending information through comparable techniques and that combining them would provide better recommendations to satisfy user needs.

The court affirmed the Board's determination that there was a reasonable expectation of success in combining Chen and Chi, as the substantial evidence supported that using content words near links to obtain accurate clustering results was a predictable application of known techniques with a reasonable likelihood of success.

The court affirmed the Board's rejection of Xerox's proffered evidence of unexpected results under the substantial evidence standard, finding that using content words to achieve accurate clustering was not surprising and that Xerox failed to identify specific unexpected results with adequate evidentiary support.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's final written decision holding claims 1–18 of U.S. Patent No. 7,043,475 unpatentable under 35 U.S.C. § 103 as obvious in light of Chen as supplemented by Chi.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's holding that the October 1988 service medical record was not "relevant" for purposes of reconsideration under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c). Under Kisor v. McDonald, a record must speak to the basis for the VA's prior decision to qualify as relevant for reconsideration; since the Board's 1991 denial rested on a factual finding that Mr. Harris lacked a chronic hip disability, the claimant failed to establish that the October 1988 record related to that specific basis, and therefore the Board did not clearly err.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Veterans Court's determination that Mr. Harris's service-connected disability for degenerative joint disease of the left hip was properly assigned an effective date of July 17, 2001 (the date the claim was reopened), rather than an earlier date based on his original 1989 claim. The claim fell within the reopening provisions and was granted based on post-2001 medical examinations, not on newly discovered service department records under § 3.156(c).

The Federal Circuit held it had jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292 to review the Veterans Court's interpretation of 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c), as a question of law, but lacked jurisdiction to review the Board's factual finding that the March 2016 grant of service connection was not based on consideration of the October 1988 record, absent a constitutional issue.

summary.holding: Affirmed the Veterans Court's decision that the claimant was not entitled to an earlier effective date for service connection because the October 1988 service record was not "relevant" under 38 C.F.R. § 3.156(c), as it did not speak to the basis for the VA's 1991 denial.

cases.origin: United States International Trade Commission

segments.text: Roku's appeal regarding the '875 patent was dismissed as moot because the Federal Circuit affirmed the Patent Trial and Appeal Board's decision on claim 10 in co-pending case No. 24-1188 on the same date, eliminating the live controversy that Roku sought to challenge.

The appeal concerning the '511 patent was vacated and remanded with instructions to dismiss as moot because the patent expired during the pendency of the appeal. Under 19 U.S.C. § 1337, the ITC can only issue prospective relief, making the claim moot once the underlying patent expires, even though the invalidity determination involved a purely legal question of indefiniteness.

cases.case_name: Chinook Landing, LLC v. United States
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Oregon

segments.text: The court affirmed that the Quiet Title Act claim was time-barred under 28 U.S.C. § 2409a(g), which requires claims to be commenced within twelve years of accrual. The court held that accrual occurred in 1955 when the 1955 easement was recorded and BPA began using Reeher Road, as the property owners knew or should have known of the government's interest at that time. The claim therefore expired in 1967, well before Mr. Lund commenced the action in 2019.

The court affirmed that the inverse condemnation claim under the Little Tucker Act was time-barred under 28 U.S.C. § 2501, which requires claims to be filed within six years of accrual. The court held that the takings claim accrued in 1955 when BPA exercised the easement rights, as all events fixing the government's liability had occurred and the property owners knew or should have known of BPA's use of Reeher Road. The claim therefore expired in 1961, before Mr. Lund purchased the property in 2004.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's grant of summary judgment on both the Quiet Title Act and inverse condemnation claims, finding both claims time-barred under their respective statutes of limitations, with accrual dating to 1955 when the easement was recorded and the government began using the access road.

cases.case_name: Roku, Inc. v. Universal Electronics, Inc.
Bpi Sports, LLC v. Thermolife International LLC

segments.text: The Court reversed the district court's denial of defendants' JMOL motion on BPI's false advertising claim under 15 U.S.C. § 1125(a)(1)(B), finding no reasonable jury could have concluded that CRTN-3's label statement of "increase vasodilation" was literally false based on the dosage disclosed. BPI failed to establish the falsity element—one of five required elements for a Lanham Act false advertising claim—which is fatal to the entire claim.

The Court affirmed the district court's Sanctions Order imposing attorneys' fees and costs against defendants for sanctions, which included fees for the motion for sanctions and two motions to compel discovery regarding the fabricated License Agreement. The sanctions were warranted based on Mr. Kramer's bad faith creation of the License Agreement on March 9, 2020, and obstruction of discovery to conceal this fabrication.

The Court dismissed BPI's cross-appeal of the district court's denial of its Rule 59 motion for a new trial as moot in light of the Court's reversal of the underlying judgment. Because the judgment was reversed, the question of whether the trial resulted in a compromised verdict became moot.

The Court did not address defendants' appeal of the district court's denial of their Rule 60(b) motion for relief from judgment and the Sanctions Order, finding it moot in light of the reversal of the underlying judgment. The district court had denied the motion as untimely.

summary.holding: The Court reversed the district court's denial of defendants' JMOL motion and entered judgment in favor of defendants on BPI's false advertising and unfair competition claims because no reasonable jury could have found that CRTN-3's label statement of "increase vasodilation" was literally false under the Lanham Act. The Court affirmed the Sanctions Order awarding attorneys' fees and costs and dismissed BPI's cross-appeal as moot.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal for lack of jurisdiction because Mr. Boynton's challenge fundamentally contested the factual findings and weight of evidence regarding his PTSD disability rating, matters outside the court's authority to review. Under Lennox v. Principi, 353 F.3d 941 (Fed. Cir. 2003), the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to determine whether application of established law to facts satisfies a clearly erroneous standard.

summary.holding: Appeal dismissed for lack of jurisdiction because the challenge constitutes an impermissible attempt to reweigh evidence and contest factual findings rather than present a legal question for Federal Circuit review.

cases.case_name: Ancora Technologies, Inc. v. Roku, Inc.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board construed the claim term 'agent' as 'a software program or routine' without limitation to OS-level use or exclusion of hardware. The Federal Circuit affirmed, finding no clear and unmistakable disclaimer in the intrinsic evidence requiring such limitations and determining the plain and ordinary meaning of 'agent' permits the Board's broader construction.

The Board found claims 1–3, 6–14, and 16 unpatentable as obvious over a combination of Hellman, Chou, and a third reference under 35 U.S.C. § 103. The Federal Circuit vacated this determination, holding that the Board erred in its analysis of secondary considerations of nonobviousness, particularly regarding the nexus between license evidence and the claimed invention.

The Board failed to properly apply Federal Circuit precedent on nexus when evaluating Ancora's objective indicia of nonobviousness based on license evidence. The court vacated and remanded on this issue, indicating that the Board must reconsider whether the licensing evidence has a sufficient nexus to the claimed invention as a whole, not merely to isolated elements or features.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that the Board must properly apply nexus analysis when evaluating objective indicia of nonobviousness tied to licensing or commercial success evidence in obviousness proceedings. The opinion reinforces that secondary considerations require a nexus between the evidence of nonobviousness (such as licensing) and the claimed invention itself, rejecting an analysis limited to individual claim elements. The holding does not change the substantive test but remands for proper application of established Federal Circuit precedent regarding the evidentiary foundation for secondary considerations in IPR proceedings.

segments.text: The court vacated the Veterans Court's decision and remanded to the Board for clarification on whether it applied the correct legal standard under 38 U.S.C. § 1116A(d)—measuring 12 nautical miles from baseline as defined by geographical coordinates—rather than 12 nautical miles from shoreline. The Board's language stating ships were "12 nautical miles or closer to the Vietnam shore" created ambiguity about which standard was applied, and the record did not affirmatively establish the correct baseline standard was used.

The court dismissed Mr. Crawford's challenges to the Board's factual findings regarding whether he set foot in Da Nang and whether his ship served in Vietnam's territorial sea, holding that these challenges constitute impermissible reviews of factual determinations and law-as-applied under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2), which lies outside the Federal Circuit's appellate jurisdiction.

The court dismissed Mr. Crawford's challenge to the Veterans Court's denial of his motion to take judicial notice of extra-record evidence about USS Hancock's location, holding that review of this discretionary evidentiary ruling constitutes an impermissible challenge to law as applied to the facts of the case under 38 U.S.C. § 7292(d)(2)(B).

summary.holding: Vacated in part and dismissed in part the Veterans Court's affirmance of the Board's denial of service connection for herbicide-related conditions; remanded for the Board to clarify which territorial sea standard it applied, but dismissed challenges to the Board's factual findings and the judicial notice ruling as outside the Federal Circuit's jurisdiction under 38 U.S.C. § 7292.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the notice of appeal for failure to pay the docketing fee required by Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) within the prescribed time period. Dismissal was entered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's procedural rules.

cases.case_name: Optis Wireless Technology, LLC v. Apple Inc.

segments.text: The court vacated the damages judgments and remanded for a new trial because the district court erred in granting a new trial limited only to damages amount while excluding evidence of Optis's FRAND licensing obligation. The court held that Apple was entitled to evidence regarding the SEPs' FRAND commitment, which is material to determining a reasonable royalty under 35 U.S.C. § 1400d and Federal Rule of Evidence 403.

The court reversed the district court's finding that claims 6 and 7 of the '332 patent are not directed to an abstract idea under 35 U.S.C. § 101. The claims directed to a PDCCH search space algorithm were determined to recite abstract ideas without sufficient inventive concept to qualify as patent-eligible subject matter.

The court reversed the district court's finding that claim 1 of the '557 patent does not invoke 35 U.S.C. § 112(f). The claim's language requiring certain functional limitations was found to trigger the means-plus-function requirement under § 112(f), necessitating corresponding structure in the specification.

The court affirmed the district court's construction of claim 8 of the '833 patent, indicating no error in the trial court's interpretation of the technical claim language regarding uplink signal transmission and resource mapping.

The court held that the district court abused its discretion under Federal Rule of Evidence 403 by admitting the Apple-Qualcomm settlement agreement and Optis's damages expert testimony concerning that agreement. The prejudicial effect of the settlement outweighed its probative value in establishing a reasonable royalty for SEP licensing.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that SEP owners asserting standard-essential patents must present evidence of their FRAND licensing obligations during damages trials, and settlement agreements with third parties may be excludable under FRE 403 in reasonable-royalty litigation. The decision also reaffirms strict application of § 101 abstract-idea doctrine to software-implemented telecommunications claims and § 112(f) to functional claim language, reversing the district court's findings on two SEPs and requiring new trials on infringement and damages.

segments.text: The Court dismissed the petition for review under Federal Circuit Rule 52(a)(1) because the petitioner failed to pay the required docketing fee and failed to file the required Statement Concerning Discrimination. Dismissal was entered for failure to prosecute in accordance with the rules.

cases.origin: United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
United States Court of Appeals for Veterans Claims
United States Patent and Trademark Office
United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The Federal Circuit adopted the parties' jointly proposed briefing schedule for the appeals, establishing deadlines for opening briefs (June 24-26, 2025), response briefs (July 8-10, 2025), reply briefs (July 18-21, 2025), and setting oral argument for July 31, 2025 at 45 minutes per side. The court permitted the V.O.S. and Oregon appellees to file separate response briefs and required compliance with Federal Circuit Rule 32(b)(1) regarding word count limitations.

cases.case_name: Novartis Pharmaceuticals Corporation v. Msn Pharmaceuticals, Inc.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal pursuant to Fed. R. App. P. 42(b) based on the parties' agreement to dismiss the proceeding. Each side bears its own costs.

segments.issue: Federal Circuit Jurisdiction over Mixed Cases
segments.text: The Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction to review MSPB decisions in cases alleging covered discrimination under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2), even after the district court dismisses the discrimination claim. Under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(2), the entire action falls within district court jurisdiction where a mixed case is involved, and the Federal Circuit has no jurisdiction to review any remaining claims.

summary.holding: The case is retransferred to the District Court for the Western District of Oklahoma under 28 U.S.C. § 1631 for the district court to conduct appropriate proceedings or enter final judgment, as the Federal Circuit lacks jurisdiction over this mixed case involving discrimination allegations under federal employment law.

segments.text: A federal employee receiving military retired pay generally cannot receive credit for that same military service when calculating a FERS civilian annuity unless one of two narrow statutory exceptions applies under 5 U.S.C. § 8411(c)(2). The Court affirmed that Mr. Stuart's military service could not be credited toward his FERS annuity because he was receiving military retired pay based on his military service and did not waive that pay or fall within either statutory exception.

Military retired pay calculated based on disability percentage, rather than years of service, still constitutes 'retired pay based on any period of military service' under 5 U.S.C. § 8411(c)(2) and triggers the bar against double crediting. The Court held that Mr. Stuart's argument that disability-calculated pay should be treated differently than service-length-calculated pay conflicted with the plain statutory language, which contemplates disability-based retirement as a type of military service-based pay subject to the double-crediting rule.

The two statutory exceptions to the double-crediting bar—for combat-incurred or war-instrumentality-caused service-connected disabilities, and for non-regular service retirement under 10 U.S.C. chapter 1223—apply only to specific categories of military retirement and cannot be extended to cover all disability-based retirements. The Court affirmed that Mr. Stuart failed to establish that his disability fell within either exception, rejecting his analogy to combat-injured service members.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that the statutory bar against double crediting military service for both FERS and military retired pay applies regardless of whether the military retired pay was calculated based on disability percentage or years of service, provided the pay is 'based on any period of military service.' The holding reinforces that the narrow statutory exceptions are exhaustive and cannot be expanded by analogy, establishing that the remedy for a federal employee seeking FERS credit for military service while receiving military retired pay is waiver of the military pay, subject only to the specified statutory exceptions.

cases.case_name: Chateau Lynch-Bages v. Chateau Angelus S.A.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

segments.text: The Board's determination that the competing marks contained house marks lacked substantial evidence and was erroneous. The Board failed to establish that either 'ANGÉLUS' or 'LYNCH BAGES' had the broad commercial use required to qualify as house marks under trademark law, relying instead on the mere existence of multiple registrations and company letterhead without citation to supporting authority or findings of actual commerce use.

Because the Board's house mark findings were critical and nearly dispositive to its conclusion that the marks were dissimilar, the Board's similarity analysis under the DuPont factors lacked substantial evidence. The court vacated and remanded because it was unclear whether the Board would have reached the same no-likelihood-of-confusion conclusion absent the erroneous house mark analysis, which received predominant weight in the overall DuPont balancing.

The Board's ultimate finding of no likelihood of confusion under Section 2(d) of the Lanham Act was vacated and remanded for reconsideration. The de novo review of the DuPont factors' weighing revealed that the Board's flawed similarity analysis, grounded in unsupported house mark findings, undermined the legal conclusion that confusion was unlikely.

summary.holding: Vacated and remanded the Board's decision dismissing the opposition to the 'ECHO D'ANGÉLUS' trademark application, holding that the Board's house mark findings lacked substantial evidence and that its resulting mark similarity analysis was therefore deficient under the DuPont likelihood-of-confusion framework.

cases.case_name: United Services Automobile Association v. Pnc Bank N.A.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment on patent eligibility, holding that claim 20 of the '638 patent is directed to an abstract idea—depositing a check using a handheld mobile device—and does not contain an inventive concept sufficient to satisfy step two of the Alice test. The court found that the claim recites routine data collection and analysis steps (reviewing checks, recognizing data, checking for errors, storing data) traditionally performed by banks and people, merely computerized through a generic handheld mobile device without sufficient specificity or nonobvious technological improvement.

segments.issue: Collateral Estoppel Effect of IPR Decisions
segments.text: The court affirmed invalidity findings from inter partes reviews of the '598 and '136 patents under 35 U.S.C. § 103 in separate decisions, which had collateral estoppel effect precluding reconsideration of the § 101 eligibility question as to those patents under the rule established in XY, LLC v. Trans Ova Genetics. Because those patents were separately determined unpatentable, the court declined to reach the § 101 issue for them in this appeal.

summary.holding: This decision clarifies that claims directed to routine business processes (such as remote check deposit) that have been traditionally performed by banks and people, merely implemented on a generic computer or mobile device without a specific technological improvement or inventive algorithmic advance actually recited in the claims themselves, constitute abstract ideas under 35 U.S.C. § 101 and fail step one of the Alice inquiry. The opinion reinforces that computer-based implementation of abstract ideas, without more, is insufficient to establish patent eligibility, and that the focus must be on whether the claims themselves demonstrate a specific improvement in computer capabilities rather than invoking generic computing devices as tools to perform traditional business functions.

cases.case_name: Mitek Systems, Inc. v. United Services Automobile Association
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The court affirmed that Mitek failed to establish reasonable apprehension of a direct infringement suit based on the factual record, including the parties' admissions about how MiSnap works, its implementation by banks, and trial evidence from the Wells Fargo case. Under the Declaratory Judgment Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2201(a), jurisdiction requires an actual case or controversy, and the district court's factual findings on this issue were reviewed for clear error.

The court affirmed the district court's finding that Mitek could not reasonably apprehend induced infringement liability because USAA never pointed to Mitek documents or manuals instructing users to perform all claim limitations, consistent with the standard in Microsoft Corp. v. DataTern, Inc., 755 F.3d 899 (Fed. Cir. 2014).

The court affirmed that no reasonable apprehension of contributory infringement existed because there was never a suggestion that MiSnap lacked substantial non-infringing uses or that Mitek knew the software was especially made or adapted for infringing use, as required under the contributory infringement standard.

The court affirmed the district court's conclusion that Mitek's indemnification agreements with its licensees did not create a reasonable potential for indemnification liability sufficient to establish subject-matter jurisdiction under the Declaratory Judgment Act.

The court affirmed that even if a case or controversy existed when Mitek's complaint was filed in 2019, it was extinguished by USAA's subsequent settlement with Wells Fargo in 2021, as permissible under Mitek I's recognition that post-filing events can show a controversy ceased to exist.

The court affirmed the district court's exercise of discretion to decline declaratory judgment jurisdiction, reviewing for abuse of discretion under Wilton v. Seven Falls Co., 515 U.S. 277 (1995), where the district court found intervention in future USAA litigation against Mitek customers was preferable and that the declaratory judgment action would require extensive involvement of end-user banks.

summary.holding: This decision confirms that under the Declaratory Judgment Act, 28 U.S.C. § 2201(a), a party must show a substantial, immediately real case or controversy with adverse legal interests, and that post-filing events extinguishing the controversy defeat jurisdiction even if one existed at filing. The court also reaffirms that even where subject-matter jurisdiction exists, a district court may discretionarily decline to entertain a declaratory judgment action based on practical and judicial economy considerations, particularly where intervention in future litigation provides an adequate alternative forum. The decision is largely fact-bound but reinforces the rigorous requirements for declaratory judgment jurisdiction in patent cases and the proper scope of post-filing event analysis.

cases.case_name: United Services Automobile Association v. Pnc Bank N.A.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the Eastern District of Texas

segments.text: The Court reversed the district court's grant of summary judgment finding the asserted claims of the '605, '681, and '432 patents patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Applying the Alice two-step test, the Court concluded the claims are directed to the abstract idea of depositing a check using a mobile device and contain no inventive concept sufficient to transform the abstract idea into a patent-eligible application, as they merely recite routine and well-known check-depositing steps implemented on generic devices without specific technical advances or software solutions.

summary.holding: The asserted claims of the '605, '681, and '432 patents are not patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101 because they are directed to an abstract idea (mobile check deposits) without an inventive concept, and the district court's summary judgment in favor of USAA was reversed. The Court also did not reach PNC's post-trial motions as moot because the claims were rendered invalid by the patent-eligibility reversal.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit dismissed the appeal under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b) upon the parties' stipulation, indicating voluntary dismissal by agreement of the parties.
Each party was ordered to bear its own costs, rejecting any shifting of appellate costs to either side.

cases.origin: United States Court of International Trade

segments.text: The Federal Circuit granted the United States's motions for a stay of the Court of International Trade's injunctions against Executive Orders imposing tariffs, applying the traditional stay factors under Fed. R. App. P. 8 and Nken v. Holder, 556 U.S. 418 (2009). The court concluded that a stay was warranted under the circumstances, noting that interim equitable relief aims to balance equities rather than conclusively determine the parties' rights.

The Federal Circuit consolidated the cases and ordered expedited en banc consideration of the merits in the first instance under 28 U.S.C. § 46 and Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 40(g), finding that the cases presented issues of exceptional importance. The court directed the parties to jointly propose an expedited briefing schedule to enable oral argument on July 31, 2025.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit stayed the Court of International Trade's injunctions enjoining certain Executive Orders imposing tariffs and ordered expedited en banc review of the underlying merits.

segments.text: The court dismissed Graham's petition for review as untimely under 5 U.S.C. § 7703(b)(1), which requires petitions to be filed within 60 days of the Board's final order. Graham's petition was filed seven days late (October 21, 2024, instead of October 14, 2024), and he failed to argue or establish equitable tolling despite the DOJ raising the issue.

The court did not address the merits of whether Graham's 30-day suspension for misuse of official position and lack of candor was proper, as the dismissal on jurisdictional grounds rendered that analysis unnecessary.

summary.holding: Petition for review dismissed as untimely filed; no decision on the underlying disciplinary charges.

cases.case_name: Agilent Technologies, Inc. v. Synthego Corp.
cases.origin: United States Patent and Trademark Office

cases.case_name: Exelixis, Inc. v. Msn Laboratories Private Ltd.
cases.origin: United States District Court for the District of Delaware

segments.text: Exelixis's cross-appeal (No. 2025-1241) was dismissed by agreement of the parties under Federal Rule of Appellate Procedure 42(b), which permits dismissal of an appeal when the parties so stipulate. Each side was ordered to bear its own costs.
The main appeal in No. 2025-1236 remains pending before the Federal Circuit, as the order addresses only the dismissal of the cross-appeal and does not dispose of the principal appellate issues.

The Court dismissed the petition for review of the MSPB decision for failure to prosecute in accordance with the Federal Circuit's rules. The petitioner failed to file both the required Statement Concerning Discrimination and the required Entry of Appearance form by an attorney admitted to the bar of this court.

summary.holding: A petition for review before the Federal Circuit may be dismissed for failure to comply with mandatory procedural requirements, including filing a Statement Concerning Discrimination and an Entry of Appearance by a court-admitted attorney.

segments.text: The court affirmed the Board's denial of Platt's individual right of action claim alleging whistleblower retaliation under 5 U.S.C. § 1221(e). Although Platt established a prima facie case that his 2011 protected disclosure was a contributing factor to his 2013 suspension, the Board properly found that TSA met its burden under the clear and convincing evidence standard to show it would have suspended Platt regardless of the disclosure, applying the three-factor Carr test.

summary.holding: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Merit Systems Protection Board's final order denying Platt's whistleblower retaliation claim under the applicable burden-shifting framework and substantial evidence standard of review.

cases.case_name: J. Star Enterprises, Inc. v. United States
cases.origin: United States Court of Federal Claims

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the judgment of the United States Court of Federal Claims in its entirety pursuant to Federal Circuit Rule 36, which permits affirmance without opinion when the decision is based on a nonprecedential disposition.

summary.holding: The Court of Federal Claims' judgment against plaintiff-appellant J. Star Enterprises, Inc. was affirmed on appeal.

cases.case_name: Gribble v. DVA, Sioux Falls Va Health System

segments.text: The arbitrator did not exceed his authority in imposing conditions of random drug testing and medical record release as part of Ms. Gribble's reinstatement remedy. Because the parties submitted the broad issue of "appropriate remedy" to arbitration, and these conditions directly related to her underlying drug misconduct, they fell within the arbitrator's broad discretion to "fashion a just award" consistent with the CBA.

Any error in the arbitrator's limitation of back pay to the date of the award rather than reinstatement was harmless because Ms. Gribble was not entitled to pay until reinstatement, which could not occur until she complied with the condition of completing an approved drug rehabilitation program—a condition for which she had produced no evidence of compliance.

The arbitrator reasonably extended random drug testing beyond the one-year limit ordinarily applicable under the EAP, as that limit applies only to employees voluntarily participating in the EAP program. Here, Ms. Gribble pursued a non-EAP program and thus was not bound by that temporal restriction, though the reasonableness of the duration remains subject to future reconsideration based on changed circumstances.

summary.holding: The arbitrator's decision mitigating Ms. Gribble's removal to a 90-day suspension and imposing conditions of drug rehabilitation program completion, random drug testing, and medical record release was affirmed as within the arbitrator's authority, supported by substantial evidence, and not arbitrary or capricious.

cases.case_name: Edwards Lifesciences Corporation v. Cardiovalve Ltd.

segments.text: The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's grant of Cardiovalve's Motions to Amend (and Revised Supplemental Motion to Amend) under 37 C.F.R. § 42.121. The Board found that Edwards failed to demonstrate by a preponderance of the evidence that the substitute claims 11–20 were unpatentable, which is the statutory standard for denying a motion to amend in inter partes review proceedings.

The Federal Circuit held that the Board made a factual finding (reviewable for substantial evidence) that Goldfarb's coupling member constitutes a single, unitary structure, and that all of its elements together—including the male element—perform the functions required by the 'support portion' limitation of substitute claim 11. The Board was not adopting an implicit claim construction excluding the male element but rather making a factual determination about Goldfarb's disclosure.

The Federal Circuit addressed Edwards' argument that Goldfarb's collar element satisfies the 'support portion' limitation but affirmed the Board's factual finding that the male element of the coupling member (not the collar alone) constitutes the relevant supporting structure that satisfies the claim element.

The Federal Circuit affirmed the Board's finding that Goldfarb discloses or renders obvious the 'advancing' limitation requiring that the ends of the clip arms be advanced out of the delivery tube before the support portion exits the tube. The Board's determination that this sequence was disclosed by the reference was a factual finding supported by substantial evidence.
